---

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

On paper my monthly budget balances, and I want to be honest about that. My parents send me CHF 220 a month and I earn CHF 816 from my job as a student assistant at the university library, where I work around seven hours a week. My expenses come to CHF 1,745, so in a normal month I have a small margin left.

The problem is that my situation is not stable, and I have no savings at all to absorb any shock. Since I arrived in Geneva I have moved four times. I have always lived in sublets because I could not get a regular lease without a Swiss guarantor or a deposit. My current room costs CHF 704 including utilities, but the sublet ends on 31 October and the main tenant is coming back. The rooms I have found so far ask for a deposit of two or three months' rent up front, which is money I simply do not have. If I do not find something in time, I will be sleeping on a friend's sofa during my final semester.

My parents run a small warung (a family restaurant) in Surabaya. Together they earn about CHF 1,230 a month, and they also support my grandmother and my younger brother, who is still in school. What they send me is almost a fifth of their income, and I know they have cut their own spending to do it. I cannot ask them for more. I also cannot increase my hours at the library, because my permit limits how much I can work during the semester and because I need the time for my bachelor thesis.

I have three semesters left. My bachelor will take ten semesters because I had to take a lighter course load in two semesters when I was working more, and I expect to finish in January 2028. I am applying to EduAll because a grant would let me pay a rental deposit and have a small safety net, so I can concentrate on finishing my degree instead of looking for a place to sleep. I have not received any other scholarship. I applied to the university's social fund last year but was told that the fund only gives one-time help in emergencies, not regular support.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I grew up in Surabaya, in East Java. Nobody in my family went to university. My parents finished primary school and have run the same small warung for more than twenty years. When I told them I wanted to study public health in Switzerland, they did not really understand what it was, but they supported me anyway.

My interest in public health started in 2019, when there was a dengue outbreak in our neighbourhood. My younger cousin was hospitalised, and I saw how little information people had about prevention. Standing water, blocked drains, no one explaining anything. It made me realise that many health problems are not about hospitals but about organisation, information and trust.

At the University of Geneva I have completed 26 courses, and my average is 80.1 out of 100 (GPA 3.25). My favourite subjects were epidemiology and health promotion. My bachelor thesis looks at how migrant communities in Geneva use community health workers, and I hope to continue with a master's in global health.

Outside of class, I have been the president of the Indonesian Students' Association in Geneva for the last year. We organise welcome events for new students, help people find housing and translate documents. Because I have moved so often myself, I have become the person others ask for help with housing, which is a little ironic. Once a month I also organise a cooking evening in my neighbourhood in Pâquis, where Indonesian students and our Swiss and migrant neighbours cook together.

Studying here has not always been easy. The housing situation has been the hardest part, more than the courses or the language. But I have learned to plan, to ask for help and to help others.

For me, education means that my family's story can change. I want to go back to Indonesia and work on community health programmes, especially in poorer urban areas like the one I grew up in. EduAll's support would help me finish this last step properly.

---

## Section 6 — Curriculum Vitae (summary)

**Education**
- 2023–present: BSc Public Health, University of Geneva (expected completion January 2028)
- 2022: Senior high school diploma, SMA Negeri, Surabaya, Indonesia

**Work experience**
- 2023–present: Student assistant, University of Geneva library (approx. 10 h/week)
- 2020–2023: Helper in the family restaurant, Surabaya

**Leadership & community engagement**
- 2025–present: President, Indonesian Students' Association Geneva
- 2024–present: Organiser of a monthly neighbourhood cooking evening, Pâquis, Geneva

**Languages**
- Indonesian (native), Javanese (native), English (fluent), French (B2)

**Skills**
- Basic statistics (R), survey design, event organisation

---

## Section 7 — Declared Circumstances (application checklist)

### Risk Factors
- ✓ First-generation student
- ✓ Housing insecurity

### Resilience & Strength Factors
- ✓ Work experience
- ✓ Leadership role
- ✓ Community engagement

**Total Resilience Factors:** 3

### Statement of Declared Circumstances

*Instructions: For each circumstance you have ticked in the checklist (risk factors and resilience/strength factors), briefly describe your situation and how it affects or has shaped your studies. You may attach supporting documents. If you have not ticked any circumstance, you may leave this section blank (max. 300 words).*

First-generation student: my parents both left school after primary school. I am the first person in my family to go to university, and I had to figure out applications, visas and the Swiss system on my own.

Housing insecurity: I have moved four times in four years and have never had my own lease. I always lived in sublets, and my current one ends on 31 October 2026. Without savings I cannot pay the two or three months' deposit most landlords ask for, so I do not know where I will live during my last semester.

Work experience: I have worked about ten hours a week at the university library since 2023. Before coming to Switzerland I helped in my parents' restaurant.

Leadership role: since 2025 I have been president of the Indonesian Students' Association in Geneva (about 60 members).

Community engagement: I help new Indonesian students find housing and understand official letters, and I organise a monthly neighbourhood cooking evening in Pâquis.

---

## References

- Academic reference: submitted directly via the online portal
- Personal reference: submitted directly via the online portal

---

- **Current Monthly Financial Need (monthly expenses minus family support and personal income; other scholarships and savings not deducted):** CHF 1,799

---

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I began my Master's in Biology at the University of Lausanne in February 2026, after four years of working to make this possible. I have just completed my first semester, and my thesis is due in July 2028, and I am applying to EduAll so that the last months of this degree are not decided by money.

My monthly costs in Lausanne come to CHF 2,479. The largest item is rent: CHF 1,299 for a small studio in Renens, plus CHF 119 for utilities. I pay CHF 290 for health insurance, and the rest goes on food, transport and the basic materials my laboratory work requires. I have kept these costs as low as the Lausanne housing market allows; shared flats near the campus rarely accept tenants without a Swiss guarantor, and I have been turned away more than once for that reason.

Against these costs, I earn CHF 414 a month as a part-time technician in a teaching laboratory on campus, preparing cultures and reagents for bachelor practicals. My two sisters in Lahore, whose households together earn about CHF 1,160, send me CHF 266 each month. It is a generous gesture from families who have children of their own in school, and I do not want to ask them for more.

The difference between what I have and what I need is CHF 1,799 each month. What I brought with me, my own savings and the money my family raised by selling a plot of land, is being drawn down steadily, and it was always meant to carry me through the degree, not beyond it.

My thesis project, on antibiotic resistance genes in wastewater bacteria, requires long days in the lab during the final semester. I cannot extend my working hours without compromising it. An EduAll grant would allow me to finish the thesis with the focus it deserves and to complete my degree on time.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was seven, my grandmother showed me a drop of pond water under a toy microscope that my uncle had brought back from Dubai. There were creatures in it, moving, feeding, dividing. I remember asking her how something so small could be alive, and her laughing and saying that most of life is too small to see. I have been trying to see it ever since.

I grew up in Faisalabad, the child of a textile worker and a mother who never learned to read. No one in my family had studied beyond secondary school. I earned a place at university through scholarships, completed a bachelor's degree in microbiology, and then worked for four years as a laboratory technician in a public hospital. I processed thousands of samples a year, and I watched infections that once responded to basic antibiotics stop responding to anything at all.

My path to Switzerland was not a straight one. As a non-binary person in Pakistan, I learned early to make myself small, at university, at work and in public. Many doors were closed to me without explanation. Coming to Switzerland to study was, in part, a decision to stop living that way. It took years of saving, two rejected applications and a great deal of stubbornness.

At UNIL I found an academic community that took me seriously. I have completed 2 courses, and I co-authored a paper on resistance genes in hospital effluent, drawing on methods I first learned in Faisalabad. My master's thesis extends this work to municipal wastewater, where resistant bacteria meet and exchange genes before reaching rivers and fields.

After graduation, I want to work in antimicrobial resistance surveillance, ideally in a programme that connects Swiss research laboratories with hospitals in South Asia. The problem does not respect borders, and the laboratories in countries like mine are where the earliest warnings appear, often unheard.

Education, for me, has been the one place where what I can do matters more than who people assume I am. I intend to make the most of the rest of this degree, and to use what I have learned where it is most needed.

---

**Education**
- 2026–present: MSc Biology (Microbiology track), University of Lausanne (expected July 2028)
- 2016–2020: BSc Microbiology, University of Agriculture, Faisalabad

**Work experience**
- 2025–present: Part-time laboratory technician, teaching labs, University of Lausanne
- 2021–2025: Laboratory technician, microbiology department, public hospital, Faisalabad

**Publications**
- Co-author, 1 article on antibiotic resistance genes in hospital effluent

**Languages**
- Urdu, Punjabi (native); English (fluent); French (B1)

---

### Risk Factors
- ✓ First-generation student

### Resilience & Strength Factors
- ✓ Work experience
- ✓ Overcame significant adversity

**Total Resilience Factors:** 2

### Statement of Declared Circumstances

*Instructions: For each circumstance you have ticked in the checklist (risk factors and resilience/strength factors), briefly describe your situation and how it affects or has shaped your studies. You may attach supporting documents. If you have not ticked any circumstance, you may leave this section blank (max. 300 words).*

First-generation student: my father worked in a textile mill and my mother could not read. I was the first in my family to go to university, supported by merit scholarships.

Work experience: four years as a hospital laboratory technician in Faisalabad (2021–2025), and since 2025 a part-time technician position in the UNIL teaching laboratories.

Overcame significant adversity: as a non-binary person in Pakistan I faced repeated discrimination in education and employment, including being passed over for promotions and advised to leave my position. I kept working, saved what I could, and rebuilt my academic life abroad.

---

## References

- Academic reference: submitted directly via the online portal
- Personal reference: submitted directly via the online portal

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I want to explain my situation honestly. I am 27 years old and I study Master in Microbiology at University of Geneva since February 2026. Before, I worked four years in Vietnam in a food laboratory. To get my student permit I had to show the money for my studies: I brought my savings and a loan from my family. But Geneva is much more expensive than I calculated, and the money was finished already after my first semester.

Now my monthly costs are CHF 2,385. The biggest problem is the rent, CHF 1,415. I know this is very high. It is a furnished studio which is rented only by short contracts of three months, because I could not find a normal flat. I sent more than 60 applications for rooms, but without Swiss salary and without guarantor, the agencies always say no. So I pay more than I should, and every three months I don't know if I can stay.

My income is CHF 363 per month from my job in a Vietnamese restaurant kitchen in Plainpalais, a few hours on weekends. As a student I can work maximum 15 hours per week, and I need the rest for the lab. My older brother has a small electronics shop in Hanoi. His family lives on about CHF 1,680 per month, and he sends me CHF 380. That is a lot for him: he also takes care of our parents, and he still pays back the loan he took for me.

Every month I miss CHF 1,642. I have no savings now. I also want to say that my grades are only average (GPA 2.98), because in the first semester I worked too many hours and was very tired.

There is one more reason why this is urgent. My permit must be renewed in February, and the migration office will ask again for proof that I can pay my living costs, about CHF 2,600 per month. Without support, I risk losing my permit before I finish.

If I receive the grant, I will use it first for the deposit of a normal room with a long contract, so my rent will be lower and more stable. Then I can finish my master in July 2028 without stopping.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Why does a person leave a stable job and start to study again, in a country where they know nobody? Many people ask me this. My answer is always the same: because of one sample.

In 2023 I worked as quality control technician in a seafood factory near Ho Chi Minh City. One day we found a Vibrio contamination which almost went to export. Nobody in the factory could explain where it came from, and the investigation was very poor. I understood that my knowledge was not enough, I only followed procedures. I wanted to understand the bacteria really.

My parents are both teachers, and they always told me that learning is the only thing nobody can take from you. Still, it took me two years to prepare: I studied French in the evenings, I saved money, and I applied two times before I was accepted in Geneva.

The study is harder than I expected. The level is high, and my classmates studied in Europe and know already the methods. But in the lab I feel useful, because I have practical experience they don't have. My project now is about Vibrio species in food chains from Southeast Asia, so I come back to the same question which brought me here.

After my master, I want to work for food safety, maybe in an international organisation or a laboratory which works with Asian exporters. In Vietnam, many small producers lose everything when one shipment is refused, and nobody explains them why. I want to be the person who explains.

For me education is my chance, and I don't want to lose it because of rent.

I sent more than 60 applications for rooms, but without Swiss salary and without guarantor, the agencies always say no. If I receive the grant, I will use it first for the deposit of a normal room with a long contract, so my rent will be lower and more stable. Then I can finish my master in July 2028 without stopping.

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I am entering the fourth semester of my Bachelor's in Business Administration at the University of Zurich, with graduation expected in July 2028. I am applying to EduAll because my studies involve costs that my regular budget was never designed to absorb, and because the support I receive from home rests on foundations that are less stable than they appear.

I have a severe hearing impairment. In lectures I rely on hearing aids connected to a wireless microphone system, and for seminars and exams I need real-time captioning or a transcript. The university covers part of these accommodations, but the equipment is mine. My current hearing aids are eight years old, and my audiologist has advised replacing them before my final exams. The replacement will cost several thousand francs, of which my insurance will only cover a fraction.

My monthly costs of CHF 1,987 include rent of CHF 746 for a room in a shared flat in Altstetten and CHF 274 for health insurance. I earn CHF 1,151 a month as a part-time assistant in the finance department of a logistics company, a position I have held for two years. My brothers, who run a building-supplies business in Erbil and together earn around CHF 1,920 a month, send me CHF 530. Their business depends on construction contracts that have slowed considerably over the past year, and they have warned me that they may need to reduce their help.

I have not received any other scholarships. A grant from EduAll would allow me to replace my hearing aids before my final semester and to complete my degree without increasing my working hours at the most demanding point of my studies.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In ten years, I want to be running the finance function of an organisation that hires people like me, people whom most employers quietly screen out. I have seen what happens when finance teams are built only by those who have never had to fight for a seat at the table: they design processes that exclude without meaning to.

I grew up in Mosul, the eldest daughter of a carpenter and a mother who managed our household and the accounts of my father's workshop by hand. Neither of my parents went to university. I lost most of my hearing to meningitis when I was six, and for years teachers assumed I was simply slow. My mother taught me to read lips at the kitchen table. She also taught me bookkeeping, and I was keeping the workshop's records by the age of fourteen.

When our city fell in 2014, my family relocated to Erbil. I was eleven, and I lost a school year. I finished school in Erbil in 2021 and worked for three years, first as an administrative assistant for an NGO, then as the finance assistant of a small women's cooperative, where I helped build their first budgeting system and trained eleven women to manage their own accounts. That role convinced me that I wanted a formal education in business.

Coming to Zurich at twenty-one was a risk. My German was basic, and my hearing makes language learning particularly hard. Today I hold a GPA of 3.29 and an average grade of 86.8, and I have completed 16 courses. At work, I have been given responsibility for monthly reporting in my team, and last year I led a project to digitise our supplier invoices, which reduced processing time by a third.

My goal after graduation is to work in corporate finance for a year or two and then pursue a master's degree focused on inclusive organisations. Ultimately, I want to bring these skills back to Iraq, where businesses owned or run by women and people with disabilities are rare and rarely financed.

EduAll's commitment to equal opportunity is exactly what I hope to practise in my own career.

---

- 2025–present: BA Business Administration, University of Zurich (expected July 2028)
- 2021: Secondary school certificate, Erbil

**Work experience**
- 2025–present: Finance assistant (part-time), logistics company, Zurich
- 2022–2024: Finance assistant, women's handicraft cooperative, Erbil

You may attach supporting documents. If you have not ticked any circumstance, you may leave this section blank (max. 300 words).*

First-generation student: my father is a carpenter and my mother never attended secondary school. I am the first in my family to study at university.

Disability: I have a severe bilateral hearing impairment since childhood. I use hearing aids with a wireless microphone system and need captioning or transcripts in seminars and exams. My aids now need replacement, which is costly.

Work experience: three years in NGO and cooperative finance in Erbil; since 2025 a part-time finance assistant role in Zurich.

Leadership role: I built the finance system of a women's cooperative and trained its members; at my current job I led a digitisation project.

Overcame significant adversity: I lost my hearing at six and was treated as a weak student for years. In 2014 my family was displaced from Mosul. I rebuilt my education from scratch, twice.

I will be honest about my budget. My parents send me CHF 290 per month and I earn CHF 885 working in a bike repair shop in Kreis 5, about 9 hours per week. My expenses are CHF 2,087, so every month CHF 912 is missing. I cover it from my savings, CHF 2,667, which I brought from Vietnam.

But this situation will change very soon, and this is why I apply. In April my father had a stroke. He was civil engineer in Can Tho and his salary was the main income of my family, together with my mother who is a teacher. Before, they earned together about CHF 1,720 per month. Now my father cannot work anymore, maybe never. My mother told me that from January she can only send me a small part of what she sends now, because the hospital and the rehabilitation cost a lot, and in Vietnam the insurance pays not much.

I calculated: without the money from my parents I will miss more than one thousand francs every month. My savings will be finished before the end of the year. I can increase my work hours a little, but not so much, because my permit allows only 15 hours in semester and I need time for my study.

I still have four semesters until July 2028. I don't have any other scholarship. With the EduAll support I could continue my bachelor normally and not go back to Vietnam in the middle.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In April this year I was standing in the Zurich main station when my sister called me. She was crying so much that I did not understand her first. My father was in hospital. I remember I looked at the big clock in the station and I thought: I am 10,000 km away and I cannot do anything.

I flew home for two weeks. My father could not speak well, but he asked me about my exams. This is typical for him. He always said that I must study the environment because Mekong Delta is sinking and salt water comes into the rice fields, and our generation must solve it.

I grew up in Can Tho. Every rainy season our street was flooded, and every dry season the water from the tap was a bit salty. When I was 15, my family's rice land in the countryside was lost because of salt intrusion. My grandfather had to sell it. This is why I chose Environmental Science.

In Zurich I study for two semesters now. My grades are medium, GPA 2.9. The first year was very difficult with German and with the system of exams, and honestly I also worked too much. Now I understand better how to study here.

Besides study and work, I help in the Vietnamese community in Zurich. We organise Tet festival and I help new students from Vietnam with apartments and with the insurance, which is very complicated.

My goal is to do a master in water management and then go back to the Mekong Delta to work on adaptation projects. I don't want to stop now, when my father is sick and my family needs me to finish more than before.

I started my Bachelor in Business at the University of Geneva in February 2026, so I have just finished my first semester.

My parents support me with CHF 1,560 a month. I want to be clear that my family is not poor by Romanian standards. I am looking for a cheaper room in a shared flat or a student residence, and I am on the waiting list for university housing. If I get a place there, my costs will go down a lot. I chose business because I have seen what happens to a family when a small company fails. My uncle ran a furniture workshop in Brașov with twelve employees. It was a good business with good products, but nobody there understood finance. When a big client paid late, everything collapsed within a year. Twelve families lost their income. I was sixteen and I remember thinking that it did not have to happen.

I want to understand how companies, especially small ones, can be managed so that one bad month does not destroy them. Later I would like to work in advising or financing small and medium enterprises in Eastern Europe, where many businesses are family-run and have very little access to good advice.

My route to university was not direct. At nineteen I had a serious car accident. I spent almost a year in hospitals and rehabilitation and had to learn to walk properly again. I lost my place at university in Bucharest and it took me a long time to believe I could start again. When I finally did, I wanted to do it properly, somewhere that would push me, and I chose Geneva.

My first semester went better than I expected. I finished with a GPA of 3.49 and an average of 91.8, even though I was studying in French, which is my third language. It gave me confidence that I made the right choice.

For me, education is proof that a bad moment does not have to decide the rest of your life. That is true for people and, I believe, also for businesses.

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I am a second-year nursing student at HES-SO La Source, and I have organised my life around a single goal: to become a registered nurse in Switzerland and, one day, to strengthen nursing education in Palestine. My financial situation is carefully managed, but it is fragile, and the most demanding part of my programme is still ahead of me.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,091, of which CHF 1,167 is rent for a small flat in Prilly and CHF 240 is health insurance. I earn CHF 1,164 a month as a nursing assistant in a care home in Lausanne, working weekend and evening shifts. My parents in Ramallah, whose combined income is around CHF 1,120 a month, send me CHF 190. They have done this every month since I arrived, even in periods when my father's work as a stonemason dried up entirely.

From the next semester, my clinical placements become full-time, with rotating shifts in hospital wards. This makes it very difficult to keep my current working hours, and my supervisors at the care home have already told me they cannot schedule around a placement timetable. The CHF 737 I lack each month today is likely to grow considerably when my income falls.

EduAll's support would allow me to complete my placements with the attention patients deserve, rather than arriving on the ward after an overnight shift elsewhere. It would also allow me to finish my degree on time, in July 2028, and begin working as a qualified nurse.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

By 2035, I want to be teaching clinical skills at a nursing school in Palestine, with the experience of working in one of the best health systems in the world behind me. Every step I have taken since I was fourteen has been towards that goal.

I grew up in Ramallah, the second of five children. My father is a stonemason and my mother raised us at home; neither of them had the chance to study beyond secondary school. When my grandmother was diagnosed with diabetes, it was a young nurse at the local clinic, not a doctor, who taught our family how to manage her insulin and diet. I was fourteen, and I followed that nurse around the clinic every afternoon for a month. I have wanted to do her job ever since.

After school I trained as a practical nurse and worked for two years at a clinic run by a women's health association. I learned how much a nurse can achieve with very little, and also how much more could be achieved with proper training and resources.

Coming to Lausanne at twenty-one meant learning French properly and starting a bachelor's degree far from my family. I have now completed two semesters and 14 courses, with a GPA of 2.85, while working part-time throughout. At the care home where I work, residents' families often ask for me by name, and I was recently asked to help train new assistants in safe mobility techniques.

I am also an active member of an Arabic-speaking women's group in Renens, where I help newcomers understand the Swiss health system and accompany them to appointments when language is a barrier.

Education, to me, is the difference between caring for people and being able to change the conditions they live in. I intend to use every part of this degree.

---

- 2021–2022: Diploma in Practical Nursing, Ramallah

You may attach supporting documents. If you have not ticked any circumstance, you may leave this section blank (max. 300 words).*

First-generation student: my father is a stonemason and my mother a homemaker. I am the first in my family to go to university.

Language barrier: I started learning French only in 2023. My clinical courses and placements are entirely in French, and medical vocabulary and documentation still require a great deal of extra work.

Work experience: two years as a practical nurse in Ramallah, and since 2025 a nursing assistant in a Lausanne care home.

Community engagement: I support Arabic-speaking women in Renens with health-related appointments and information.

Overcame significant adversity: I grew up under the restrictions of the occupation, with regular checkpoint closures that made even getting to school unpredictable. I trained and worked in difficult conditions and started again in a new language at twenty-one.

I asked myself this question during my years as a technician in a hospital in Hue, when I saw a dialysis machine which was broken for three months because nobody could repair it and the spare part was too expensive.

I grew up in a small village near the Perfume River, in Thua Thien Hue. Every few years the floods came. In 2015 the water reached the second floor of our house, and we lost almost everything, including all my school books one month before my exams. I studied from photos of a friend's notes on my phone and passed the exam anyway. My parents are teachers, and for them education was always the first thing, even when we had to rebuild the house.

In Bern I study Engineering with focus on biomedical technology. My GPA is 3.77 and average 95.4. I am proud of this, because I study in German and English, both not my mother language. I am also the president of the Vietnamese Students Association in Bern, and I organised this year a workshop about medical device repair together with an NGO.

My dream is to design medical devices which are simple, robust and repairable in low-resource hospitals. In Vietnam and in many countries, expensive machines from Europe stay unused because of one small broken part.

For me education is not only personal success. It is a responsibility to bring back what I learn.

I grew up in a small village near the Perfume River, in Thua Thien Hue. Every few years the floods came. In 2015 the water reached the second floor of our house, and we lost almost everything, including all my school books one month before my exams. I studied from photos of a friend's notes on my phone and passed the exam anyway. My parents are teachers, and for them education was always the first thing, even when we had to rebuild the house.

In Bern I study Engineering with focus on biomedical technology. My GPA is 3.77 and average 95.4. I am proud of this, because I study in German and English, both not my mother language. I am also the president of the Vietnamese Students Association in Bern, and I organised this year a workshop about medical device repair together with an NGO.

My dream is to design medical devices which are simple, robust and repairable in low-resource hospitals. In Vietnam and in many countries, expensive machines from Europe stay unused because of one small broken part.

For me education is not only personal success. It is a responsibility to bring back what I learn.

I will be candid about my choices, because I think they matter for understanding my application. From February to May 2026, in my first semester, I worked twelve hours a week as a research assistant in a polymer lab at the Adolphe Merkle Institute. In June I decided to stop, because my laboratory courses require full days, and I was falling behind. That decision was mine, and it means I currently have no personal income.

My parents, both civil servants in Yogyakarta, have a combined monthly income of about CHF 1,320. They send me CHF 280, which is about a fifth of what they earn, and they also support my younger brother at university in Indonesia. I have no savings: what I earned from my assistant job went directly into my living costs.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,892, of which CHF 957 is rent for a room in a shared flat in Fribourg's Pérolles district and CHF 372 is food. I have tried to keep everything else modest. The result is a shortfall of CHF 1,612 each month.

I have applied to the university's social fund and am waiting for an answer, although I was told support there is usually limited to one-off payments. I have not received any other scholarship.

My thesis is due in July 2028. An EduAll grant would allow me to complete it in 2027/28 without returning to paid work in the most intensive phase, and to graduate on time. I would rather tell you plainly that this is, in part, a situation I chose, than pretend otherwise: I chose it because finishing well matters more to me than finishing comfortably.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

The job that taught me the most was not in a laboratory. For two years after my bachelor's degree, I worked for a waste bank cooperative in Yogyakarta, where households bring sorted plastic and receive small credits in return. I weighed bags, kept records and talked with the women who ran the collection points. Every week I saw the same thing: a mountain of thin plastic films that nobody would buy, because nobody could recycle them.

I grew up in a family of civil servants. My mother works at the regional education office and my father at the land registry. They gave me a steady, unremarkable childhood, and the belief that public service is a worthy life. I studied chemistry at Gadjah Mada University and expected to become a teacher. The waste bank changed my plans.

I came to Fribourg in February 2026 for a Master's in Materials Science because of the university's strength in polymer research. It has been demanding, but also the most rewarding time of my life. I have a GPA of 3.65 and an average of 90.2, and my thesis supervisor has invited me to present my first results at the institute's internal symposium in November.

My research focuses on films made from cassava starch and agricultural waste, materials that are abundant in Indonesia and could replace some of the packaging that ends up in waste banks with nowhere to go. After graduating I would like to work in applied research, ideally in a partnership between a European institute and Indonesian manufacturers.

Outside the lab, I coordinate a monthly clean-up of the Sarine riverbanks with other students and residents, and I help organise the Indonesian community's Independence Day gathering in Fribourg.

For me, education is not an escape from where I come from. It is a way of bringing better tools back to it.

I want to be upfront: right now my income is higher than my expenses. I study part-time and work about 23 hours a week as a support worker in a residential home for people with intellectual disabilities, and I earn CHF 2,577 a month. My partner, who works as a logistics coordinator in Bern and earns about CHF 5,030 a month, contributes CHF 320 to my share of our costs. If my partner does not find a new job quickly, we will both live on what I earn. In 2027/28 I also have a clinical internship that is part of the master, and I will have to reduce my care work to about 18 hours a week, so my income will go down to around CHF 2,060.

I have no savings. Before starting my master's I worked full-time, but most of that money went into language courses, the recognition of my Romanian degree and moving costs. I have not received any other scholarship.

My master's in Psychology, part-time, runs until January 2029. I would like EduAll to consider my application with that date in mind, and I will of course report any change in our situation, positive or negative.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Do you remember the moment you understood what you wanted to do with your life? For me it was a Tuesday night shift in 2021, when one of the residents I cared for, a man in his fifties who does not speak, took my hand and led me to the window to show me the snow. Nobody had ever told me he could communicate like that. I realised how much we miss when we only listen to words.

I grew up in Iași, in north-eastern Romania. My mother works in a bakery and my father drove trucks until his back gave out. Nobody in my family studied at a university before me. I finished a bachelor's in psychology in Iași while working evenings in a call centre, and then came to Switzerland in 2019 to work in social care, because the pay in Romania did not allow me to live independently.

For five years I worked in care homes and residential services around Bern. I learned German on the job, first standard German and then, with a lot of patience from my colleagues, enough Bernese to understand the residents. In February 2026 I started the Master's in Psychology at the University of Bern. My first semester went well: GPA 3.43, average 83.8. Academic German is still hard for me, and I need much longer than my classmates for reading and writing, but I am getting there.

Outside of work and study I volunteer with a peer-support group for Romanian care workers in Switzerland, and I help run a monthly language café in my neighbourhood.

I want to work as a psychologist in disability services, focusing on non-verbal communication. For me education is a way to turn what I learned in care work into something that can help many more people than I can reach alone.

I should say clearly at the outset that my monthly budget is almost balanced today, and that I have some resources that many applicants will not. I want the committee to see the full picture.

I study Business Administration part-time and work about 13 hours a week as a bookkeeping assistant for a small accounting office, earning CHF 1,452 a month. My spouse, who works as a hotel receptionist in Zurich and earns about CHF 3,700 a month, contributes CHF 310 towards my personal costs; the rest of the household income goes to our five-year-old child and the flat. I also receive a scholarship of CHF 4,444 a year from a Moroccan diaspora association. My own monthly expenses are CHF 2,249, which leaves a gap of CHF 487 before the scholarship. We also have savings of CHF 11,923, built up over several years before I returned to studying.

Why apply, then? Because at this pace my degree would take until July 2030. From September 2027 I want to study full-time and keep only about five hours a week of bookkeeping, which means my income would fall to around CHF 560 and my gap would grow to CHF 1,379 a month before the scholarship. The savings are our family's only reserve, set aside for our child, and my scholarship is renewed only year by year.

An EduAll grant would allow me to switch to full-time and finish in July 2029, a year earlier, without touching the money we have set aside. If the committee decides my need is less urgent than others', I will understand.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In fifteen years, I want to run a small consultancy that helps immigrant-owned businesses in Switzerland grow beyond survival. Kebab shops, cleaning companies, hair salons, grocery stores: they are everywhere in Zurich, and most of them are one bad year away from closing, not because the owners are not capable, but because nobody has ever explained VAT, cash flow or credit to them in a language they understand.

I know this because my family lived it. I grew up in Fès, where my father ran a small leather workshop that was always one missing payment from ruin. As a teenager I kept the accounts in a school notebook. When I came to Switzerland in 2016 to join my spouse, I spent my first years cleaning offices at night, then working in a laundry, while learning German from free courses at the library.

In 2020 our child was born, very prematurely. We spent three months in the neonatal unit of the Triemli hospital. It was the most frightening period of my life, and it was also when I decided that I would not spend the rest of it in jobs that left no room for a future. When our child started kindergarten, I began preparing for the university entrance exam, and I passed on my first attempt.

I have now completed three semesters in Business Administration at the University of Zurich, with a GPA of 3.01, while working and raising a child. My bookkeeping job has become the practical side of my degree: I now handle the monthly accounts of fourteen small clients, most of them immigrants like me.

I am in the first year of my Master of Law at the University of Zurich, specialising in international economic law, and I am applying to EduAll to make sure that the last stage of my degree, my thesis, receives the time it requires.

My monthly costs amount to CHF 2,431. The largest item is rent: CHF 1,417 for a studio in Wiedikon, which I took after two previous shared flats ended abruptly. In Zurich, a student without a Swiss guarantor has very little choice. Tuition and semester fees add CHF 203 a month, and the remainder covers food, insurance and transport.

I earn CHF 935 a month as a student assistant at a legal-aid organisation for migrants, where I prepare case files and translate for Bengali- and Hindi-speaking clients. My father, a district court advocate in Sylhet, and my mother, a secondary school teacher, have a combined income of around CHF 700. They send me CHF 120 every month, which is about a sixth of what they earn, and they are also putting my younger brother through engineering school.

This leaves a monthly gap of CHF 1,376. Over the past semester I have filled it by taking on extra hours, but my thesis on the enforcement of labour standards in global garment supply chains requires sustained research, including interviews with NGOs in Geneva.

A grant from EduAll would allow me to hold my working hours at a sustainable level and to complete my degree in January 2028 with a thesis I am proud of.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Last November, I sat in the public gallery of the Federal Supreme Court in Lausanne and watched five judges deliberate openly on a case involving a Bangladeshi textile supplier. I had read about Swiss public deliberations, but seeing it was something else: judges disagreeing respectfully, in public, on the reasoning behind a decision that would affect workers thousands of kilometres away. I took the train back to Zurich knowing exactly what I wanted my thesis to be about.

I grew up in Sylhet, in north-eastern Bangladesh. When I was sixteen, my father was arrested for representing a group of garment workers in a wage dispute and held for four months without charge. Our family's income stopped overnight. My mother kept us going on her teacher's salary, and I tutored younger students to pay for my own school fees. I watched my father's colleagues, and later the courts, eventually secure his release. That experience made me believe in law, and also showed me how fragile it can be.

I completed my LLB at the University of Dhaka and came to Zurich in February 2026. Studying law in a new legal system, partly in German, has been demanding, but I have completed 4 courses, and my work at the legal-aid organisation has taught me as much as any seminar.

I serve as president of the Bangladeshi Students' Association in Zurich, where I organised a series of information evenings on tenant rights and employment law for newly arrived students and workers, together with volunteer lawyers.

After graduating, I want to work on corporate accountability for supply chains, first in an international organisation in Geneva and eventually back in Bangladesh, where millions of workers depend on standards that exist mainly on paper. Education, for me, is the means to make those standards real.

I trained at a medical college in Kharkiv. My parents worked in a tractor factory; nobody in my family had studied before. For the first ten years I worked on a cardiology ward. Then I became head nurse of the ward, responsible for 26 nurses. I introduced a structured discharge plan for heart failure patients, and our readmissions went down. I was very proud of this, but I did not have the scientific training to measure it properly or to publish it.

We came to Switzerland in 2021, when my spouse got a job offer in Basel. My Ukrainian nursing diploma was only partly recognised, so I decided to go back to university and do it properly. I did bridging courses, then the master's programme. I have completed 4 courses, with an average of 88.2.

My goal is to work as an advanced practice nurse in cardiology and to develop nurse-led programmes for chronic patients. In Ukraine, after the war, there will be enormous need for this kind of care, because many doctors have left. I want to be able to teach it.

Education for me is not a new start. It is the continuation of what I did for twenty years, with better tools.

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

Every month, my costs of studying in Zurich exceed the support available to me by CHF 2,411. That single figure has shaped almost every decision I have made since arriving at ETH, and it is the reason I am writing to EduAll.

My expenses total CHF 2,581 a month. Rent is CHF 1,363 for a studio in Oerlikon, close enough to the Hönggerberg campus that I can walk when I cannot afford the tram. Tuition and semester fees amount to CHF 243 a month, and health insurance to CHF 355. I have kept everything else to the minimum.

My younger brother, a pharmacist in Accra, sends me CHF 170 every month out of a household income of about CHF 1,100. That is a sixth of what his family lives on, and he does it because, for four years, I paid for his own university fees from my teacher's salary. It is a debt he insists on repaying, but it is not one I want to extend.

The Master's in Physics at ETH is a full-time programme in the most literal sense. Laboratory courses, problem sets and my semester project leave very little room for paid work, and the few student jobs I have found clash with compulsory lab sessions. For a semester I have tried to make the numbers work by cutting costs, but I have reached the limit of what cutting can do.

I have three semesters left before completing my degree in January 2028. A grant from EduAll would allow me to finish it with my full attention on physics, rather than on the gap at the end of each month.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

For five years, I taught physics to teenagers in Kumasi, in a school where the laboratory consisted of a single cupboard. We built pendulums from string and bottle caps, measured the speed of sound by clapping against the school wall, and assembled a working spectroscope from a broken DVD. My students called me "Mr Improvise". Some of my first students now study engineering and medicine.

My father was a primary school headmaster and my mother a nurse, and they raised us to believe that knowledge belongs to whoever is willing to work for it. I studied physics at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology and always intended to continue, but family responsibilities came first: my salary paid for my younger brother's studies.

When he graduated, I decided that if I did not pursue advanced study then, I never would. I was admitted to the Master's in Physics at ETH Zurich and began in February 2026. The step from a Ghanaian classroom to one of the world's most demanding physics programmes has been enormous, and I have had to rebuild mathematics that I had not used since my bachelor's. I have met that challenge with the same approach I took in Kumasi: patience, repetition and a lot of improvisation.

My semester project, in the group for quantum optics, involves building a low-cost interferometer for teaching purposes, work that connects directly to my years in the classroom. After graduating, I want to return to Ghana and help establish teacher-training programmes in experimental physics, so that no school laboratory has to depend on a single cupboard.

In Zurich, I help run a weekly study group for African students in science and engineering, where newer students can ask the questions they are too embarrassed to ask in lectures.

Education gave me my career once. I want it to give the same to many more students.

My situation right now: I spend CHF 2,368 a month and I have CHF 376 coming in. The gap is CHF 1,992. I have no savings left and no job at the moment.

I grew up in Korail, one of the biggest informal settlements in Dhaka. My father pulled a rickshaw for thirty years and my mother worked as a domestic helper. Neither of them can read. I was the first person in my family, and one of the first in my lane, to finish secondary school.

What pushed me towards psychology was my brothers. They left for the Gulf when they were very young to support us. When they came home on leave, they were different: quiet, exhausted, sometimes angry. Nobody in our community talked about mental health. I wanted to understand what was happening to them.

With scholarships from an NGO school and later from the university, I studied psychology at the University of Dhaka. I worked as a research assistant in a lab studying the mental health of garment workers, and I co-authored two papers from that project. That is how I got the chance to apply to Basel.

Basel has been harder than I expected. I came in February 2025 with little money and almost no German. I have moved four times. But my grades are good (GPA 3.64), and my supervisor has encouraged me to think about a PhD.

I am also involved in the Bangladeshi community in Basel, helping newly arrived workers and students with forms and appointments.

I want to do research on the mental health of labour migrants, people like my brothers, who carry whole families on their backs and never get asked how they are.

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I have been studying Economics at the University of Zurich part-time for three years now, and I want to tell you honestly how my money works, because it has never been simple.

Each month I need CHF 2,135. My rent is CHF 861 for a small room in Schwamendingen, and my health insurance is CHF 490, which is a lot for me, but with my illness I cannot choose the cheapest model. I work about 21 hours a week: I clean offices in the early morning and I work two evenings in a care home. Together this gives me CHF 2,365. My older sister, who works as a care assistant in Paris and lives on about CHF 2,500 with her two children, still sends me CHF 300, even though I asked her to stop.

So on paper I cover my costs, and I want to say this clearly. I also have CHF 1,341 on my account. But this balance only works when I am healthy. When I am in hospital I lose my income from one day to the next; last winter it happened twice. And in May my mother in Thiès was told her kidneys are failing. She needs dialysis three times a week, and every franc I send to Senegal is a franc less for my studies.

I have six semesters left and I finish in July 2029. I am asking EduAll for a safety margin, so that one hospital stay or one more bill from Thiès does not force me to stop my studies.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

There is a bench at the Zurich Stadelhofen station where I sat one evening in February 2023 and almost decided to give up. I had just come out of the hospital after a sickle-cell crisis. I had missed two exams. I did not understand half of what the professor said in German, and I was thirty-six years old among students who could be my children. I sat there for maybe an hour. Then I took the tram home, opened my notes and started again.

I was born in Thiès, in Senegal. My mother sold fabric at the market, my father repaired radios. I have lived with sickle-cell disease all my life. As a child I missed school for weeks every year. Teachers told my mother not to waste money on my education. She did not listen to them.

I came to Switzerland in 2011 for marriage. The marriage ended, but I stayed, and I worked. I cleaned hotel rooms, I worked in a laundry, I cared for old people. For ten years I learned German in the evenings. When I obtained my C permit, I decided it was finally my turn to study.

Studying economics was a promise I made to the women of my mother's market. They borrowed money at crazy interest rates, and nobody explained anything to them. I want to understand how credit can help poor women instead of trapping them.

My grades are not brilliant. My GPA is 2.99. Every semester I lose weeks to my illness. But I have completed 22 courses, one by one, and I am still here.

After my degree I want to work for a microfinance institution in West Africa, or for an organisation in Switzerland that supports women's economic projects. I want to show the teachers of my childhood that my mother was right.

---

I am 29 years old and I come from Multan, in the south of Punjab. My father was headmaster of a government school for 30 years. He taught me that the best thing a person can have is curiosity.

For five years I worked as a laboratory officer at an agricultural research institute in Multan. We worked on cotton, which is the main crop of our region. Every year I saw farmers losing their harvest because of the whitefly and the leaf curl virus. We tried many things, but our research was limited, we had old equipment and little training in molecular methods.

So I decided to learn this properly. I saved for three years and I was admitted to ETH Zurich in February 2026, in Master of Biology with focus on plant sciences. It is a dream but also very difficult. The level of the students is very high and I had to learn a lot of new methods, like CRISPR and bioinformatics, which I never used before.

My master thesis is about the resistance of cotton plants to leaf curl virus. My supervisor is very supportive and says my practical skills in the lab are strong.

After my master I want to go back to Pakistan and work in plant breeding for small farmers. Our farmers need seeds which can resist climate change and disease, and Pakistan needs people who can develop them.

For me education is not for my CV. It is for the farmers of Multan.

I am a doctoral student in Mathematics at ETH Zurich, now in my third semester. ## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

My parents own two pharmacies in Ruse, and together they earn around CHF 3,270 a month. Since February, when I began my Master's in Biochemistry in Bern, they have sent me CHF 940 every month, which covers my rent of CHF 856, my tuition and everything else I need.

But in April, everything in our family changed. My father was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He is in treatment now in Sofia, and the prognosis is not good. My mother is running both pharmacies alone while driving to Sofia three times a week, and we have already talked, as a family, about selling one of them. My father's treatment is only partly covered by the Bulgarian health system, and the private clinic costs are growing every month.

My parents have told me not to worry and to stay in Bern. But I am not a child, and I can see the numbers. I know that the support I receive now takes money that my father's treatment may soon need, and that it may not continue for the whole of my programme, which runs until July 2028.

I am applying to EduAll so that my studies do not become one more weight on my family during the hardest time of our lives. Before starting my master's, I worked for three years as a laboratory technician in Sofia. I am ready to take on work again here, and I am applying for research assistant positions. A grant would give me the stability to look after my studies while my family looks after my father.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Ruse is a city on the Danube, on the border with Romania. It has beautiful old buildings from the time when it was the most modern city in Bulgaria, and it has emptied out in the last thirty years. Half of my school class now lives abroad. The chemical plant where my grandfather worked is closed. Every summer, when I go home, there are more windows without lights.

I grew up in the back room of my parents' pharmacy, doing my homework between shelves of medicines. I learned the names of drugs before I learned my multiplication tables. My father would explain to me how each medicine worked, what it did inside the body. I think that is where it all started: the feeling that there is a hidden world of molecules deciding whether we are healthy or sick.

I studied molecular biology in Sofia and then worked three years in a research laboratory on antibiotic resistance, where I became the lab coordinator for a team of six technicians. We published one article on resistant Klebsiella strains in Bulgarian hospitals, and I was proud to see my name on it.

In Bern I study biochemistry with a focus on drug development. Now, of course, my interest has a new and painful meaning. Pancreatic cancer is one of the diseases where medicine has advanced the least. When I sit with my father in the hospital, he asks me about my courses. He still explains things to me. He still wants to know how everything works.

I want to do a PhD in cancer biochemistry after my master's. Maybe it will not help my father. But it may help somebody else's father.

For me, education is the most valuable thing my family gave me, more than any money. I want to honour it.

---

I would like to be transparent about my finances, because they are unusual for an EduAll applicant. At the moment my household can cover my costs, and I also have savings of CHF 10,320.

My husband works as a sous-chef in a hotel in Lausanne and earns around CHF 4,790 a month. He contributes CHF 1,280 to my part of our costs. I earn CHF 764 as a part-time drafting assistant for a small architecture office in Renens. My personal expenses come to CHF 1,649 a month. My share of the rent is only CHF 488, because we live in a subsidised family flat.

So why do I apply? Our savings are the money we put aside, over many years, for our two children. We have no family in Switzerland to help if anything happens, and my husband's contract is renewed every season. My last semester at EPFL is also the most expensive one: the diploma project requires models, large-format printing and site visits, and the studio hours make it impossible to keep working at the same level. From October I will reduce my job to a few hours a month.

I understand that other applicants may be in more urgent need. If the committee decides to support me, the grant would let me finish my diploma project in July 2028 without touching our children's savings.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My first job in architecture was carrying cement bags. At nineteen, in Surabaya, I worked on a construction site because my family needed the money. My father was a fisherman, my mother sold vegetables at the market, and none of us had been to university. On that site I watched a young architect walk through the half-finished building, pointing at things, changing things. I remember thinking: I want to be the person who decides.

It took me a long time. I worked as a draftswoman in an architecture office in Jakarta for eight years, learning everything by watching and asking. I married, and we had our first child. In 2018 my husband found work in Switzerland, and a year later we followed him. I spent two years learning French, caring for our children, and preparing the admission exam for EPFL, which I passed on the second try, at thirty-four.

Studying architecture at EPFL with two small children has been the hardest thing I have ever done. There were nights in the studio when I was the oldest person in the room by fifteen years. But I have completed 23 courses, with a GPA of 3.18, and my work on low-cost housing was selected for the semester exhibition.

My diploma project is a design for flood-resilient housing for fishing communities on the north coast of Java, communities like the one I come from. Every year, the sea takes a little more of their land.

After graduating, I want to work in an office that designs social housing, and one day to open a small practice in Indonesia that builds for people who cannot afford architects.

I think of the young architect on that construction site often. I would like, one day, to be that person for someone else.

---

Right now I have CHF 130 a month and I need CHF 2,354. That is a gap of CHF 2,214. I have no savings.

Until June I worked as a care assistant in a nursing home in Köniz, about 12 hours a week. I had to stop, because my clinical placement started in August. It is full-time with rotating shifts on a surgical ward at the Inselspital, the University Hospital of Bern, and the nursing home could not give me shifts that fit. I did not choose this lightly, but I could not do both.

The CHF 130 comes from my uncle in Gaziantep, Turkey. He has a small tailoring shop and his family lives on around CHF 550 a month. He has helped me since I left Syria. My parents cannot send anything. After the earthquake in February 2023 our family house in Aleppo was badly damaged, and my father was injured and has not been able to work properly since. Since then I have also been sending money home when I could, which is why I have nothing saved.

My rent is CHF 1,195 plus CHF 130 for utilities for a small studio. I know this is expensive. I took it in 2023 when I urgently needed a place, and I have been looking for something cheaper since, so far without success.

I will be honest: I have been paying the last two months' rent with a loan from a friend. My placement ends in December and I graduate in July 2028. After that I can work as a nurse, and I already have a job offer from the hospital if I pass. I only need to get through these last four semesters.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I was thirteen when my school in Aleppo was hit. I was not inside, but my best friend was. I spent the next day in a field hospital, trying to find him. He survived, but I will never forget the nurses in that hospital. They had nothing, no electricity, few medicines, and still they were calm, and they held people's hands.

My parents run a small grocery shop, and neither of them went to university. When the war made school impossible, I went to live with my uncle in Gaziantep and finished my secondary school in Turkey. I volunteered with a Syrian community clinic there, translating for patients and helping with registration.

In 2023, at nineteen, I came to Bern to study nursing. I was lucky to have an admission and a student permit. The first year was very hard. I studied German every evening and worked in a nursing home on weekends, which helped my language more than any course. I have completed 25 courses now, with a GPA of 3.02.

Since 2023 I also volunteer with the Red Cross in Bern as an interpreter for Arabic-speaking patients.

The earthquake in 2023 was the worst time. For three days I did not know if my family was alive. I still went to my exams that week. I passed them. I don't really know how.

After I graduate, I want to work in emergency and surgical nursing. Later, I hope to work with humanitarian organisations in the Middle East. I want to be, for someone else, what those nurses in Aleppo were for me.

I will describe my finances plainly, including the parts that may count against me.

I study Data Science part-time at the University of Lausanne and work about 12 hours a week as a data-entry assistant at a medical laboratory, where I earn CHF 1,315 a month. My monthly expenses are CHF 1,956, of which CHF 1,012 is rent for a studio in Chailly and CHF 245 is health insurance. I have not received any other scholarship; the university's social fund gave me a one-off payment last year, which I used for a laptop that can run the software my courses require.

At my current pace, my degree would take until January 2030. From September 2027 I would like to study full-time and stop working, because the final part of the programme includes a practical data project with a partner organisation that is incompatible with my job. Without my salary, my monthly gap would become CHF 1,686. An EduAll grant would allow me to make this switch, finish in January 2029, and keep a small margin for the months between graduation and my first job.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When does a life actually begin? For me, I think it began at thirty-three, in a small office of a women's counselling centre in Lausanne, when a social worker asked me what I would like to do if nobody else's opinion mattered. Nobody had ever asked me that before.

I grew up in Hyderabad, in Sindh. I was a good student, especially in mathematics, but I was married at nineteen and my education stopped there. For many years my life was organised around my husband's family and their decisions. When we moved to Switzerland for his work in 2019, I spoke no French, had no friends, and depended completely on him. The marriage was not a safe place. In 2020 I left, with the help of that counselling centre.

The years after that were difficult: temporary housing, legal procedures, and work in a hotel laundry, where I folded sheets for eight hours a day and practised French with my colleagues. But I also started, slowly, to remember who I had been before, the girl who loved numbers.

In February 2025 I began a Bachelor's in Data Science at the University of Lausanne. French is still my fourth language and many courses are a struggle for me, but I have completed 15 courses with a GPA of 3.1. I am proudest of a project in which I analysed data on the use of domestic violence helplines in Vaud, which the counselling centre now uses in its reports.

After graduating, I want to work as a data analyst in the public or non-profit sector, helping social services understand who they reach and who they miss. I know from experience how many women never reach anyone.

Education, for me, is the life I was not allowed to have. I intend to live it fully.

Education, for me, is the life I was not allowed to have. I intend to live it fully.

I am entering the last four semesters of my Bachelor's in Educational Sciences at the University of Basel, and I am applying to EduAll to ensure that the most important part of my degree, the practical teaching placement and my thesis, can be completed without financial pressure dictating my choices.

My monthly expenses amount to CHF 1,828: CHF 757 for a room in a shared flat in Gundeldingen, CHF 285 for health insurance, CHF 142 for tuition and semester fees, and modest costs for food, transport and study materials. I earn CHF 752 a month as a classroom assistant in a day school in Basel, where I support children who are learning German as an additional language. My sister and her husband, both teachers in Peshawar with a combined income of around CHF 900 a month, send me CHF 240. They have three children of their own; this is a sacrifice I do not take lightly.

This leaves a gap of CHF 836 each month. My placement this autumn requires me to be in a partner school four days a week, which means reducing my hours at the day school substantially. Without additional support, the gap will widen exactly when I most need to concentrate on teaching well.

An EduAll grant would allow me to complete my placement and thesis on schedule, graduating in July 2028, and to begin working in education immediately afterwards.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I grew up in Peshawar, in a family of teachers. My mother taught in a government primary school with classes of fifty children in rooms built for thirty, one blackboard and a box of chalk that had to last the term. As a girl I corrected her pupils' copybooks on the kitchen floor. I learned early that a child who is seen by a teacher, even for a moment each day, learns differently from a child who is not.

In December 2014, when I was fourteen, a school in our city was attacked. Among those killed were children from our street and a teacher my mother had trained with. For months afterwards, parents were afraid to send their children to any school, and teachers were afraid to go. My mother kept teaching. In the evenings I went with her to visit families at home and persuade them to let their children return. By the end of that school year, almost all of her pupils were back.

That period taught me that education is not only about curriculum. It is about trust, safety and the relationship between a school and its community. I became a teacher myself, taught for two years, and wanted to study these questions seriously. In 2024 I came to Basel, which has a strong tradition in comparative and inclusive education.

Studying in German, far from home, has been a humbling experience. But my work as a classroom assistant has given me daily contact with Swiss schools and with children from Afghanistan, Eritrea, Syria and Ukraine who are navigating a new language, as I am. My thesis examines how Swiss day schools build relationships with refugee families, and it draws on everything I learned in Peshawar.

After graduating, I want to work in teacher training focused on schools in crisis-affected regions, and eventually to return to Pakistan to support teachers working in insecure areas.

Education, to me, is an act of courage by children, parents and teachers alike. I want to spend my career supporting that courage.

My mother cried in the kitchen at night. I remember visiting him in a big room full of beds, and thinking that the people there were not bad or cursed, only very, very alone.

My parents did not go to university. My father worked in a sugar mill and my mother at home. After my father died when I was eighteen, I stayed at home to look after my mother, whose health was poor. For years, the only thing I did for myself was read, mostly psychology books from the library.

This has been my life so far: caring and studying.

I want to become a clinical psychologist and work on reducing the stigma of mental illness in rural India. I think about my father often, and the big lonely room.
