I am a third-year Bachelor's student in Physics at the University of Fribourg, and I am applying to EduAll because my housing situation has become precarious at the most important stage of my degree.

My monthly expenses total CHF 2,174. I rent a studio in Fribourg's Beauregard district for CHF 1,000 plus CHF 140 in utilities. In May, the building's owner informed all tenants that the building will be fully renovated from July 2028, and our leases will not be renewed. I have been searching since then, but affordable rooms near the university are scarce, and most landlords ask for a Swiss guarantor, which I do not have.

I cover part of my costs through two sources. I earn CHF 1,002 a month as a weekend receptionist at a hotel near the station. My father, a petroleum engineer in Basra, supports me with CHF 360 a month from a household income of around CHF 1,720; he is also paying for my two younger sisters' education in Iraq. The remaining CHF 812 a month I have covered until now with loans from friends and with extra shifts in the holidays.

My final semester includes an experimental bachelor project that requires regular evening and weekend work in the laboratory, which will conflict with my reception shifts. Moving house in the middle of it, with a deposit of two or three months' rent to find, is the risk I am trying to guard against.

An EduAll grant would allow me to secure new accommodation, reduce my working hours during my project, and graduate on time in July 2028.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

The summer I turned eleven, the electricity in Basra failed almost every afternoon. At fifty degrees, the city stopped. My father brought home a car battery and a small solar panel from his work, and together we built a fan that ran for three hours a day. It was the first thing I ever built, and I have never forgotten the feeling when the blades started turning.

I grew up asking why things work. My father answered what he could and then bought me books when he could not. At school I was the student who stayed after class to argue with the physics teacher. At nineteen, I was accepted to study physics in Fribourg, and I arrived in February 2025 with two suitcases and a French phrasebook.

Studying in French and German, as a teenager alone in a new country, was harder than I expected. There were weeks in my first year when I did not speak to anyone outside class. But I found my place in the laboratory. I have completed 18 courses, and my work on thin-film solar cells in a second-year project was selected for presentation at the department's student day.

Outside my studies, I volunteer with a homework-help programme run by Caritas in Fribourg, working with Arabic-speaking secondary school students on mathematics and science. Several of them arrived in Switzerland as I did, with more ambition than language.

My goal is to complete a master's in physics with a specialisation in photovoltaics and to work on solar energy for hot, grid-poor regions like southern Iraq, where the sun is the one resource that never fails.

Education, for me, began with a fan in a hot room. I would like it to lead to something that keeps the lights on for millions.

Medan is a big city in North Sumatra, hot and noisy, with many rivers that are very dirty. When I was a child, every rainy season my neighbours' children got diarrhoea, and some were very sick. My mother was a nurse in the public hospital. She came home and told us to always boil the water, always. I did not understand then why the water was dangerous when it looked clean.

After school I worked two years as assistant in a laboratory for water quality of the provincial health office in Medan. I tested water from wells, rivers and hospitals. It was good work, but I always wanted to understand more, not only to test.

When my husband got a job in Switzerland in 2021, I came with him and decided to use the chance. I learned German for two years and at twenty-two I started at ETH. People told me it was too difficult. Maybe. But I passed every exam until now, and my GPA is 3.37. I think my experience in the laboratory helps me very much, and I enjoy to help other students in the practical courses.

In my free time I volunteer at the Indonesian church community in Zurich, where I teach Indonesian to children of mixed families on Saturday afternoons.

My plan after the bachelor is a master in microbiology with focus on environmental microbes and water. Then I want to work for water safety, maybe in Switzerland or in Indonesia. Many children in Medan still drink water that is not safe.

For me education came after a detour, but it came, and I am very thankful.

I want to say it directly: at this moment I don't have a monthly deficit. I study Law part-time and I work about 19 hours a week as delivery driver for a pharmacy, where I earn CHF 2,165. My parents live in Lausanne and give me CHF 280 per month. I also have a scholarship of CHF 6,388 per year from a Bulgarian cultural foundation. Also, I want to change to full-time study from September 2027, so I can finish in July 2028 and not in January 2029. For this I will drive only on Saturdays, about CHF 900 per month. I calculated it: with my parents' help and the scholarship I can almost manage, but only if my parents continue to send the same.

I am honest that my need is not urgent like for other students. If the committee thinks other students need it more, I accept it. But if my father does not find work, our family will be in a difficult situation, and the grant would protect my last year.

In ten years I want to be a lawyer who defends workers from Eastern Europe in Switzerland. There are thousands of them: in construction, cleaning, care. Many of them don't know their rights, don't speak French, and accept everything because they are afraid.

I know them because I grew up with them. My father is a civil engineer and my mother a trained primary teacher, but their Bulgarian diplomas were never recognised here. They came to Lausanne from Pleven in 2010 to work, and I stayed with my grandmother in Bulgaria until I was twelve. When I joined them in 2013, I did not speak one word of French. I was put in a class for foreign students, and then in a normal class where I was the one who did not understand anything. I repeated one year. Many teachers thought I will do an apprenticeship at best.

I didn't accept this. I studied French every day, and later I passed the maturité. Since I was sixteen I also worked in summer on construction sites with my father, and later as a delivery driver for a pharmacy. I saw workers not paid for extra hours, working without protection, dismissed with one phone call.

At the university my results are average, I have a GPA of 2.85. Law in French is very difficult with so much text, and I still write slower than my classmates. But I am close to the end. My bachelor thesis is about the protection of posted workers in Swiss labour law.

After my bachelor I want to do the master in law and the lawyer's exam. For me education means that the son of a foreman and a cleaner can be the lawyer in the room.

They came to Lausanne from Pleven in 2010 to work, and I stayed with my grandmother in Bulgaria until I was twelve. When I joined them in 2013, I did not speak one word of French. I was put in a class for foreign students, and then in a normal class where I was the one who did not understand anything. I repeated one year. Many teachers thought I will do an apprenticeship at best.

I didn't accept this. I studied French every day, and later I passed the maturité. Since I was sixteen I also worked in summer on construction sites with my father, and later as a delivery driver for a pharmacy. I saw workers not paid for extra hours, working without protection, dismissed with one phone call.

At the university my results are average, I have a GPA of 2.85. Law in French is very difficult with so much text, and I still write slower than my classmates. But I am close to the end. My bachelor thesis is about the protection of posted workers in Swiss labour law.

After my bachelor I want to do the master in law and the lawyer's exam. For me education means that the son of a foreman and a cleaner can be the lawyer in the room.

My goal is to work on the economics of disability and employment in the Middle East. In Palestine, and in the region more broadly, people with disabilities are among the poorest, and most of them never find stable work. I want to produce research that helps governments and organisations change this.

I grew up in Hebron. My father drove a delivery truck and my mother raised seven children. None of them had been to university before me. When I was nineteen, I was injured in a fall at a construction site where I worked during the summer. I spent a year in rehabilitation and was told I would probably never walk again. I learned to walk with crutches after two years of physiotherapy.

After the injury, I went back to school, completed a bachelor's in economics at Birzeit University and worked for three years for a vocational training organisation, helping people with disabilities find jobs. I also volunteered with a sports club for wheelchair basketball, and I helped organise a campaign to make public buildings in Hebron accessible.

I came to Lugano in 2026. My GPA is 3.03. Here I volunteer with an association that tests the accessibility of restaurants and shops and publishes the results online.

Education changed my life after the injury. I want to use it to change the lives of others.

At dinner I told her the answer was "too many". She laughed and said: "Then find a way to count them without counting." This was my first combinatorics problem, and in some way I am still solving it.

I grew up in Cluj. My parents are doctors, and they expected that I become a doctor too. I tried one year of medicine and I was miserable. Then I changed to mathematics at Babeș-Bolyai University. It was the best decision in my life.

During my bachelor I was the coordinator of the mathematics circle for high school students in Cluj, where we prepared students for olympiads. I also volunteered with an NGO which gives free lessons to Roma children in villages near Cluj. After graduating I taught mathematics for one year in a high school.

In Basel I study combinatorics and discrete probability. With my professor from Cluj I published two papers during my bachelor, on permutation patterns. My GPA here is 3.27.

After the master I want to do a PhD and later teach at university. I also want to start a mathematics circle for children in Basel who come from families without university background.

For me education is something to give further, like my grandmother gave me the buttons.

I began my Bachelor of Law at the University of St. Gallen in February 2026, after three years of full-time work, and I am determined to complete it. To do so, I need a stable financial basis for the next two and a half years.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,847. Tuition and semester fees at HSG are higher than at most Swiss universities and come to CHF 205 a month. My rent is CHF 911 for a furnished room that I found at short notice when I moved to St. Gallen; it is on a month-to-month basis, and the landlord has already said he may need it back in the spring.

My mother, who works part-time in a care home in Wil, earns around CHF 2,100 a month and gives me CHF 750 of it. It is far more than she can comfortably spare, and she does it because she never had the opportunity to study herself. I also receive a small scholarship of CHF 1,559 a year from my home municipality.

The difference between my expenses and my monthly support is CHF 1,097. HSG's first-year assessment is known for its intensity, and I have deliberately not taken a job during it, so that I can pass. From my second year, I plan to work part-time again.

An EduAll grant would give me the security to complete the assessment year, find a stable room, and continue towards my degree, expected in January 2029.

I came to Switzerland at eleven, when my mother received her residence permit after years of working here while I stayed with my grandmother in Ghana. I arrived speaking English and Twi, and I was placed in a class where I understood nothing. Swiss German was a wall. But I learned it, and when I finished secondary school, I did what was expected of a child in my position: a commercial apprenticeship.

I spent three years as an apprentice and then three more as a commercial employee in the legal department of an insurance company in St. Gallen. I prepared files, checked contracts and took minutes in meetings with lawyers. I noticed that I understood the cases better than I was supposed to. One of the lawyers, a woman who had also come to law late, encouraged me to take the university entrance exam. I passed it on my first attempt while working full-time.

At HSG, I am often the only person in the room whose parents did not go to university and who has already worked for a living. I see that as a strength. I know how organisations actually function, and I know what it means for a contract to affect a real person's income.

I want to specialise in labour and social insurance law, and eventually to work for an organisation that helps people, especially migrants, navigate the social insurance system, which I watched my mother struggle with for years.

Education, for me, is the chance my mother worked so hard to give me. I intend to use it well.

I also receive a small scholarship of CHF 1,559 a year from my home municipality.

I am twenty-three, I grew up between Kumasi and Wil, and I am the first person in my family to study at a university.

I came to Switzerland at eleven, when my mother received her residence permit after years of working here while I stayed with my grandmother in Ghana. I arrived speaking English and Twi, and I was placed in a class where I understood nothing. Swiss German was a wall. But I learned it, and when I finished secondary school, I did what was expected of a child in my position: a commercial apprenticeship.

I spent three years as an apprentice and then three more as a commercial employee in the legal department of an insurance company in St. Gallen. I prepared files, checked contracts and took minutes in meetings with lawyers. I noticed that I understood the cases better than I was supposed to. One of the lawyers, a woman who had also come to law late, encouraged me to take the university entrance exam. I passed it on my first attempt while working full-time.

I want to specialise in labour and social insurance law, and eventually to work for an organisation that helps people, especially migrants, navigate the social insurance system, which I watched my mother struggle with for years.

Education, for me, is the chance my mother worked so hard to give me. I intend to use it well.

In the interest of full transparency, I should begin with what I have, before explaining what I lack.

My father, who runs a car-parts shop in Sulaymaniyah, has supported me throughout my studies. Our family's income is around CHF 1,750 a month, and he sends me CHF 340. I also have savings of CHF 5,134, most of which he gave me when I first came to Switzerland, as a reserve for emergencies. My monthly expenses are CHF 2,148, which leaves a modest gap of CHF 1,808. I do not have a job; my chemistry programme, with its long laboratory days, has made it very difficult to hold one, and I have never worked before.

Two things have changed this year. First, in April my older brother was seriously injured in a road accident. He needed several operations, and my family has been paying for private treatment, which the public system could not provide in time. My father has told me that he may have to reduce what he sends me from the new year.

Second, I have lost my housing. The owner of my flat in St. Johann is selling it, and I must leave by the end of November. I will need to pay a deposit on a new room and, most likely, a higher rent than the CHF 1,055 I pay now.

My savings were meant for emergencies, and this year has produced two at once. I am applying to EduAll so that I can finish my degree in July 2028 without asking my family for money they now need for my brother.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

The first time I saw snow was on the Münsterplatz in Basel, in December 2023. I was nineteen, it was eleven at night, and I had just come out of the laboratory after my first successful synthesis. I remember standing there, looking at the snow falling on the cathedral, and thinking that I had come a very long way from my father's shop.

I grew up in Sulaymaniyah, in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, in a family where nobody had studied beyond secondary school. My father left school at fourteen to support his siblings. My mother never went to school at all. They have always said that my education is their project too.

My childhood was marked by instability. In 2014, when I was ten, the war with ISIS brought thousands of displaced families to our city, and for a year our house was shared with three families of relatives from Mosul. I learned then what it means to lose everything, and how much people depend on each other.

In Basel, I have found a second community. I help organise the Kurdish Students' Society, where we run study groups and welcome events for new students, and I help newly arrived Kurdish families in our neighbourhood with official letters.

My studies have been demanding. My GPA is 2.93, and I have had semesters where I struggled, particularly in physical chemistry, where the German terminology still slows me down. But I have completed 24 courses, and in the laboratory I have found where I belong.

After my bachelor's, I want to do a master's in environmental chemistry and work on water and soil contamination in Kurdistan, where oil production has poisoned land that families have farmed for generations.

I will be completely open about my finances, because I think my application should be judged on accurate information.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,955, including CHF 984 in rent for a room in a shared flat in Lausanne and CHF 245 in health insurance. I earn CHF 1,173 a month as a laboratory technician at a research institute in Épalinges, working the maximum hours my permit allows. ## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I am thirty-one years old, a biochemist in training, and a person who was raised by an aunt, a grandmother and a whole village.

My parents both died when I was twelve, within a year of each other, from illnesses that were treatable but not treated. I went to live with my aunt in Kisumu, who took in three children in addition to her own. She had trained as a teacher at a college, but in our family no one had ever been to a university. When I was admitted to Maseno University, she sold two of her goats to pay my first fees.

After my bachelor's degree I worked for seven years as a laboratory technician at a malaria research station near Kisumu. I ran assays, maintained mosquito colonies and trained younger technicians. I also co-founded a community science club that brought secondary school students into the laboratory on Saturdays, many of them girls who had never seen a microscope.

In 2025 I came to Lausanne for a Master's in Molecular Life Sciences, focusing on biochemistry. It has been an extraordinary experience. My GPA is 3.78, with an average of 98.0, and my supervisor has encouraged me to apply for doctoral positions. My thesis examines how the malaria parasite regulates its metabolism under drug pressure, a question I first encountered in Kisumu.

In Lausanne I help coordinate the East African community association's mentoring programme for new students.

My goal is to lead a research group in East Africa working on drug resistance in malaria. For me, education is the repayment of a debt to my aunt and to every person who decided that an orphan from Kisumu was worth investing in.

In summer 2025 I stood for the first time on the Gemmi pass, at 2,300 metres, with a net in my hand and a cold wind in my face. Around me there were hundreds of butterflies, of species I knew only from books. I sat on a stone and I cried a little. Not from sadness. From the feeling that I finally arrived where I wanted to be.

The way to there was long. I grew up in Brăila, in eastern Romania. My father was an engineer at the shipyard and my mother a chemistry teacher, but after the shipyard closed my father started to drink, and our home became a place I did not want to be. At seventeen I left and moved to my aunt in Bucharest. I finished high school while working in a supermarket in the evenings.

I studied biology in Bucharest and worked in parallel all the time: in a pet shop, in a laboratory for water analysis, later as field assistant in a project on the Danube Delta. There I discovered insects, and how they tell us everything about the health of an ecosystem.

After some years of work I decided to do a master abroad. I came to Bern in 2025. My GPA is 3.35. My thesis is about how the butterflies of the Alpine meadows react to the earlier melting of snow.

After my master I want to do a PhD and work in conservation of insects, maybe in Switzerland, maybe back in the Danube Delta.

For me education was always the way out, and now it is the way forward.

My financial need is small, and I want to say this first. I study the Master in History part-time. My expenses are CHF 1,757 per month. I earn CHF 1,947 as a research assistant for a professor at the History department and as a teacher at a Saturday Vietnamese school, about 17 hours a week together. My spouse, who owns a small Vietnamese restaurant in Zurich with a household income of about CHF 4,940, gives CHF 370 for my part of our costs. I have no savings.

So why do I apply? The restaurant is our only family income besides my work, and since the construction work on our street started this spring, we have lost about a third of our customers. The work will continue until summer 2027.

And in 2027/28 I must spend several weeks in archives in Paris and Aix-en-Provence, because my research is on colonial documents about Vietnam. During these weeks I cannot work, so my income will go down to about CHF 1,190 on average, and I will miss around CHF 197 per month, plus the travel.

A grant, even a small one, would allow me to do this archive work and would mean that my studies are not a burden on the restaurant in a difficult year.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My goal is to write the history of ordinary Vietnamese people under French colonial rule, using documents that no Vietnamese researcher has read before. Most of these archives are in France, written in French, and until now mostly read by Western historians.

I am 44 years old. I grew up in Nam Dinh, in the north. My parents were rice farmers, and I was the first in the family to go to university. I studied journalism in Hanoi and worked for sixteen years as a journalist and later editor for a history magazine. I led a team of six writers. We published stories about villages, old crafts, and people forgotten in official history.

In 2019 I moved to Zurich, where my spouse had opened a restaurant. I learned German and French, and I volunteered at a Vietnamese language school for children every Saturday. In 2026 I started my master's at the University of Zurich.

My first semester went well, my GPA is 3.6, and I have already published two articles in history journals, based on work I began as a journalist.

After the master I want to do a PhD. I would like to make these archives accessible to Vietnamese readers, and to write books for the public, not only for academics.

For me education means to give back to my people their own stories.

I study Biology part-time at the University of Basel, and I work about 19 hours a week in a warehouse in Basel. I earn CHF 2,113 a month. My grandfather had a pomegranate orchard outside Kandahar. When I was a boy, I spent every summer there. He showed me how to graft branches, and which insects were good and which were bad for the trees. I asked him why some trees gave fruit and others did not. He said, "Ask the soil." I think biology started there for me.

My parents never went to school. My father was a mechanic and my mother raised eight children. I finished school in Kandahar and worked as a laboratory assistant in a small agricultural office, testing soil and seeds for farmers. When the security situation became impossible, I left. After some difficult years, I came to Switzerland in 2019 to join my wife, who has lived in Basel since she was a child.

For five years I worked in a warehouse, full-time, and learned German in the evenings. I also volunteered as an interpreter for Afghan families at a migrant counselling office. In 2025, at thirty-one, I passed the university admission exam and started Biology at the University of Basel.

My first year went very well. I have a GPA of 3.66 and an average of 95.8. I love the laboratory work. I want to specialise in plant biology and soil science.

My dream is to help Afghan farmers one day, maybe through an international organisation. Afghanistan has good soil and hard-working people, but very little knowledge support.

For me education is the promise I made to my grandfather's trees.

Herat is an old city of blue tiles and gardens, and for a short time in my life it was a city where girls could study. I was lucky to be young in that time. My father was a teacher of literature and my mother a midwife, and they wanted all their daughters to go to university.

I studied economics in Herat. In 2017, during an internship in Kabul, a bomb exploded near our building. I was injured in my back and my left leg. Since then I have chronic pain and difficulty walking long distances. After my degree I worked for three years for an international organisation, managing small loans for women's businesses.

After 2021, women in Afghanistan could no longer work or study. I continued to teach girls in secret in my home in Herat, economics and English, for one year. Then it became too dangerous. In 2022 I was admitted to a preparation programme at the University of Fribourg, and I came to Switzerland with a student permit.

Studying in a new language, with pain, was very hard. But I am close now. My thesis examines how women's employment changes after conflicts, comparing Afghanistan, Iraq and Bosnia.

I hope to work for an international organisation or a research institute on gender and economic policy. When Afghanistan opens again for women, I want to be ready.

I am in the first year of my Master's in Biology at the University of Zurich, which I study part-time. My thesis is due in January 2030.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,402. Rent is CHF 1,222 for a room in a shared flat in Wipkingen, tuition CHF 203, health insurance CHF 420. EduAll's support would let me move without panic, keep my working hours reasonable and finish my master's on time.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Cassava feeds more than 500 million people in Africa. In my village near Nsukka, it was what we ate almost every day. When I was twelve, a disease went through the fields. The leaves turned yellow and twisted, and the roots were small and bitter. That year my family ate once a day. My father, a farmer, did not know what had happened, and no one came to explain it.

That disease was cassava mosaic virus. Today it is the subject of my master's thesis, in a plant virology group at the University of Zurich. I am studying how resistance genes behave in cassava varieties grown by smallholder farmers.

I am the first in my family to go to university. I studied biology at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka, and worked five years as a research assistant at an agricultural research institute. I co-authored a paper on virus-resistant cassava lines. I also taught farmers in extension programmes how to recognise infected plants.

When a political conflict in our region turned violent in 2021, our family home was burned. We lost everything. I left Nigeria in 2022. My asylum application was rejected, because the violence was not directed at me personally, but I was provisionally admitted, since a return to my region is not considered safe. After a difficult year I was admitted to UZH.

In Zurich I volunteer with a food-sharing association, collecting leftover food from bakeries, and I help coordinate the Nigerian community's welcome group for new students.

After my master's I want to do a PhD on plant disease resistance and then return to Nigeria to work on crop protection for small farmers.

For me, biology is not abstract. It is the difference between eating once a day and three times.

I will explain my money honestly. My costs are CHF 1,633 per month, it is not so much because I live in a small room in a student house in Lausanne, CHF 657 with everything. I work as a cleaner in a school in the evenings and earn CHF 746. My older brother works as electrician in Doha, Qatar. His family has about CHF 1,400 per month, and he send me CHF 360. *Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother could not read, but she could count very fast. She sold eggs and vegetables at the market in our village near Savar, and she did all the calculation in her head. She always told me: "If you can count, nobody can cheat you. If you can read, nobody can lie to you." She died in 2015. I think of her every day.

I started to work in a garment factory when I was fourteen, because we needed the money. In 2013 I was working in Rana Plaza. When the building collapsed, I was on the third floor. I was under the concrete for eleven hours before they found me. Many of my friends died. I had injuries in my arm, but I was lucky.

After this, I decided I will not go back to the factory. With the help of an NGO I finished my school, and I started to work for them as a community health worker, visiting families of injured workers and teaching about hygiene and nutrition. I did this for six years.

In 2023, I came to Lausanne to study Public Health. It was very hard, because I did not speak French. I learned day and night. Now I have GPA 3.2 and I finish my bachelor this winter.

Also in Lausanne I am active in the Bangladeshi association, I help women who are new here to find doctors and to understand the health insurance.

I want to work in occupational health, for the safety of workers in factories. What happened in Rana Plaza should never happen again.

My parents did not go to university. My father drives trucks between Bulgaria and Germany, and my mother works in Germany as a live-in carer for an elderly woman. Together they earn about CHF 6,780, which is a good income for our region, but they work very hard for it, far from home.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Vidin is the poorest region of Bulgaria, maybe of the whole EU. My town has lost half its population since I was born. When I was a child, most of my friends' parents worked abroad, and the children stayed with grandparents. I was one of them. My parents left when I was eight, and my grandmother raised me.

My grandmother kept chickens, and one summer many of them died of a disease. Nobody knew what it was. The vet came from the city once, took samples, and never called back. I was thirteen and I read everything I could find about bird diseases on my phone. That is when I became interested in microbes.

I came to Basel in February 2025 to study microbiology. My parents were very proud: I am the first in our family to study at a university. But the first year was very difficult. My German was only B1 when I arrived, and the lectures were fast. My GPA is 2.7. I know this is not high, but it has improved every semester.

I have not yet had the time or the courage to join clubs or volunteer. I spend my days in lectures and in the library, and my evenings with German exercises.

I want to work in veterinary or food microbiology, maybe in a laboratory that protects animals and people from infectious diseases. I would like one day to go back to north-west Bulgaria, where such knowledge is badly missing.

Education for me means that, one day, my own family will not have to be split between countries to earn a living.

My goal is to work for a development bank, on financing for small businesses in North Africa. In Morocco, most small enterprises never get a bank loan. They grow slowly, or they die. I want to change this, even a little.

I grew up in Meknes. My father sold spices in the medina and my mother did not work outside the house. My father died when I was fifteen, and I became the one who helped my mother with my younger brothers. I worked in the shop after school. Nobody in my family studied before me.

After my bachelor in economics in Fès, I worked seven years in a microcredit association in Meknes, first as loan officer and then as branch assistant. I met hundreds of women and men who had good ideas and no capital. I saw also the dangers of microcredit when it is badly designed.

I came to Neuchâtel in 2025 for the master, because the programme has a good focus on development economics and it is in French. I am writing now my master thesis on the effect of microcredit interest rates on small business survival in Morocco, with data from my old employer.

For me education is the tool to understand why some people succeed and others not, and to make the system more fair.

In my first lecture, in epidemiology, I understood maybe one word out of ten. I cried in the toilet afterwards. For the whole first year I was translating every slide with my phone. I failed two exams and passed others only just.

But something changed this year. I found a study group, three Swiss students who explain things to me in simple German, and I help them with the statistics, which I understand well. My German is now B2. My last exams were my best ever. I believe my grades will rise.

Why public health? In my estate in Nairobi, when I was sixteen, there was a cholera outbreak. Our neighbour's baby died. It was because of the water, and everybody knew it, and nobody did anything. I want to be the person who does something.

I don't have a long CV. I did not have jobs or big activities before, I was in school and then preparing to come here. But I have a family who believes in me and a clear goal.

Education means to me that my siblings will see that it is possible. I really, really want to finish this.

I study Environmental Science at the University of Geneva, part-time since 2024, and I work about 23 hours a week at the reception of a sports centre, earning CHF 2,583 a month.

My parents both work in Geneva. My mother is a nanny for a family in Champel and my father a driver for a delivery company. Together they earn around CHF 5,000 a month and give me CHF 240. My expenses are CHF 1,981, including CHF 1,008 for a room in Plainpalais.

I moved out of my parents' flat in 2024 because it has two rooms for five people, and my two younger brothers needed the space. That is also when I started working so many hours. Since then I have lived in three different sublets; the current one ends in December.

From September 2027 I want to study full-time and finish in July 2028 instead of January 2029. My bachelor thesis on urban biodiversity needs field surveys through the spring, and I cannot do them with 23 hours at the reception. I will keep only the Sunday shifts, about CHF 560 a month, which leaves CHF 1,181 a month uncovered.

An EduAll grant would let me make this switch, find a stable room, and finish my degree a semester earlier.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother has cared for other people's children in Geneva for sixteen years. She has taught three Swiss children to read, to ride a bicycle, to swim. She never went to university, and neither did my father. When I was a child, she used to take me with her to the parks where she worked, and she always said: "One day, you will have your own garden."

I was born in Batangas, in the Philippines, and came to Geneva at twelve to join my parents. I did not speak French. I spent my first year in a welcome class, and I remember the feeling of standing at the edge of every conversation. But I learned fast, and I finished the Collège with good grades.

At university I discovered environmental science, and especially coastal ecosystems. In Batangas, the coral reefs where my grandfather fished are dying. My bachelor's thesis is on the effect of rising water temperature on seagrass meadows, using data from the Philippines.

I am president of the Filipino Students' Association in Geneva, and every year we organise a cultural day for the Filipino community, which is large in Geneva but almost invisible. I also help younger Filipino teenagers with their homework in French.

After my bachelor I want to do a master's in marine ecology, and one day work on coastal protection in South-East Asia.

Education, for me, is the garden my mother talked about.

Every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon I tutor mathematics to secondary school students in Neuchâtel, and on Saturdays I work in a bakery. Together this gives me CHF 825 a month. My two older brothers work as seafarers on cruise ships. Their incomes together are around CHF 3,270, and they send me CHF 800 every month, because I am the first in our family who has the chance to study at this level, and they want me to succeed.

Last year this happened for almost four months, and I had to borrow from friends to pay rent. It was a very frightening time. I was afraid every day that I would have to go home.

My master's in mathematics runs until July 2028. I am asking EduAll to help me build a small foundation for these periods without income, so that I do not have to leave my studies because of the rhythm of the sea.

In Banda Aceh, before I came here, I taught mathematics for five years at an Islamic boarding school for girls. Many of my students were orphans. Some of them had lost their parents, like I did, in the tsunami of 2004. I was six. I remember the water, the sound of it, and then the silence. My father and my little sister were never found.

My mother raised my brothers and me alone, selling cakes in front of our house. None of us went to university, except me, many years later, with a scholarship from a local foundation. I studied mathematics at Syiah Kuala University. Mathematics was my safe place. Numbers do not change, they do not disappear. When everything around me was uncertain, a proof was always true.

At the boarding school, I also started, as a volunteer, a small afternoon club where girls could do mathematics puzzles and games. Some of them had never been told that they were good at mathematics. By the end, three of them went to university to study science.

I came to Neuchâtel in February 2026. French is still very difficult for me, and I study every evening with a dictionary. But my first semester went well, GPA 3.46. I discovered statistics, and I want to specialise in it.

My dream is to go back to Aceh and train mathematics teachers, especially for girls' schools. I want the girls of Aceh to know that numbers belong to them too.

The Mesopotamian marshes, where the Tigris and Euphrates meet, were once one of the largest wetlands in the world. In the 1990s they were drained almost completely, and a whole way of life disappeared with them. When I was a child in Basra, my grandmother still told stories of the reed houses and the water buffalo. When I finally saw the marshes myself, as an engineer in 2010, they were cracked mud. That image is the reason I study environmental science.

My parents ran a small grocery shop and never studied. I was the first in my family at university, where I studied civil engineering. For six years I worked on water projects in southern Iraq, including a restoration project in the marshes. Two articles came out of that work, on salinity and on water flow in restored areas.

I came to Switzerland in 2012 through marriage. Those years were not easy: my qualifications were not recognised, I worked in cleaning and in kitchens, and the marriage ended badly. I also spent those years volunteering as an Arabic interpreter for a women's shelter in Zurich, which taught me how many people are rebuilding their lives quietly, as I was.

In February 2026 I started my master's in Environmental Science at the University of Zurich, at forty. My first semester, GPA 2.98, was a return to academic work after eighteen years, and I expect my results to rise as I regain my footing.

My goal is to work on wetland restoration and water governance in the Middle East. The marshes are slowly coming back, and they need people who understand both the science and the region.

I study Mathematics part-time at the University of Fribourg, and I work about 22 hours a week in a supermarket, where I earn CHF 2,515 a month. My monthly costs are CHF 1,890. What would have happened if I had stayed in Mosul? I ask myself this question sometimes. I was sixteen when I came to Switzerland in 2010 to join my father, who had been working here for some years. Four years later, Mosul was taken by ISIS. Many of my school friends who stayed are dead or scattered.

My parents did not go to university. My father left school at twelve. When I arrived in Bulle, I spoke Arabic and some English, no French. I was placed in a class for newcomers, and then did an apprenticeship as a logistician, because everybody told me that was realistic for someone like me. I worked for four years in a warehouse.

But I always liked mathematics. In the evenings I did the maturité for adults, and at twenty-nine I started university in Fribourg. I love it. My thesis is on graph colouring problems.

For many years I have volunteered with a football club for refugee children in Bulle, as a coach on Saturdays. Many of them are in the same situation I was in.

I am in my second year of the Bachelor's in Chemistry at the University of Geneva, which I study part-time. At forty-two, I am one of the oldest students in my programme, and my financial circumstances reflect a life that has already been long and full of responsibilities.

I work about 20 hours a week as a laboratory assistant for a water-testing company in Vernier and earn CHF 2,273 a month. My wife works as a nursing assistant at the Geneva University Hospitals, and our household income is around CHF 4,400 a month; she contributes CHF 240 towards my share of our costs. My own monthly expenses come to CHF 1,678, with a modest share of our rent of CHF 661 in a cooperative flat in Les Libellules.

The second half of my degree is considerably more laboratory-intensive, with practical courses that take entire afternoons, four days a week. From September 2027 I intend to study full-time, which would allow me to graduate in January 2029 rather than a year later. I will keep one day a week with my employer, which reduces my income to about CHF 1,010.

An EduAll grant would cover the resulting gap and allow me to keep studying at full pace through the laboratory years, without placing the weight on my wife's salary, which also supports her elderly mother in Morocco.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was ten, I spent my summers in the tanneries of Fès, carrying skins between the dye pits for a few dirhams a day. The smell was terrible, and the colours were magical. I remember asking an old tanner why the water in one pit turned red and in the other yellow. He laughed and said "God's chemistry." I wanted to know the chemistry behind God's chemistry.

I left school at fourteen to work full-time; my father was a porter in the medina and my mother could not read. Nobody in my family had studied. For many years I worked in the tanneries and then in a textile factory in Casablanca, where I saw workers lose their health to chemicals that nobody explained to them.

In 2008 I came to Geneva with my wife. I worked in construction and cleaning, learned French and, at thirty-six, began evening classes to obtain my maturité. It took four years. In 2025 I entered the University of Geneva. My first three semesters have gone better than I dared hope: my GPA is 3.64, with an average of 95.1.

For ten years I have been active in the Moroccan association of Geneva, where I organise Arabic literacy classes for adults who, like my mother, never had the chance to learn to read.

My goal is to work in environmental and occupational chemistry, on reducing toxic exposure in industries like the tanneries of my childhood. I would also like to show the young people of my community that it is never too late to start.

Education, for me, is the answer to the question that old tanner could not answer.

I am in my second year of the Bachelor's in Chemistry at the University of Geneva, which I study part-time. At forty-two, I am one of the oldest students in my programme, and my financial circumstances reflect a life that has already been long and full of responsibilities.

I work about 20 hours a week as a laboratory assistant for a water-testing company in Vernier and earn CHF 2,273 a month. My wife works as a nursing assistant at the Geneva University Hospitals, and our household income is around CHF 4,400 a month; she contributes CHF 240 towards my share of our costs. My own monthly expenses come to CHF 1,678, with a modest share of our rent of CHF 661 in a cooperative flat in Les Libellules.

The second half of my degree is considerably more laboratory-intensive, with practical courses that take entire afternoons, four days a week. From September 2027 I intend to study full-time, which would allow me to graduate in January 2029 rather than a year later. I will keep one day a week with my employer, which reduces my income to about CHF 1,010.

An EduAll grant would cover the resulting gap and allow me to keep studying at full pace through the laboratory years, without placing the weight on my wife's salary, which also supports her elderly mother in Morocco.
STU000055.personal_statement:
When I was ten, I spent my summers in the tanneries of Fès, carrying skins between the dye pits for a few dirhams a day. The smell was terrible, and the colours were magical. I remember asking an old tanner why the water in one pit turned red and in the other yellow. He laughed and said "God's chemistry." I wanted to know the chemistry behind God's chemistry.

I left school at fourteen to work full-time; my father was a porter in the medina and my mother could not read. Nobody in my family had studied. For many years I worked in the tanneries and then in a textile factory in Casablanca, where I saw workers lose their health to chemicals that nobody explained to them.

In 2008 I came to Geneva with my wife. I worked in construction and cleaning, learned French and, at thirty-six, began evening classes to obtain my maturité. It took four years. In 2025 I entered the University of Geneva. My first three semesters have gone better than I dared hope: my GPA is 3.64, with an average of 95.1.

For ten years I have been active in the Moroccan association of Geneva, where I organise Arabic literacy classes for adults who, like my mother, never had the chance to learn to read.

My goal is to work in environmental and occupational chemistry, on reducing toxic exposure in industries like the tanneries of my childhood. I would also like to show the young people of my community that it is never too late to start.

Education, for me, is the answer to the question that old tanner could not answer.

I will list everything, because I want the committee to see the full picture.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,410. Rent is CHF 1,328 for a small ground-floor studio in Zurich-Wollishofen. I chose it because I have limited use of my right hand and arm, and I cannot manage stairs with shopping and laboratory bags easily. Health insurance is CHF 470.

I also have savings of CHF 12,371. This is what I saved in eight years of work as a hospital laboratory technician in Zurich before starting my doctorate. I am using these savings to cover the gap of CHF 2,020 per month, but at this rate they will last less than a year, and my doctorate runs until July 2029.

I have applied for a Swiss National Science Foundation fellowship for next year. If I receive it, I will inform EduAll immediately. Until then, a grant would slow down the loss of my savings and give me time.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In ten years I want to lead a research group on antimicrobial resistance in South-East Asia, and train young Filipino scientists in modern microbiology.

I studied microbiology in Manila and worked as a public health laboratory scientist. I was also active in a community health organisation that documented the health effects of mining on indigenous communities in Mindanao. In 2013 several of our members were "red-tagged", accused of being communist rebels. In 2014 I was attacked on my way home. The attack damaged the nerves of my right arm. I fled to Switzerland and was recognised as a refugee.

I started again from nothing. I learned German, had my degree recognised, and worked for eight years as a laboratory technician in a hospital in Zurich, learning to work with my left hand and with adapted equipment. I also helped found a support group for Filipino workers in Zurich, many of them domestic workers without anyone to turn to.

In 2025 I started my doctorate on resistance genes in hospital wastewater. My first two semesters have gone very well, with top marks in the doctoral courses.

I know I am older than most doctoral students. But I believe my experience, as a scientist, as a refugee and as a person with a disability, makes me a better researcher and teacher.

I am entering the second year of my Master's in Environmental Science at the University of Geneva, which I have so far studied part-time. I am applying to EduAll to complete it full-time from September 2027, with my thesis due in July 2028.

My monthly expenses are CHF 2,287, including CHF 985 for a small studio in Carouge and CHF 560 for health insurance. *Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My ambition is to work on climate adaptation in cities, making urban spaces cooler, greener and more accessible for everyone, including people who, like me, navigate them with a disability.

I was born in Lahore and came to Geneva at the age of eight, when my father took up a position as a driver for the Pakistani mission. He had studied commerce at university in Lahore, but in Geneva he drove diplomats for twenty years. He never complained. He simply insisted that we study.

I was diagnosed with retinitis pigmentosa at sixteen. It is a slow narrowing of vision, and it will continue. I was told I should perhaps avoid science. I chose environmental science anyway, with a bachelor's at the University of Geneva and now the master's programme. My thesis examines heat exposure in Geneva's suburbs, where housing is dense and green spaces are rare, and I published a first article on this topic from my bachelor's research.

For four years I chaired the student commission on accessibility at the University of Geneva, where we worked with the administration to improve accessible materials and exam accommodations for students with disabilities. I also volunteer with an association that trains guide dogs, helping at weekend training sessions in parks.

After graduating, I would like to work for a cantonal environment office or an international organisation on urban climate adaptation. I intend to make the case, from the inside, that inclusive cities and climate-resilient cities are the same project.

Right now, on paper, I am not in deficit. I want to say that first, because it is true, and because the reason I am writing is that this will not stay true for long.

I study Biology part-time and work about 15 hours a week, childminding for two families and cleaning a small office. I earn CHF 1,700 a month. For the last six years I have lived with my partner in his flat in Bern-Bethlehem. He earns around CHF 5,000 a month and pays CHF 230 towards my share of the rent. My expenses are CHF 1,598, and I have CHF 2,024 saved.

In June, we decided to separate. It is peaceful, but it means that at the end of December I must move out, and his support will end. I have been looking for a room since July. Everything I can afford is far from the university, and every landlord asks for a deposit of two or three months' rent, which is more than my savings.

In 2027/28 I also have to retake one exam and do the laboratory courses of the third year, and I will have to reduce my work to about CHF 930 a month. My costs will not become smaller; probably bigger. My bachelor ends in January 2030.

I am forty-one. I have started over before. I am not afraid of work. But I cannot work enough hours to pay for a room in Bern alone and still pass my exams. Please help me cross this part.

I came to Switzerland in 2008 to work as a nanny for a family in Geneva. I was twenty-three. I sent almost all my salary home to my parents in Leyte, who are rice farmers and never finished school, and to pay for my younger brothers' education. Both of them are now engineers. I am very proud of that.

For nine years, I looked after other people's children. I loved them, but I always had a dream of my own. When I was a child, I collected insects in jars and drew them in a notebook. My teacher said I should become a biologist. We laughed, because in our village nobody became anything like that.

In 2013, when typhoon Haiyan destroyed our village, I lost my grandmother and our house. I felt helpless in Geneva. I organised a collection among the Filipino workers in Switzerland, and we sent more than two tons of goods and money. That was the first time I led something big. Afterwards I became coordinator of the Filipino domestic workers' association in Bern, where I still help women who have problems with employers, pay or permits.

In 2025, after years of evening school, I started biology at the University of Bern. It is very hard. My grades are low, GPA 2.54, and I need to retake one exam. I work slowly, and many students are half my age. But I have never missed a class.

I want to work in entomology, maybe in a museum or in a laboratory on pollinators. I still have the notebook with the insect drawings. I keep it on my desk.

Right now, on paper, I am not in deficit. I want to say that first, because it is true, and because the reason I am writing is that this will not stay true for long.

I study Biology part-time and work about 15 hours a week, childminding for two families and cleaning a small office. I earn CHF 1,700 a month. For the last six years I have lived with my partner in his flat in Bern-Bethlehem. He earns around CHF 5,000 a month and pays CHF 230 towards my share of the rent. My expenses are CHF 1,598, and I have CHF 2,024 saved.

In June, we decided to separate. It is peaceful, but it means that at the end of December I must move out, and his support will end. I have been looking for a room since July. Everything I can afford is far from the university, and every landlord asks for a deposit of two or three months' rent, which is more than my savings.

In 2027/28 I also have to retake one exam and do the laboratory courses of the third year, and I will have to reduce my work to about CHF 930 a month. My costs will not become smaller; probably bigger. My bachelor ends in January 2030.

I am forty-one. I have started over before. I am not afraid of work. But I cannot work enough hours to pay for a room in Bern alone and still pass my exams. Please help me cross this part.
STU000061.personal_statement:
I came to Switzerland in 2008 to work as a nanny for a family in Geneva. I was twenty-three. I sent almost all my salary home to my parents in Leyte, who are rice farmers and never finished school, and to pay for my younger brothers' education. Both of them are now engineers. I am very proud of that.

For nine years, I looked after other people's children. I loved them, but I always had a dream of my own. When I was a child, I collected insects in jars and drew them in a notebook. My teacher said I should become a biologist. We laughed, because in our village nobody became anything like that.

In 2013, when typhoon Haiyan destroyed our village, I lost my grandmother and our house. I felt helpless in Geneva. I organised a collection among the Filipino workers in Switzerland, and we sent more than two tons of goods and money. That was the first time I led something big. Afterwards I became coordinator of the Filipino domestic workers' association in Bern, where I still help women who have problems with employers, pay or permits.

In 2025, after years of evening school, I started biology at the University of Bern. It is very hard. My grades are low, GPA 2.54, and I need to retake one exam. I work slowly, and many students are half my age. But I have never missed a class.

I want to work in entomology, maybe in a museum or in a laboratory on pollinators. I still have the notebook with the insect drawings. I keep it on my desk.

I came to Geneva at nine with my parents, who emigrated from Vietnam to join my uncle. I grew up here, went to school here, and I have a C permit. My father was an engineer in Saigon; here he worked in a factory.

My brother had just started his business, so I stayed home and cared for both of them, for sixteen years. I never had a paid job until 2024, when my brother gave me work in his salon. At night, I read physics: first popular books, then textbooks, then online university courses.

After my parents died, in 2018 and 2020, I started a bachelor in physics at the University of Geneva, and now the master. I published my first co-authored article this year, on optical properties of thin films.

I am doctoral student in Materials Science at University of Fribourg since September 2025. When I started, my position was paid from a research project of my supervisor for one year. This project finished in July 2026 and the new project proposal is still in evaluation, the answer is expected only in spring 2028. My supervisor wrote a letter which confirm that at this moment there is no salary for me from the department, I attached it to this application. So since September I am practically without funding, but I want to continue because I am in the middle of my experiments.

My monthly costs are CHF 1,925. The biggest part is my rent, CHF 1,009 for a small studio plus CHF 126 for electricity and heating. I looked for a room in shared flat but in Fribourg many landlords don't want to rent to a student without a work contract. Also I pay CHF 70 each month for materials and samples which the lab cannot cover anymore after the project ended.

For income, I have CHF 357 per month as teaching assistant in the practical course for bachelor students (about three hours per week). My two older brothers live in Istanbul and work together in a textile workshop. Together they earn around CHF 760 and they send me CHF 170 each month. They have their own families, so it is really the maximum they can give. My parents are still in Homs and they cannot support me, in the opposite, sometimes they need help.

So I have a gap of CHF 1,398 every month and I have no savings. I applied for two other scholarships (one from the university, one from a private foundation) but the university one is only for bachelor and master students and the other one I did not receive answer yet.

Without support, I will have to stop my doctorate and search full-time work, and I will lose my permit as student. With EduAll grant I can bridge this period until the new project is decided, and continue my research. I will inform you immediately if I receive other funding.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I was born in Homs, Syria in 2002. My father is electrician and my mother is housewife, nobody in my family studied in university before me. During the war our neighbourhood was damaged and we moved two times inside the city. I remember that in many winters we have only few hours of electricity per day. Maybe this is why I became interested in energy and materials, I wanted to understand how we can store energy better and cheaper.

I studied Materials Engineering at Damascus University and after I came to Fribourg in 2023 for master in Chemistry with specialisation in materials. The system is very different from Syria, the exams also, but in research I felt immediately that I am in my place. My master thesis on porous polymer membranes became one article, and one conference paper, both with my supervisor.

Now in my doctorate I work on low-cost materials for sodium-ion batteries. Sodium is much more available than lithium, and I think this can be important for countries like Syria where the energy grid is broken and people need cheap solutions for storage.

Next to my studies I am active in the Syrian association in Fribourg. I help new arrived families with translation of letters from the commune and with registration of children in school. I know how it feels when you receive a letter and you cannot understand it.

For me education is the only way I see to rebuild something, for me and for my country later. I don't want to stop at the middle because of money. I am ready to work hard, I just need some time until the funding situation is clear.

Nobody in my family went to university. I was the first. I studied Bengali literature in Dhaka and became a teacher, and I started to write a blog about religion, freedom and reason. I also volunteer as a translator for Bengali-speaking asylum seekers at a legal counselling service.

In 2024 I started Philosophy at the university. It is my dream. Reading Kant or Spinoza in French is very hard for me, but I am learning every day. My thesis is about freedom of expression and the duty of states to protect those who speak.

I will be honest with every number, because I have learned that honesty is the only thing that makes help possible.

I study my Master in Data Science part-time. For almost twenty years my life was the life of a wife at home, first in Morocco and then in Switzerland. When my marriage ended in 2021, I had nothing of my own except my C permit and a bachelor's degree from 2003 that I had never used. Today I have my first paid job: I work about 19 hours a week as a data assistant in an insurance office in St. Gallen, and I earn CHF 2,149 a month. I am proud of every franc of it.

My costs in St. Gallen are CHF 2,385 a month. The tuition at HSG is high, CHF 522 per month, and my small flat costs CHF 1,026 plus CHF 49 of heating. My brother in Casablanca, who works as a taxi driver and whose family lives on about CHF 1,910, sends me CHF 460. I also receive a scholarship of CHF 7,144 per year from a foundation for women in data and technology, and I want to declare it clearly. I have no savings.

From September 2027 I want to study full-time, so that I finish in July 2028 and not a year later. My thesis needs all my time. I will keep only a few hours at the insurance office, about CHF 790 a month, and I will miss CHF 1,135 a month.

After that, I will work in my field, for the first time in my life. I only need to reach that day.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Every Wednesday afternoon for eight years I sat in a small room of the Arabic women's association in St. Gallen and helped women fill out forms. Tax declarations. Health insurance. School letters. Many of them could not read German, some could not read at all. I became the woman who understands the papers. At first I did it as a volunteer because I was lonely. Then I realised that it was the only place where I felt useful.

I grew up in Casablanca. My father was a docker, my mother a housewife. I was the first in my family to go to university; I studied mathematics and graduated in 2003. Then I married, and my husband did not want me to work. I followed him to Switzerland in 2008. For years I lived inside four walls, and my German stayed very poor.

When the marriage ended, I was thirty-nine. People told me to find a cleaning job. Instead, with the help of the women's association, I took a German course, then a bridge course in statistics, and in 2025 I was admitted to the Master in Data Science at HSG. I was the oldest person in the room, and my German was the worst. But mathematics came back to me like an old friend. My GPA is 3.2.

My thesis uses data from social services to understand why so many migrant women do not claim the benefits they have a right to. I know the answer from the Wednesday afternoons. Now I want to prove it with numbers.

For me, education is freedom. I found it late, but I found it.

---

I want to be clear: my budget now is not in deficit. My older sister, who is nurse in Lausanne, and her husband, together earn about CHF 9,800, and they give me CHF 1,760 each month. I live in a small room in their flat, CHF 496. My costs are CHF 1,643. I have also CHF 10,749 of savings, from my years working as draftsperson in Manila and Dubai.

I stopped working in 2024 when I began EPFL, because architecture studio takes day and night. I finish in July 2028. After I will work again.

My parents are fishermen and never studied beyond elementary school. I was the first in my family to go to college. ## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

What does a mountain city do when its water runs out? In Baguio, where I grew up, this is not an abstract question. Every dry season, taps in our neighbourhood run dry for days. Families queue for water trucks. At the same time, the springs that once fed the city have been lost to construction and poor planning.

I was twelve when I first asked my father where the water in the ground comes from. He did not know; neither of my parents went to college. So I went to find out. I studied geology at the University of the Philippines Baguio, where I was the first in my family to graduate.

For four years I worked as a research assistant at a geotechnical company, mapping aquifers and landslide risks in the Cordillera. On weekends I volunteered with a local organisation teaching schoolchildren about water conservation, visiting mountain schools where children walked an hour to reach a water source.

I chose Neuchâtel because of its strength in hydrogeology, and especially karst systems, which are similar in some ways to the limestone formations near Baguio. My studies have gone well: I have a GPA of 3.23 and have completed 3 courses.

After my master's, I want to work on groundwater management for mountain cities in South-East Asia. No child in Baguio should have to queue for water that lies under their feet.

I must explain first my residence situation, because it is connected with my money. My student permit B expired in June 2026. In May 2025, I stood in a laboratory at the University of Zurich and saw a protein structure on the screen that I had purified myself, after six months of failed attempts. My supervisor shook my hand. I went outside, sat on a bench at the Irchel park and called my mother. She did not understand what a protein is, but she understood that I was happy.

I come from Faisalabad. My parents never went to school. My father sold cloth in the bazaar, and after he died in 2010, my uncle took care of our family. I was the only one of five children who finished college. I studied biochemistry at the University of Agriculture in Faisalabad, and then a master's in Lahore.

For four years I could not continue because the family needed me in the shop. But in the evenings I taught free chemistry classes to boys and girls in our mohalla who could not pay for tuition. I also organised blood donation camps with a youth group.

In 2024, at twenty-eight, I got the chance to come to Zurich. German is still very difficult for me. My courses are in English, but everything outside, the migration office, the landlord, the health insurance, is in German, and I often misunderstand letters.

My research is on enzymes that break down plastic. I want to go back to Pakistan one day and work on the plastic waste problem, which is terrible in our cities.

For me, education is the thing my father could not have, and that he wanted most for us.

For three years, every weekend and many evenings, I have worked as a nursing aide in a care home in Bern. I wash, feed and turn residents who can no longer do these things themselves. I earn CHF 1,079 a month, and together with CHF 130 that my parents send me from Accra, this has been exactly enough. My father is a pharmacist and my mother a midwife; their household income is around CHF 810, and they are also supporting my two younger sisters at university in Ghana.

But from January, my medical master's enters the clinical rotations. Each rotation lasts several weeks, full days in the hospital, with night and weekend duties. My employer has been kind, but a care home cannot schedule around a medical student's rotation plan. I will lose most of my shifts, and with them most of my income.

My monthly costs are CHF 1,648: a room in a shared flat in Länggasse for CHF 652, health insurance of CHF 235, tuition and the rest. I have kept them as low as I can.

What I am asking for is simple: the chance to spend my clinical years learning to be a doctor, and not calculating how many night shifts I need to pay my rent. I have worked for everything I have. I will keep working as much as the rotations allow. I just need a bridge until I qualify in January 2028.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

There is a resident at the care home, Frau M., who is ninety-three and does not remember my name. Every Saturday she asks me where I come from, and every Saturday I say "Ghana," and she smiles and says "so far." Last month she held my hand and said, "You have good hands for a doctor." She does not know I am studying medicine. I had never told her.

I grew up in Accra, in a house full of medicine: my father's pharmacy on the ground floor, my mother coming home from night shifts at the maternity ward with stories of births that went right and births that went wrong. When I was fourteen, a fire destroyed the pharmacy and most of our home. We lived with relatives for two years while my parents rebuilt everything from zero. I learned then that you can lose almost everything and still keep going.

I came to Switzerland at twenty-three, after working two years as a laboratory technician in Accra. I completed my bachelor of medicine at the University of Fribourg, while working the whole time, and now I am in the master's programme in Bern.

At the university, I was elected class representative for two years, and I co-founded a peer group for international medical students, who often feel very alone in the Swiss system. I also help organise health information evenings for the Ghanaian community in Bern.

I want to become a general practitioner, and later work in rural health in Ghana, where one doctor serves tens of thousands of people.

I have good hands, Frau M. says. I want to give them the chance to become a doctor's hands.

I began the Master's in Sociology at the University of Bern in February 2026. My monthly costs are CHF 2,215, of which CHF 976 is rent for a room in Bümpliz and CHF 415 is health insurance.

I work as a night receptionist at a youth hostel two nights a week, earning CHF 467. My older brother, a civil servant in Ibadan whose household income is around CHF 1,050, sends me CHF 233. The gap is CHF 1,515 a month.

My eyesight limits the kind of work I can do. I have oculocutaneous albinism, with low vision, and I rely on magnification software and large-print materials. Many student jobs, such as delivery, cashier work or anything involving reading small print quickly, are not possible for me. The reception job is one of the few that works.

A grant from EduAll would allow me to focus on my coursework and research without taking on more night shifts, which already leave me exhausted in morning seminars.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Let me introduce myself: a sociologist in training, from Ibadan, Nigeria, thirty-two years old, born with albinism.

In Nigeria, people with albinism are often seen as cursed or magical. As a child I was called names on the street; some people would not touch me. My parents, a market trader and a carpenter who had never gone to university, protected me as well as they could. My mother went to my school every term to explain to teachers why I needed to sit in the front row.

I studied sociology at the University of Ibadan, where I was the first person in my family to graduate. Then I worked for nine years for a disability rights organisation, first as a field officer and then as a programme officer, documenting discrimination against people with albinism and running awareness campaigns in schools.

My master's research will study how stigma against visible difference affects access to employment in West Africa and among African migrants in Europe.

I want to continue to a doctorate and then teach and research in Nigeria, where disability studies is still a young field. I want the next child with albinism in Ibadan to grow up hearing different words.

My parents, a market trader and a carpenter who had never gone to university, protected me as well as they could. My master's research will study how stigma against visible difference affects access to employment in West Africa and among African migrants in Europe.

The more pressing problem is housing. My room in Wipkingen, at CHF 1,003, is a sublet that ends in December, and the tenant has told me it will not be renewed. In Zurich, finding a room without Swiss references or a guarantor is extremely difficult, and every option requires a deposit I would have to take from my savings.

I could tutor more hours, and I will try. But ETH's master's courses in physics leave little room, and I do not want to repeat the mistake I made during my bachelor's, when I worked too much and my grades suffered.

An EduAll grant would give me a stable room and the time to finish my master's by July 2028.
STU000082.personal_statement:
For four years, every Friday, I taught physics to girls in a small community centre in Imbaba, one of Cairo's poorest neighbourhoods. None of them expected to study science. Most of their families expected them to marry at eighteen. On Fridays, we built circuits, dropped eggs from the roof, and measured the speed of falling things. One of those girls is now studying engineering at Cairo University.

I understand those girls because I was one of them. I grew up in Asyut, in Upper Egypt. My parents are teachers, and they believed in education, but our extended family did not believe in it for girls. When I was eighteen, relatives arranged an engagement for me. I refused, and I left for Cairo to study physics with almost no support. For two years, my family barely spoke to me. I paid for my studies by working in a call centre at night.

Today my parents are my strongest supporters. My mother keeps a photo of my ETH admission letter on her phone.

After my bachelor's, I worked for four years as a research assistant at the Egyptian National Research Centre, on solar materials, and taught at the community centre on Fridays. In 2026 I came to ETH for the Master's in Physics. My GPA is 3.42.

I want to work on renewable energy materials, and to return one day to Upper Egypt to teach, so that girls there know that physics is a door, not a wall.
