I am entering the seventh semester of my Bachelor's in Architecture at ETH Zurich, and I am applying to EduAll because my housing, which has made my studies affordable until now, is about to disappear.

For three years I have lived in a temporary-use building in Zurich-West, an old office block rented to students and artists at a low rent while it waits for demolition. My room costs CHF 482 a month. The demolition has now been scheduled for December 2026. On the open market, a room within reach of the ETH campus costs at least twice as much, and I will need a deposit.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,538. I earn CHF 656 a month as a part-time model-builder for an architecture office in Kreis 4. My cousin in Lahore, who runs a construction supply business with a household income of around CHF 850, sends me CHF 250 each month.

The last semester is also the most expensive. My bachelor's thesis project requires physical models, printing and material samples, and the studio schedule makes it impossible to work more hours.

A grant from EduAll would allow me to keep stable accommodation and finish my degree without compromising my final project.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Architecture matters because buildings outlive the people who design them, and they shape the lives of people who never chose them. I grew up in a one-room house in the old city of Lahore, with nine family members, one window and a courtyard we shared with four other families. That courtyard was everything: our kitchen, playground, meeting room. I have been thinking about courtyards ever since.

My father was a tailor and my mother never learned to read. I left school at fourteen to work in a construction crew, carrying bricks. At nineteen I became a site foreman, and over the next years I built houses, schools and a small health centre in Punjab. I learned how buildings are made, but I always had to follow drawings made by others, often badly adapted to the heat, the families and the way people really live.

I finished secondary school in evening classes at twenty-one. In 2023, at twenty-three, I was admitted to ETH Zurich. The first year was the hardest of my life: new language, new mathematics, and classmates who had never held a brick. I have completed 21 courses with a GPA of 3.26.

My thesis project is a design for affordable courtyard housing for low-income families in Lahore, using passive cooling and local brick. It is, in a way, a design for the house I grew up in.

After graduation, I want to complete a master's and then work on climate-adapted social housing in South Asia.

My financial situation depends almost entirely on factors outside my control, and I am applying to EduAll to give my studies a foundation that does not disappear overnight.

I study my Master in Psychology part-time, and I contribute CHF 2,002 a month myself, working about 18 hours a week as a community interpreter for a refugee support organisation in Neuchâtel. The work is meaningful, but my contract is renewed every three months, depending on the organisation's funding and the number of new arrivals.

My father, a software engineer, stayed in Lviv when my mother and I left Ukraine in 2022. He works for an IT company that serves foreign clients, and together my parents earn around CHF 3,060 a month. They send me CHF 360. In the past year his company has lost two major contracts, and staff in his department have already been let go. My mother, who is with me in Switzerland, has not been able to work in her profession here.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,140, including CHF 1,034 in rent and CHF 173 in tuition and semester fees. From September 2027 I intend to study full-time, which would allow me to finish in January 2029 instead of a year later; I would keep only about ten hours of interpreting a week, around CHF 1,130 a month. The resulting budget is balanced only if every other source continues, which is exactly what I cannot guarantee.

There is also the question of status. Protection status S is renewed year by year, and my plans depend on decisions that are not mine. An EduAll grant would give my final year the stability to be completed regardless of what happens elsewhere.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was nine, my grandmother, a school psychologist in Kyiv, let me sit in the corner of her office while she talked with a boy who had stopped speaking after his parents' divorce. I did not understand much of what was said. What I remember is that, by the end of the hour, he was laughing. I decided then that I wanted to do whatever she was doing.

I completed my bachelor's degree in psychology at Taras Shevchenko National University in Kyiv, writing my thesis on adolescent anxiety. When the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, my mother and I left within weeks and arrived in Neuchâtel that spring. I finished my degree remotely, sometimes submitting assignments from the waiting room of the cantonal migration office. In February 2026 I began the Master of Science in Psychology at the University of Neuchâtel, and I have now completed my first semester.

My work as an interpreter has shaped my studies more than anything I have read. I sit in rooms with doctors, social workers and families who have lost their homes, and I translate not just words but fear, exhaustion and sometimes silence. I have seen how often trauma goes unrecognised simply because nobody shares a language with the person in front of them.

This is what I want to change. My goal is to specialise in clinical psychology, with a focus on trauma in displaced children and adolescents, and to develop culturally adapted, low-threshold interventions that do not depend on a patient speaking the local language. Whether I eventually return to Ukraine or remain in Switzerland, there will be a generation of young people who need this kind of support for many years.

Education has been the one continuous thread through a period in which almost everything else was interrupted. I would be grateful if EduAll could help me protect it, so that I can complete my degree and put it to use where it is most needed.

When the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, my mother and I left within weeks and arrived in Neuchâtel that spring. I finished my degree remotely, sometimes submitting assignments from the waiting room of the cantonal migration office. In February 2026 I began the Master of Science in Psychology at the University of Neuchâtel, and I have now completed my first semester.

My work as an interpreter has shaped my studies more than anything I have read. I sit in rooms with doctors, social workers and families who have lost their homes, and I translate not just words but fear, exhaustion and sometimes silence. I have seen how often trauma goes unrecognised simply because nobody shares a language with the person in front of them.

This is what I want to change. My goal is to specialise in clinical psychology, with a focus on trauma in displaced children and adolescents, and to develop culturally adapted, low-threshold interventions that do not depend on a patient speaking the local language. Whether I eventually return to Ukraine or remain in Switzerland, there will be a generation of young people who need this kind of support for many years.

Education has been the one continuous thread through a period in which almost everything else was interrupted. I would be grateful if EduAll could help me protect it, so that I can complete my degree and put it to use where it is most needed.

Mosul's old city was nine hundred years old. There were houses with courtyards and carved wooden balconies, the al-Nuri mosque with its leaning minaret, narrow streets where neighbours knew each other for generations. I grew up there. In 2017, during the battle to retake the city, almost all of it was destroyed.

My parents were a baker and a housewife. Nobody in my family went to university before me. I studied architecture at the University of Mosul and worked ten years in an engineering office, designing schools and houses. When ISIS took the city in 2014, I fled with my family. After years in camps in Kurdistan, I came to Switzerland in 2019 and received provisional admission.

In Zurich, I started from nothing. I learned German, had my degree partly recognised, and entered the ETH master's programme in 2026. My GPA is 3.11, and I published one article on post-war reconstruction.

My thesis is about rebuilding Mosul's old city: how to rebuild houses for returning families, respecting the old structure but with modern safety and climate needs.

I am in the first year of my Master's in Physics at the University of Fribourg, and I will finish in July 2028.

My monthly costs are CHF 1,882. My room in a shared flat near Pérolles costs CHF 885, and my health insurance CHF 285. My only support is CHF 190 each month from my older sister in Dakar, who sells fabrics at the Sandaga market and whose household lives on about CHF 1,120. She gives me about a sixth of everything she earns. Every month when the money arrives, I feel both grateful and ashamed.

I do not have a job. The master's courses and laboratory work fill my days, and my French, although good, is not enough for the few student jobs that are available in Fribourg, where most employers want German as well.

This leaves CHF 1,692 missing every month. I have nothing saved. Until now I have survived with small loans from friends in our community, which I will repay the day I earn a salary.

With a grant from EduAll, I could stop counting coins before buying bread, and give all my strength to my thesis on solar cells. I have come a very long way to reach this classroom. I would like to be allowed to finish.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In ten years, I want to lead a small laboratory in Dakar that designs cheap solar panels for villages. I want the children of those villages to do their homework under electric light, and not under a streetlamp, as I did.

When I was seven, my father, a poor farmer in the region of Kaolack, sent me to a Quranic school in Dakar. I was a talibé. Like thousands of children in Senegal, I spent my days begging in the streets for my marabout, barefoot, with a tomato can for coins. I did not go to a real school. At night, I sat under a streetlamp near the Place de l'Indépendance and copied letters from old newspapers.

At twelve, a social worker from an association found me. She took me to a shelter and enrolled me in school. I was the oldest in my class by five years. I will never forget her. Nobody in my family had ever gone to school. I finished my baccalaureate at twenty-one and studied physics at Cheikh Anta Diop University. The university was often closed by strikes, and it took me many years. But I finished.

Since then, I have given every free day to the same association that saved me. With other former talibés, we created a group that walks the streets of Dakar on Friday evenings, talking to children, bringing them food and telling them there is another way.

In Fribourg, I discovered the physics of solar cells, and I discovered that I am good at it.

For me, education is not a privilege. It is the streetlamp I read under, finally turned into real light.

For me, education is not a privilege. It is the streetlamp I read under, finally turned into real light.

Each month, my costs of studying in Fribourg exceed my support by CHF 1,747. That is the situation in a single figure, and it is why I am writing to EduAll.

My expenses total CHF 2,034: a room in a shared flat for CHF 965, health insurance at CHF 250, tuition and fees at CHF 167 a month, and modest costs for food and transport. A grant would allow me to complete my degree in January 2028 and move directly into doctoral research or industry.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I grew up in Maiduguri, in north-eastern Nigeria. My parents, a trader and a seamstress, never went to school. When the Boko Haram insurgency reached our city in 2009, I was twelve. Our neighbourhood was attacked twice. My father's shop was burned. For three years we lived in an internally displaced persons camp outside the city, twelve people in one tent.

In that camp, I organised a study group for teenagers who, like me, had lost their schools. We had one mathematics textbook, which we copied by hand. Nine of us eventually passed the national exams, and four went to university.

I studied materials engineering at the University of Lagos, where I was elected president of the Nigerian Society of Engineering Students, representing more than 3,000 members, and led a campaign for better laboratory equipment. Afterwards I completed a master's degree and spent two years as an unpaid visiting researcher, applying for doctoral positions abroad.

In 2026 I was admitted to Fribourg. My thesis addresses a problem I saw every day in the camp: corroded pipes that made water unsafe.

I want to work on affordable, durable materials for water infrastructure in regions like north-eastern Nigeria, where clean water is still a matter of life and death.

I want to be honest: right now my costs are covered. I study Environmental Science part-time, and I work about 15 hours a week: as a field assistant for an environmental consultancy and at a Ukrainian Saturday school. I earn CHF 1,686. My husband works as an IT project manager in Zurich and earns around CHF 9,400 a month; he pays CHF 370 of my costs. My own expenses are CHF 1,504. My rent share is only CHF 489, because we live in a furnished flat provided by his employer.

The problem is that this flat is temporary. The employer's relocation package ends in March 2027, and we have to leave. We have been looking for a flat since spring, but with a foreign permit, no Swiss rental history and short contracts, landlords always choose other people. If we find a normal flat in Zurich, my share of the rent will be two or three times higher, and we will need a large deposit. We have no savings: we left almost everything in Mariupol.

I started my bachelor in February 2026, part-time, and it will take until January 2032. I know my current situation is not urgent compared with other applicants. I apply because I want to be prepared for the move and not have to interrupt my studies.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Mariupol was a city of steel and sea. Two huge metallurgical plants, and the smell of the Azov sea. As a child I saw orange smoke over the city every day. Many people, including my grandmother, had lung disease. Nobody talked about it; the plants gave everyone work.

In 2022 the city was almost completely destroyed. I left in March through a humanitarian corridor, after four weeks in a basement. My parents stayed and I did not hear from them for two months. They survived, and now live with relatives in Dnipro.

Before the war, I worked for twelve years as an environmental inspector for the city. I led a team of five people measuring air quality, and I organised a citizens' group that published pollution data online, because official data was often hidden. It was not popular with the plants.

In 2023 I came to Zurich, where my husband found a job. I learned German, and in 2026 I started studying environmental science properly, to get the scientific foundation I never had.

In Zurich I help organise the Ukrainian community's Saturday school, where children keep their language.

I want to work on air quality and industrial pollution, and one day help rebuild Mariupol as a cleaner city.

My mother used to say that a family is like a pot: everyone puts in what they can, and everyone eats. Our pot has always been small, and today it is stretched further than ever.

I am in the second year of my Master's in Computer Science at ETH Zurich. My costs are CHF 2,518 a month. The biggest part is rent: CHF 1,411 for a studio in Altstetten. When I arrived in Zurich I could not find a shared flat that would accept me, and I have been on waiting lists for student housing ever since.

My uncle in Dubai, a taxi driver, contributes CHF 380 every month, although the whole household lives on roughly CHF 1,560. He does this because my father cannot, and because he promised my mother, years ago, that he would make sure I studied.

Every month I am missing CHF 1,508. My master's thesis, on privacy-preserving machine learning for medical data, needs my full attention in the next months, and I cannot take on more hours without risking it.

I am so close. Four semesters. A grant from EduAll would carry me across the finish line.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother could not go to school. She was born in Afghanistan, fled to Iran as a child, and grew up in Mashhad as a refugee, cleaning other people's houses from the age of ten. When I was born, she decided one thing: her children would go to school, whatever it cost.

It cost a lot. As Afghans in Iran, we were not allowed in regular schools for many years. My mother paid for an informal school run by volunteers in a basement. I learned to read there, on donated books, with fifty other Afghan children. When the rules changed, I entered a regular school, and I was top of my class in mathematics.

I taught myself programming on a second-hand laptop my uncle sent from Dubai. At eighteen I was admitted to ETH Zurich. It felt impossible. It still does, some mornings.

I finished my bachelor at ETH in 2025 and started the master directly. In Zurich I help organise a free coding workshop for young refugees at a community centre, because I know how much one working laptop and one patient person can change.

My mother died in 2023, of an illness that could have been treated if she had had access to proper care. I work on medical data because of her.

I want to build technology that makes healthcare fairer, for people with no papers, no records and no voice. My mother put everything she had into the pot. I want to show her it was worth it.

I want to be truthful about our finances, because I know that on paper we do not look like a family in need.

I study my Master's in Environmental Science part-time, and I work about 21 hours a week as a freelance GIS analyst for an engineering office, mostly from home, and earn CHF 2,341 a month. My husband works as a risk analyst at a bank in Zurich and earns around CHF 9,500 a month; he pays CHF 220 towards my costs. I have savings of CHF 11,714. My own monthly expenses are CHF 2,392. By the usual measure, I have no monthly shortfall, and I will not pretend otherwise.

But in January our daughter, who is nine, was diagnosed with leukaemia. Since then our life has been the children's hospital. Health insurance covers the treatment itself, but not everything around it: the taxis for daily visits, the hours my husband has had to cut, the private help at home for our younger son while we are at the hospital. My savings are going into this, month after month, and so is the money that was meant to carry me through my master's. I work from home because it is the only way to be at the hospital every day.

I did not stop my studies. I thought about it. But my daughter asked me not to. She says she wants to see me graduate.

My master's runs until January 2030. I am applying for my own study costs only, so that my studies do not take money that her care needs. If the committee decides that others need it more, I will understand completely.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Environmental science matters to me because I have seen what happens when a river dies. I grew up in Ruse, on the Danube. As a child, I swam in it every summer. In 2000, when I was seventeen, a cyanide spill from a mine upstream reached the river, and fish floated on the surface all the way to the Black Sea. My grandfather, a fisherman, cried. I had never seen him cry.

I studied chemistry in Sofia. After graduating, I went back to Ruse to care for my mother, who was ill for many years, and later my own children were born. I never had the chance to work in my field. In 2020 we moved to Zurich for my husband's work. I learned German, joined a parents' association at my children's school, and later helped organise the Bulgarian community's language classes for children. That community was our family in Switzerland.

In February 2026 I started a Master's in Environmental Science at the University of Zurich, focusing on river ecology. One month before, our daughter had been diagnosed. I study in hospital corridors, in waiting rooms, at night next to her bed. My first semester went better than I dared hope: my GPA is 3.33.

My thesis will be on micropollutants in Swiss rivers. I want to work in water protection, maybe for a cantonal office, maybe for the international Danube commission.

My daughter asks me every day what I learned. Explaining it to her is my favourite part of the day.

I am thirty years old, a husband and a former bank credit officer, and this year I became a student again.

I grew up in Enugu. My father was a school principal and my mother a nurse. They taught me that education is never finished. I studied accounting, and worked five years in banking in Enugu, the last two leading the branch's team of six credit officers.

In 2021, armed men attacked my branch. Two of my colleagues were killed. I survived because I was in the vault room. For a long time after, I could not enter a bank. I resigned in 2023.

I decided to use this break to do something I had always wanted: study business properly, especially how small businesses are financed. In banking, I refused so many loans to good small entrepreneurs, only because the rules did not fit them.

My research is about how firms and regions adapt when a major employer closes: which workers find new jobs, and which do not. I have published two articles, one on Romanian steel towns and one on retraining programmes.

I will tell you everything, because I have nothing to hide and I have very little left to protect.

My monthly costs in Fribourg are CHF 2,188: rent of CHF 1,002 for a small studio, CHF 139 of utilities, and health insurance of CHF 230, which is expensive because I am thirty and no longer eligible for student insurance. My older sister and her husband, a technician in Riyadh, send me CHF 700 every month from a household income of about CHF 2,440. That is almost a third of what they have.

In Egypt this is not covered for him. My sister now has to send money to our parents too. She told me, crying on the phone, that she cannot continue sending me the same amount.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Education is the only thing that ever changed anything in my family. My grandmother married at thirteen. My mother at sixteen. Neither could read. I was the first person in my family to hold a pen with confidence, and the first to go to university. I know, in my body, what one good teacher can do.

Mine was Ms. Samia, in a crowded government school in Minya. Seventy children in the class. She noticed that I read everything I could find, and she gave me her own books. When my father wanted me to leave school at fourteen to work, she came to our house and argued with him for two hours. I stayed.

I became a teacher myself, and taught Arabic and English for five years in schools in Minya and Cairo. I saw classrooms of seventy, eighty, a hundred children, and teachers with no training for it. I wanted to learn how to change that.

In Fribourg I study how teachers can be supported in very large and very diverse classrooms. My thesis follows three teachers in Fribourg schools with many refugee children, and I compare their strategies with those I knew in Egypt. My GPA is 3.51. My German and French are still not strong enough, and I often feel like a child again in seminars. But I am learning, like my students used to learn.

When I finish, I want to train teachers, in Switzerland or in Egypt. I want to be Ms. Samia for many teachers, who will each be Ms. Samia for seventy children.

When I was fifteen, the bus I was travelling in with my cousin fell into a ravine near Huancayo. Nine people died, including my cousin. I spent five weeks in the hospital with a broken pelvis. The doctors were busy and rushed. The nurses were the ones who sat with me when I cried at night, who explained things, who remembered my name.

I decided then what I would become. It took a long time. My mother raised me and my brother alone after my father left, on her teacher's salary. After school I started nursing in Lima while working in a pharmacy, but I had to stop after one year when money ran out. For almost two years I worked as a nursing assistant in a private clinic, saving every sol I could.

In 2024, I came to Lausanne to study nursing again, from the beginning, in French. It was very hard, but it has also been the best time of my life. My GPA is 3.58. My supervisors say I am calm under pressure. I think it is because I remember what it is like to be the frightened one in the bed.

I want to work in trauma and emergency care. And someday I want to go back to the Andes, where a bus accident still means hours of waiting for help, and where a good nurse can be the difference between life and death.

I am entering the last four semesters of my Bachelor's in Public Health at the University of Lausanne, and I am applying to EduAll to finish this degree on the strongest possible footing.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I am forty-four years old, an interpreter, a former midwife's assistant, and soon, I hope, a public health professional.

I grew up in Kabul in the 1990s. During the first Taliban period, I was a teenager, and my schooling happened in secret, in a neighbour's living room, with curtains closed. My mother, a doctor who was forbidden to practise, taught us biology from her old textbooks. I still remember the fear of every knock at the door.

After 2001, I trained and worked for many years alongside midwives in a maternity hospital in Kabul. I saw women die from causes that basic prevention and access could have avoided: bleeding, infection, eclampsia. I understood that medicine alone is not enough. Health is decided long before a woman reaches the hospital.

In 2018 I came to Geneva to work for an international health NGO, and later settled in Lausanne. In 2024 I began my bachelor's in public health. Studying in French, while working as an interpreter, has been demanding, but deeply meaningful. Every week I interpret for Afghan women in Swiss hospitals, and I see the same barriers to care that I saw in Kabul, in a different form.

Outside my studies and work, I co-founded an Afghan women's circle in Lausanne, which meets monthly to share information about health, rights and services.

After graduating, I want to work in migrant health, helping public health services reach women who are too often invisible to them.

How does gold change a village? I have asked this question all my life. I was born in Kédougou, in the south-east of Senegal, where gold mining is everywhere. When I was small, my uncles dug in artisanal mines with their hands. Some died in collapses. The rivers became brown and the fish disappeared. The money came fast and went fast.

My father was a school teacher, and he pushed me to study. I studied geology in Dakar and worked six years for the national geological service, mapping mineral deposits, and later advising on the safety of artisanal mines. I published one article about mercury pollution near mines.

My life was not easy. In 2020 my husband died in a road accident, and I kept our household alone, with my mother, while continuing to work. It took me a long time to feel strong again.

At thirty I decided to study again, to learn modern methods of environmental geology. In Zurich everything is in German and English, and my German is still very weak; the first semester was hard, but I passed (GPA 3.18).

I want to go back to Kédougou and help to make mining safer and cleaner for the people who live there.

I am a doctoral student in Chemistry at the University of Bern, in my second year. My doctorate is supposed to be funded by a Nigerian federal research scholarship. My older brother, a clerk in Ibadan with a household income of around CHF 560, sends me CHF 120.

A grant from EduAll would count as proof of means for my permit and would allow me to continue my research until funding is secured.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Chemistry matters because in the Niger Delta, where I grew up, the water and soil are poisoned by oil. I grew up in Warri, where gas flares burn day and night, and where my mother's fish from the creeks started to taste of petrol. I wanted to understand how to clean what had been destroyed.

My parents are both secondary school teachers. When I was fourteen, militants attacked our neighbourhood during the oil conflict, and we lived for almost a year with relatives in Benin City. I missed a full year of school and caught up by studying at night by candlelight.

I studied industrial chemistry in Benin City and worked four years as a laboratory analyst for an environmental testing company, measuring hydrocarbons in soil and water. I was elected president of the young chemists' association of our state, and organised community workshops about water safety in oil-affected villages.

My doctoral research is on materials that can absorb oil from water, and it has already produced a first publication. I want to return to the Niger Delta and apply this work where it is most needed.

In the interest of accuracy, I should say plainly that my household currently covers my costs.

I study Nursing part-time at BFH, which the school offers precisely for people who already work in care. I work about 24 hours a week as a care assistant in a home for people with dementia and earn CHF 2,702 a month. My spouse works in logistics at a pharmaceutical company in Bern, with a household income of around CHF 5,200, and contributes CHF 390 to my share of our expenses. I also receive a scholarship of CHF 4,321 a year from an Indonesian nursing foundation, and have savings of CHF 3,225. My own monthly costs are CHF 1,887.

My reason for applying is the structure of the coming years. From 2027/28 the programme includes clinical placements of several weeks each, which are full-time and unpaid, with rotating shifts. During those weeks I cannot work at the care home, and my scholarship ends in December. My spouse's income must also cover our car loan and support for my parents in Surabaya. My degree runs until July 2030, and a stable contribution in the placement year would allow me to keep my job without falling behind.

If the committee decides that others need the support more urgently, I will fully understand.

I had been a nurse for nine years. I had worked through a pandemic. And here I was, starting again, unable to read my own textbook.

That was the moment I decided to treat my studies the way I had treated my toughest shifts: one task at a time. Two and a half years later I have completed 11 courses, and I am about to begin my final placement in intensive care.

I grew up in Surabaya. My father is an engineer and my mother a teacher. I trained as a nurse and worked in a public hospital, becoming head nurse of the emergency department at twenty-eight, leading a team of fifteen. During the COVID-19 pandemic our hospital was overwhelmed. We lost patients, and colleagues, in numbers I still cannot say out loud. I worked for six months without a real day off. Afterwards, I struggled with exhaustion and grief, and it took me a long time to recover.

When my spouse found work in Bern, I decided to use the move to become the nurse I wanted to be: one with a scientific foundation, able to lead change, not only survive it.

After graduating, I want to work in intensive care and later specialise in crisis preparedness for hospitals, so that no nursing team is left as unprepared as mine was.

My spouse works in logistics at a pharmaceutical company in Bern, with a household income of around CHF 5,200, and contributes CHF 390 to my share of our expenses. I also receive a scholarship of CHF 4,321 a year from an Indonesian nursing foundation, and have savings of CHF 3,225. My own monthly costs are CHF 1,887.

My reason for applying is the structure of the coming years. From 2027/28 the programme includes clinical placements of several weeks each, which are full-time and unpaid, with rotating shifts. During those weeks I cannot work at the care home, and my scholarship ends in December. My spouse's income must also cover our car loan and support for my parents in Surabaya. My degree runs until July 2030, and a stable contribution in the placement year would allow me to keep my job without falling behind.

If the committee decides that others need the support more urgently, I will fully understand.
STU000107.personal_statement:
On a cold evening in February 2025, in my first week at the Bern University of Applied Sciences (BFH), I stood outside the BFH health building on Murtenstrasse with a stack of German anatomy notes and realised that I understood almost none of it. I had been a nurse for nine years. I had worked through a pandemic. And here I was, starting again, unable to read my own textbook.

That was the moment I decided to treat my studies the way I had treated my toughest shifts: one task at a time. Two and a half years later I have completed 11 courses, and I am about to begin my final placement in intensive care.

I grew up in Surabaya. My father is an engineer and my mother a teacher. I trained as a nurse and worked in a public hospital, becoming head nurse of the emergency department at twenty-eight, leading a team of fifteen. During the COVID-19 pandemic our hospital was overwhelmed. We lost patients, and colleagues, in numbers I still cannot say out loud. I worked for six months without a real day off. Afterwards, I struggled with exhaustion and grief, and it took me a long time to recover.

When my spouse found work in Bern, I decided to use the move to become the nurse I wanted to be: one with a scientific foundation, able to lead change, not only survive it.

After graduating, I want to work in intensive care and later specialise in crisis preparedness for hospitals, so that no nursing team is left as unprepared as mine was.

I explain my money situation honestly. My costs are CHF 2,099 per month. I live in a room in a shared flat in Schwamendingen for CHF 862. The tuition at ETH is CHF 243 per month.

My parents did not go to school, my father was a blacksmith. In his workshop I learned to feel metal, how it bends and breaks. In 2015 my family fled to Germany. I finished school in Hamburg, did an apprenticeship in metal construction, and worked as welder in a shipyard. I learned German there.

In Hamburg I also volunteered with an association that helped new refugees with language and papers. I know how it feels to arrive with nothing.

In 2022 I moved to Zurich for work, and in 2025 I was admitted to ETH. At twenty-four I began my bachelor, after years in workshops, with students who came straight from school. My GPA is 3.45. I am proud of this.

I want to work on materials for affordable and earthquake-resistant housing. Syria will need to be rebuilt, and it must be rebuilt stronger.

Every evening she counted the coins twice, and put a few aside in a tin for my school fees. This tin paid my primary school.

My parents did not go to university; my mother died when I was ten and my father worked as a fisherman far away. My grandmother raised me. When she died, I was sixteen, and I lived with my aunt.

I studied economics at the University of Cape Coast with a scholarship, and worked five years at a rural bank, giving small loans to market women like my grandmother. I also volunteered with a savings group project for women in villages, teaching them to keep simple records. With my supervisor at the bank I wrote a paper on women's savings groups, which was published.

In Lucerne I help in the African students' group, organising welcome days and information about jobs.

My goal is to work on financial inclusion for women in West Africa. The tin of my grandmother is my first lesson in economics.

I was born in Makassar, in Indonesia. My father was a fisherman who died at sea when I was six. My mother worked as a domestic worker, and nobody in my family studied. In 2012, when I was eighteen, my mother married a Swiss man she met through work, and we came to Lucerne.

It was very hard for me. I did not speak German. I felt lost, and soon I became ill, a long illness that took me many years to recover from. I spent a lot of time in clinics. There, I saw how much the way people are treated depends on money, language and where they come from.

When I became healthy again, I learned German, did the passerelle, and at thirty-one I started university.

I want to work in health promotion for migrants, especially women who don't speak the language and who are alone, like my mother and I were.

I am in the first year of my Master's in Physics at the University of Geneva, and I am applying to EduAll because my housing and my finances have both become fragile at the same time.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,788, including CHF 846 for a room and CHF 300 for health insurance. I earn CHF 223 a month tutoring secondary school students in mathematics. My younger brother, a school teacher in Hyderabad (household income around CHF 510), sends me CHF 100. It is a fifth of his income, and he does it without complaint.

My room is a sublet in Carouge. The main tenant has told me that she is returning in November, and I have not yet found another place I can afford. Most listings ask for a Swiss guarantor or three months' deposit.

The monthly gap is CHF 1,465. My master's programme includes an experimental project that requires long laboratory hours, which limits how much I can work. A grant from EduAll would secure a stable room and allow me to complete my degree by January 2028.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother taught physics in a girls' school in Hyderabad, Sindh, for thirty years, with a single set of lab equipment she had bought with her own savings. She would carry a box of batteries, wires and lenses from classroom to classroom. When I was a child, I carried it with her.

She died when I was twenty-two. I took over her classes at the same school, and I became head of the science department at twenty-seven, leading a team of nine teachers. Over those years I trained young teachers, rebuilt the laboratory after it was damaged in the 2022 floods, and ran a small physics club that sent students to national competitions.

The floods of 2022 were the hardest period of my life. Our house and the school were under water for weeks. We lost almost everything. I spent months with colleagues cleaning, rebuilding and teaching in tents. It was then that I decided to study again, to deepen my own understanding of physics and come back able to teach it at a higher level.

In Geneva, I study condensed matter physics. My goal is to return to Sindh and help develop physics teaching at the university level, where there is a severe lack of trained staff.

My mother's box of equipment is still in my brother's house. One day I would like to replace it with a real laboratory.

Every Tuesday evening for four years in Lyon, I served soup at a night shelter, and I learned how quickly a life can slide from stable to fragile. I think about this often now, because I am honest enough to see that my own situation is not stable.

I started my Master's in Sociology at the University of St. Gallen in February 2026. My monthly costs are CHF 2,488. Tuition at HSG is high, CHF 522 a month, and my studio costs CHF 1,035 plus CHF 91 for heating. I work as a student assistant in the university library, earning CHF 811. My aunt in Paris, a nurse, gives me CHF 652 every month, a large share of the roughly CHF 2,580 the household has. She pays my share because my parents in Dakar cannot.

I have four semesters left in Geology at the University of Neuchâtel, and in July 2028, if everything goes well, I will be the first geologist from my village.

My costs are CHF 2,054 a month. My room costs CHF 935. I work in a supermarket warehouse on Saturdays and some evenings, and earn CHF 630. My older brother in Dakar, a mechanic whose household earns about CHF 1,180, sends me CHF 330.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

The first time I held a real fossil was in the geology museum of Neuchâtel, in my first month here. It was an ammonite, 180 million years old, from the Jura. I held it in my hand and thought of my father's fields near Kolda, and wondered what stories were under them too. I was nineteen, alone, cold, and very far from home, and I suddenly felt that I was in the right place.

My father studied agronomy in Dakar and went back to farm our family land, and I grew up in the village helping in the fields. When I was twelve, a drought killed almost all our harvest. We ate one meal a day for months. I understood then that everything depends on water and soil. My teacher in Kolda told me about geology. I did not know it was a job.

After school I came to Neuchâtel to study, with the savings of my whole family. I have worked since my first semester, and I have volunteered every summer back home with a project that helps villages find and protect groundwater wells.

My studies have not been easy. I study in French, which I speak, but the sciences at this level were new and difficult for me, and I have had to fight for every exam. But I never stopped.

After my bachelor, I want to work in hydrogeology, finding water for villages in the Sahel. I want no child in Kolda to eat one meal a day because of a drought.

I am in the first year of my Master's in Physics at the University of Fribourg, which I study part-time. My thesis is due in January 2030.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,052. I rent a room for CHF 1,007; health insurance costs CHF 210. I work about 16 hours a week as a hotel night porter, two nights at the weekend, and earn CHF 1,774. My cousin in Paris, a hospital technician, sends me CHF 360 every month out of a household income of about CHF 2,500.

My budget is balanced, but only just. My housing is also uncertain: my room is in a building that has been sold, and the new owner has given all tenants notice for the end of December. I must find a new place, and rooms in Fribourg now cost more, with a deposit.

Studying part-time was my choice, so that I could keep working. A grant from EduAll would allow me to secure new housing and to complete my master's with the focus it needs.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Physics matters because it explains the world without asking who you are. In my village near Tambacounda, where my parents farmed peanuts and millet, the world was explained by elders, by God, by tradition. When a teacher showed me, at eleven, why the moon changes shape, using a torch and a football, I felt that the universe had opened a door that nobody could close.

Nobody in my family had gone to school. I was sent to live with an uncle in Dakar for secondary school. I studied physics at university there, but had to stop at twenty-five to work. In 2010 I came to Switzerland, where I worked for many years in hotels and in a watch factory in the Jura, learning precision in a very literal sense.

I also founded a football club for African youth in Fribourg, which I led for eight years, and I volunteer as a tutor for mathematics at a community centre.

In 2025 I resumed my studies. My professors have been very supportive, and my thesis on thin superconducting films has already produced a co-authored publication.

After graduating, I want to do a PhD and later teach physics, ideally in Senegal, where universities need more trained staff. Every child should have the chance to see the moon explained with a torch and a football.

I will present my finances completely, including the elements that may weaken my application.

My monthly expenses in Neuchâtel are CHF 1,965. My younger brother, a primary school teacher in Ibadan with a household income of around CHF 360, sends me CHF 70 a month, which is a fifth of what his family has. I have no employment.

I do have savings of CHF 14,028. They come from the sale of my late father's plot of land in Ibadan, which my family agreed I should use for my education. I am drawing on them to cover the monthly gap of CHF 1,895. At that rate, they will last less than eight months, while my bachelor's degree runs until January 2029.

I should also explain why I have no work history. After secondary school I married young and spent many years running a household and caring for my husband's family. I have never held a paid position. Since coming to Switzerland, I have been learning French intensively, and I am now looking for part-time work, but without experience or fluent French, it has been difficult.

I am applying to EduAll so that my father's legacy can carry me through my degree, rather than disappear in its first year.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was eight, my father, a secondary school economics teacher, used to bring the newspaper home and read the market prices to me: yams, palm oil, cement, petrol. He would ask me why the price of petrol went up when the country was full of oil. I did not know. He said, "One day you will explain it to me." He died in 2023. I am still trying to answer his question.

After my marriage ended in 2021, I decided that I would not let the rest of my life pass without doing what I had always wanted. I came to Neuchâtel in 2025 and started my Bachelor's in Economics in February 2026. French is my great challenge; I study every evening with recordings of lectures. My first semester went well, with a GPA of 3.09.

For many years in Ibadan I volunteered with my church's women's group, teaching basic bookkeeping and savings to market women. Here in Neuchâtel I continue this with an African women's association.

I want to work on public finance and resource economics in Nigeria, where oil wealth has too often bypassed ordinary people. My father asked me the question. I intend to answer it.

My monthly costs in Geneva total CHF 2,080. Today I cover them myself, and I would like to explain why that will stop in September 2027.

I study my Master's in Biology part-time and work about 20 hours a week as a laboratory helper in a biology department, earning CHF 2,241. My parents, who live in Geneva, contribute CHF 280. My father works as a kitchen assistant and my mother cleans offices; together they earn around CHF 5,500, and they have my three younger siblings at home. My rent is CHF 1,166 for a small room, since there is no space for me in my parents' two-room flat.

Since 2024 my parents have also been sending money to our relatives in Gaza, who lost their homes. This year, my grandmother and two cousins were killed. The money my family could spare for me is now going to those who survived.

From September 2027 my thesis in a plant genetics laboratory requires full days, so I will switch to full-time study and leave my job. This would allow me to complete my degree in January 2029 rather than a year later, but it leaves CHF 1,800 a month uncovered. A grant from EduAll would make that final year possible without adding to my parents' burden at the hardest time our family has known.

I was sixteen when I left Gaza in 2019 to join my father, who had been working in Geneva for several years. I arrived speaking Arabic and school English. Nobody in my family had been to university: my father was a fisherman before the blockade ended his work, and my mother never finished school.

In Geneva I was placed in a welcome class. I learned French in eighteen months and finished the Collège. I studied biology at the University of Geneva, and I am now in my master's, working on drought-resistant wheat. In Gaza, I watched my grandmother grow vegetables in a tiny courtyard with water that was often salty. I want to develop crops that grow where water is scarce and poor.

I have worked since I was seventeen: in a supermarket, in a restaurant, and now in a laboratory. I have learned to study on buses, at night, and in hospital waiting rooms.

The past two years have been the hardest of my life. Every morning I read the news before I read anything else. But I have finished every course, and my GPA is 3.36. I carry my family's hope, and my grandmother's courtyard, with me.

I will be transparent about my situation, including where I could have done things differently.

My monthly expenses in Zurich are CHF 2,317. My room costs CHF 1,164, which is more than I should pay; I took it in my first week because I was afraid of having nowhere to sleep, and I have been on waiting lists for student housing since. ETH tuition adds CHF 243 a month.

I earn CHF 477 a month as a tutor for first-year chemistry students. My father, a tailor in Patna (household income around CHF 430), sends me CHF 80, which is almost a fifth of what my family lives on. The gap is CHF 1,760 every month. I have no savings: I came to Switzerland with a loan from relatives, which I am still repaying from my tutoring income.

I could have chosen a cheaper university town. I chose ETH because it offered me admission and because its biochemistry programme is among the best in the world. I do not regret it, but I know it makes my need larger.

A grant would allow me to move into cheaper housing when a room becomes available, and to complete my degree by July 2028.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

On my first night in Zurich, in September 2025, I walked from the Hauptbahnhof to the ETH main building and stood in front of it at midnight. I had seen it only on a phone screen, in a cyber café in Patna. I remember thinking that my father had never seen a building like this in his life, and that I was standing in front of it for both of us.

I come from a Dalit family in Bihar. My father is a tailor, my mother makes bangles at home. Neither went to school beyond a few years. At school I was often made to sit apart from the other children. Some teachers refused to check my notebooks. I learned early that I would have to be twice as good to be treated as equal.

I was. I finished school as the top student in my district in chemistry and biology, and I founded a free study circle for Dalit children in our neighbourhood, which I led for three years. I worked in a pharmacy for two years after school to save money for my applications.

At ETH I study biochemistry. My GPA is 3.45. I am interested in enzymes that could make medicines cheaper to produce. In Bihar, many people cannot afford even basic drugs.

For me education is the only thing in India that caste cannot fully take away.

Nursing matters because it is where health care actually touches people. From the age of fifteen I served as a volunteer health helper with a church outreach programme in Lagos, visiting sick and elderly people in their homes in Ajegunle, one of the poorest neighbourhoods of the city. My father was a secondary school teacher and my mother a trader. They wanted me to become a doctor, but after school I could not afford medical studies, and I gave my time to the outreach programme instead.

In 2024, with the support of friends from my church in Switzerland, I came to Lausanne, learned French and began to study to become the nurse I had been trying to be since I was a teenager. French is still a challenge, but I have passed all my first-year modules, with a GPA of 3.37.

Architecture matters because the shape of a city decides who belongs in it. In Manila, I grew up in Tondo, where families of eight live in rooms of ten square metres, and where every few years a fire or a demolition erases whole neighbourhoods overnight. I saw my own street disappear when I was twelve.

My parents sold fish at the market and never went to school beyond a few years. I trained as a draftsperson and worked for two years in an architecture firm in Makati, drawing condominiums for people who would never set foot in Tondo. I want to give a complete picture of my finances, including my own choices.

I study Data Science part-time at the University of Neuchâtel. My monthly expenses are CHF 1,993, including CHF 1,006 for my share of our flat and CHF 110 for utilities. I work about 22 hours a week, in the evenings and on Saturdays, sorting parcels at a logistics centre, and earn CHF 2,453. I have no savings.

In practice, it works only because we never see each other: I study in the mornings, care for our four-year-old in the afternoons, and leave for the logistics centre when my partner comes home. I chose a reduced course load for this reason, which also explains why my GPA of 2.58 is lower than I would like.

This autumn the restaurant was sold, and my partner's contract is only guaranteed until the end of the year. If she loses her job, our arrangement collapses. The grant would allow our small family to hold together while I build a degree that will, in the long run, double our household's earning capacity. I graduate in January 2031.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

What happens to a young person's plans when they become a parent at twenty? In my neighbourhood of Villa El Salvador, on the edge of Lima, the answer was usually: they end. I decided mine would not.

My parents sell vegetables in a market stall. Neither finished secondary school. I was the first in my family to be admitted to university, in statistics, in Lima. Then, at twenty, I became a father. I left my studies to work and help care for my daughter, and my partner, who had family in Switzerland, found work here. In 2024 we joined her.

The first year here was hard: new language, no friends, a small child, and the feeling that my chance had passed. What saved me was a parents' group at a community centre in Neuchâtel, where I began helping other Spanish-speaking parents with school registrations and administrative letters. I realised I was good at organising information, at making numbers and forms make sense for people.

That is why I chose data science. I want to work with data from public services, schools, health, social support, to make them easier to use for families like mine.

My daughter now goes to kindergarten. Every morning she asks if I have "school" too. Yes, I tell her. We both do.

Kolomyia is a small town at the foot of the Carpathians, where every family seems to own a guesthouse, or wishes it did. My grandmother ran one with four rooms. As a child, I helped her change sheets, cook for guests and write the bills by hand. She had no business training, and she lost money every winter.

My parents, both engineers, wanted me to follow them. I studied economics in Lviv instead, and worked in tourism development for the regional administration, helping small family businesses apply for grants and training. On weekends, I volunteered with an organisation teaching digital skills to rural women who ran guesthouses.

In 2016 I moved to Switzerland with my husband, and later completed a bachelor's degree here while working. My master's research at Lucerne looks at how small, family-run hospitality businesses can survive seasonal crises, comparing Central Switzerland and the Carpathians. I have published two papers on rural tourism resilience.

Since 2022, the war has changed everything for the region I come from. The Carpathians have become a refuge for displaced families, and the guesthouses of my grandmother's generation are now shelters. I want to use my knowledge to help these businesses rebuild when the war ends.

For eleven years I have worked in care homes, and I still do: about 19 hours a week, three evenings and one weekend day, as a care assistant in a home for elderly people in Köniz. I earn CHF 2,151. This is why I study nursing part-time. My partner, who works as a bus driver in Bern and earns about CHF 5,300, gives CHF 330 for my share of our life. Together this covers my costs of CHF 1,690.

So why do I write to you? Because my body is telling me I cannot continue like this. I have a chronic back condition, two herniated discs, from years of lifting residents. The care home work that pays my share is exactly the work that damages me. My doctor has told me I must reduce the physical work, and from September 2027 I will drop one evening, so I will earn about CHF 1,510. And in June my mother in Tangier was diagnosed with cancer; my partner and I now send money for her treatment.

I began my bachelor in nursing in February 2026, at thirty-nine. It is a long road until January 2032. I want to become a nurse so that I can care for people in a way that does not destroy me, and with knowledge that I did not have for eleven years.

A grant would let me reduce my hours in the care home before my back decides for me.

I grew up in Tangier. My father was a teacher, my mother a seamstress. I came to Switzerland at twenty-eight, and I started in care homes because it was the work I could find. I discovered that I love it. I love the old people, their stories, their stubbornness, their fear and their jokes.

But after eleven years I also know the limits of a care assistant. I see the nurses make decisions I do not understand, and I want to understand. I want to recognise when a resident's confusion is an infection and not "just age".

In Bern I am also active in the Moroccan association, where I organise information evenings about care for elderly immigrants, who often end their lives very alone.

My first semester was hard. After twenty years away from school, I had to learn how to study again, in German. But I will learn, as I learned everything else.

For eleven years I have worked in care homes, and I still do: about 19 hours a week, three evenings and one weekend day, as a care assistant in a home for elderly people in Köniz. I earn CHF 2,151. This is why I study nursing part-time. My partner, who works as a bus driver in Bern and earns about CHF 5,300, gives CHF 330 for my share of our life. Together this covers my costs of CHF 1,690.

So why do I write to you? Because my body is telling me I cannot continue like this. I have a chronic back condition, two herniated discs, from years of lifting residents. The care home work that pays my share is exactly the work that damages me. My doctor has told me I must reduce the physical work, and from September 2027 I will drop one evening, so I will earn about CHF 1,510. And in June my mother in Tangier was diagnosed with cancer; my partner and I now send money for her treatment.

I began my bachelor in nursing in February 2026, at thirty-nine. It is a long road until January 2032. I want to become a nurse so that I can care for people in a way that does not destroy me, and with knowledge that I did not have for eleven years.

I grew up in Tangier. My father was a teacher, my mother a seamstress. I came to Switzerland at twenty-eight, and I started in care homes because it was the work I could find. I discovered that I love it. I love the old people, their stories, their stubbornness, their fear and their jokes.

But after eleven years I also know the limits of a care assistant. I see the nurses make decisions I do not understand, and I want to understand. I want to recognise when a resident's confusion is an infection and not "just age".

In Bern I am also active in the Moroccan association, where I organise information evenings about care for elderly immigrants, who often end their lives very alone.

My first semester was hard. After twenty years away from school, I had to learn how to study again, in German. But I will learn, as I learned everything else.

For two years I lived in a temporary shelter camp. I worked as an assistant coordinator for an NGO distributing aid, and I became the person other women came to at night, when they could not sleep, when their children screamed in dreams. I had no training. I just listened. I also helped organise a women's group in the camp, which is still active today.

My father was a teacher and my mother a nurse; they always said I should study. The earthquake came one month after I finished school.

I am in my second year of the Bachelor in Physics at the University of Zurich. My monthly costs are CHF 2,113, with rent of CHF 1,017 for a room in Wipkingen.

I work as a kitchen assistant in a hospital cafeteria on weekends and earn CHF 690. My older brother in Kanpur, who runs a small mobile-phone shop and whose household earns about CHF 1,090, sends me CHF 200 every month.

The gap is CHF 1,223 a month. From next semester, my laboratory courses and bachelor project take more time, and I will not be able to work as many weekend shifts.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Kanpur is an old industrial city on the Ganges, once famous for its leather and textile mills. Most of the mills are closed now. The river is grey, the air is heavy, and in summer the power goes off for hours. I did my homework under a kerosene lamp more often than under a bulb. Maybe this is why I became interested in physics: I wanted to understand light.

My father worked in a tannery until it closed, and my mother stitched school uniforms at home. Neither went to school beyond a few years. I was the first in my family to finish secondary school, with top marks in physics and mathematics.

After school I could not afford university in India, so I worked for four years: first in my brother's phone shop, then as a technician repairing solar panels in villages around Kanpur. This work taught me more than any book: how a photon becomes a current, and how a broken panel means a village in darkness.

In 2025 I was admitted to the University of Zurich. It has been the most exciting time of my life. My results are good, and I am thinking about a master's in condensed matter physics.

I want to work on solar cell materials, and one day bring better and cheaper solar technology back to the villages where I once repaired panels by hand.

I am a doctoral student in Mathematics at the University of Bern, and I am applying to EduAll to secure the continuation of research that has, until now, been funded by a scholarship for scholars at risk.

That scholarship covered my first year and ended in February 2026. My supervisor has confirmed in writing that the institute cannot offer me a salaried position before a new grant application is decided in 2028. Since then, I have lived on CHF 150 a month from my cousin in Sylhet, a bank officer with a household income of around CHF 910, and on what I had set aside from my scholarship.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,053, of which CHF 1,162 is rent for a studio in Bern. I chose a studio because, as a refugee who has faced targeted threats, I value a private and secure place to live.

The monthly gap is CHF 1,903. An EduAll grant would allow me to continue my research without interruption until my position is funded, and to complete my doctorate by January 2029.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In fifteen years, I hope to lead a research group in algebraic topology and to be an openly queer mathematician whom young people in South Asia can look to. Neither of those futures seemed possible when I was growing up in Sylhet.

My parents are a rickshaw mechanic and a housewife; neither finished school. I found mathematics through a free olympiad training programme and won a place at the University of Dhaka. There, I co-founded a discreet support network for LGBTQ students and led it for three years. In 2016, two activists I knew were murdered in Dhaka. In 2020, after my name appeared on a list online, I left the country. I was recognised as a refugee in Switzerland in 2021.

In Bern I completed a master's in mathematics while working as a tutor, and began my doctorate in 2025. I volunteer with an organisation supporting LGBTQ asylum seekers, accompanying them to appointments and interviews.

Mathematics has always been the place where I am judged only by the correctness of my reasoning. I want to open that place to others.

I will be honest with you about everything, the good and the difficult.

My costs are CHF 2,266 a month. I earn CHF 1,183 as a night receptionist in a hotel near Cornavin, four nights a week. My older sister, a seamstress in Kumasi, gives me CHF 180, a large share of the roughly CHF 1,080 the household has. I have CHF 1,078 in savings. So the gap is CHF 903 a month. I know this is smaller than for many others.

But I am tired. In 2023 I was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Some weeks my legs are weak and my eyes blur, and after a night shift I need a whole day to recover. My neurologist has told me that the night work is making my condition worse, and that I should stop. If I stop, the gap becomes much larger. If I don't stop, I may not finish.

And in May my younger brother's kidneys failed. He needs dialysis three times a week in Kumasi, and my sister and I are paying for it. My savings will go there.

My master's thesis is due in July 2028. I am asking EduAll to help me leave the night shifts for the last months, so that I can finish my degree before my body forces me to stop.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was seven, I stammered so badly that the other children laughed whenever I opened my mouth. A teacher, Mr. Owusu, kept me after school every day for a year and made me read aloud to him, slowly, one sentence at a time. He never laughed. By the end of the year I could read a whole page. I have wanted to be that kind of person for someone else ever since.

My parents are a teacher and a nurse. I studied psychology in Accra and worked for seven years as a counsellor in a secondary school, and later as head of the student counselling unit, leading a team of five. I came to Geneva in 2026 for my master's, to train in clinical psychology.

French is my greatest difficulty. I understand lectures, but writing clinical reports in French takes me twice as long. My results are nevertheless very good, with a GPA of 3.7.

The diagnosis of MS changed my life. But it has also made me a better listener. I know now what it is like to fear your own body.

I want to work as a clinical psychologist with people living with chronic illness, and one day return to Ghana, where psychological support for them hardly exists.

My younger brother, a mechanic in Sialkot, sends me CHF 220 out of a household income of about CHF 1,030. I do not work at the moment. The first year at ETH, the "Basisprüfung", decides whether a student can continue, and I have put all my time into it.

The gap is CHF 1,631 a month. With support from EduAll I could continue my studies through the first-year examinations and beyond.
STU000146.personal_statement:
I am twenty-five, from Sialkot, and for eight years I made footballs.

Sialkot produces most of the world's hand-stitched footballs. I started stitching panels at fourteen in a small workshop, after my father, a labourer, fell ill. Neither of my parents went to school. At eighteen I became a quality inspector in a sports goods factory, responsible for testing materials: leather, synthetic panels, bladders. I became fascinated by why one material lasts and another cracks.

I also volunteered for five years with an organisation that fought child labour in the football industry, the same industry that had taken my own childhood. We visited villages and helped children return to school. I organised evening literacy classes for workers in our neighbourhood.

In 2023 I decided to finally study what I had been learning by hand for so long. I prepared for two years, learned German, passed the ETH entrance exam, and in February 2026, at twenty-four, I sat in my first lecture on materials science.

I want to work on sustainable materials for sporting goods and textiles, and to help Sialkot's industry become cleaner and fairer.

Materials matter because, when the water comes, the only thing that decides whether your house stands is what it is made of. In August 2022, the floods in Sindh put a third of Pakistan under water. Our town, Larkana, was surrounded for weeks. The mud-brick houses in the villages around us simply dissolved. The concrete houses stood.

My family was lucky: our house was damaged but not destroyed. Many of my relatives lost everything. For three months, I helped organise a relief camp at my school, helping to coordinate food distribution for four hundred families and teaching younger children in makeshift classrooms. My grandfather took me on walks above Cusco and showed me the stones of the Inca walls, cut so precisely that no knife fits between them. He told me each stone had a story millions of years old. My father, an engineer, died when I was eight. My mother came to Zurich in 2010, when I was ten, to marry my stepfather, and I followed her.

I want to specialise in natural hazards in mountain regions, in Switzerland and in the Andes, where landslides destroy villages every rainy season.

My parents never went to school. My father worked as a porter at the market. In 2018, when I was fifteen, we joined him in Switzerland after he had been working here for several years. I did not speak German. Within three years I completed the gymnasium and was admitted to ETH.

During my bachelor at ETH I worked in a supermarket and later as a tutor. I was elected president of the Afghan students' association in Zurich, and I organise free coding workshops for Afghan girls, online, since girls in Afghanistan can no longer attend secondary school.

Every morning I take the tram past the Basel Zoo to the Biozentrum, and every morning I think of how improbable it is that I am here.

I study the Master's in Microbiology at the University of Basel, and I will finish in January 2028. My costs are CHF 2,229 a month. My rent is CHF 1,217, and health insurance CHF 260. I work as a laboratory technician twelve hours a week, earning CHF 1,149, and my older brother, an electrician in Bielefeld whose household earns about CHF 5,000, sends me CHF 1,260. He has done this since the day I arrived.

But my brother has just learned that our youngest sister, who was taken by ISIS in 2014 and has been missing ever since, may be alive in a camp in north-eastern Syria. He is spending everything on lawyers, intermediaries and travel to bring her home. I told him to stop sending me money. He refused. I cannot let him choose between us.

A grant from EduAll would let me release my brother from carrying me, so that all his strength can go to finding our sister.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In August 2014, when I was eighteen, ISIS came to Sinjar. I am Yazidi. My family fled up the mountain with thousands of others. We had no water. I saw children die of thirst. My youngest sister was taken on the road. We never saw her again.

After two years in a camp in Kurdistan, I came to Switzerland in 2016 as a refugee. I had just finished secondary school and wanted to study biology in Mosul. I started from zero: German, bridging courses, a bachelor's in biology in Basel. I worked in laboratories, cleaning glassware at first, then as a technician. At the Biozentrum I now train new technicians, and I led the organisation of our laboratory's move to the new building last year.

In the camp, I saw cholera spread through the tents. Microbiology became my way to fight something I could finally understand. My master's thesis is on waterborne pathogens in refugee camps.

I want to work in outbreak response for humanitarian organisations. I have seen what happens when there is no clean water. I want to be the one who brings it.

I am in my second year of the Bachelor's in Chemistry at the University of Basel, and I am applying to EduAll because the support that made my studies possible has suddenly become uncertain.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,733: a room in a shared flat for CHF 865, tuition and fees of CHF 142 a month, and modest costs for food, transport and insurance. My parents are teachers. They rebuilt slowly. My sister went to work abroad to help the family. After secondary school I stayed two years to help my parents rebuild the house and to care for my father when he became ill. My family needed me at home.

Years later, a friend showed me data maps of the typhoon damage, made by volunteers from satellite images. I understood that data can save lives: where to send water, where to send doctors. I decided to study data science. In 2025 I came to Lausanne.

My studies go well, GPA 3.69. I want to work in disaster response with data, for organisations that help after typhoons and floods.

How long can a person live on savings that were never meant to be savings? I ask myself this every month.

The CHF 6,608 in my account is what is left from the sale of my late grandmother's land in the Volta region, which my family agreed to use for my education. It is not a safety net. I also must be honest about my grades. My GPA is 2.4, and my standing is at risk. French is still hard for me, and the first year of nursing was a shock. I passed the practical modules well, but I failed two theory exams and must retake them.

I have not found a student job yet, although I am applying everywhere. If EduAll can help me, I will not waste it. I have waited too long for this chance.

For three years I lay in a hospital bed in Ho, in eastern Ghana, with tuberculosis in my spine. I was twenty-two when it began. The doctors were busy and tired. It was the nurses who kept me alive, and not only with medicine. One nurse, Sister Abena, came every evening, even when she was not on duty, and read the newspaper to me. She told me I would walk again. I did not believe her. She was right.

My parents are teachers. They spent everything on my treatment. When I finally walked out of that hospital, slowly, with a cane, I knew what I would do with my life.

It took a long time. I had to rebuild my strength, then find a way to study. In 2025 I came to Lausanne to begin nursing. I am older than almost everyone, I speak French with difficulty, and I am slower than the others in exams. But on the wards, patients trust me. I think they can see that I know what it is to be in their bed.

I want to be Sister Abena for someone else. I want to become a nurse in rehabilitation, for people who have to learn to walk again.

I was born in the Balata camp, near Nablus, and I have lived in camps, rented rooms and borrowed apartments most of my life. When I was fourteen, during a raid on the camp, our house was demolished. My family moved in with relatives, fourteen people in three rooms. I learned then that a home is not walls. It is the people who hold you.

German is still very hard for me, especially in the academic readings and exams. But in the interviews for my thesis, I have found my strength: women open their hearts to me because they know I have lived what they have lived.

Every Wednesday I volunteer with a refugee women's group in Zurich, where I help organise language exchange and support circles.
