When I was ten, I spent every weekend at my grandfather's fish pond in Iloilo, watching the water change colour with the seasons. One year all the fish died in a single night. The water had turned red. My grandfather lost his income for a year. Nobody could explain it to him. Years later I learned it was a toxic algal bloom.

I studied biology in Iloilo and did my master's in marine science in Manila, on harmful algae in fish ponds. During my studies I worked as a research assistant in an aquaculture centre and as a lab technician.

In 2019, during my second year of university, typhoon Phanfone destroyed our house. We lived with relatives for a year, and I studied in a shared room with five cousins. I still finished at the top of my class.

My doctoral project in Zurich studies how warming water changes the toxicity of algae. I want to return to the Philippines to build early warning systems for fish farmers, like my grandfather.

I am a doctoral student in Philosophy at the University of Lausanne, in my third year, and I am applying to EduAll to ensure that I can complete my doctorate while supporting my young family.

For my first two years I held a part-time assistant position in the philosophy department. It was a fixed-term replacement contract that ended in June 2026, and the department has confirmed in writing that no new assistant position will be available before autumn 2028. My monthly expenses are CHF 2,396, including my share of our family's rent and our son's food and clothing. My uncle, a pharmacist in Beirut whose household earns around CHF 1,280, supports me with CHF 360 a month. My wife cares for our son, who is two, and is taking French courses.

A grant would allow me to finish my doctorate without abandoning it for full-time work just before completion.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was nine, in Raqqa, my father, a tailor who had never been to school, would sit with me in the evenings and ask me questions I could not answer: why good people suffer, whether a promise binds you forever, what we owe strangers. He did not expect answers. He simply liked the questions.

I studied philosophy in Beirut, the first in my family to go to university, while working as a translator of Arabic and English texts. I volunteered for three years in a school for Syrian refugee children in the Bekaa valley, teaching reading and critical thinking.

My doctoral thesis is on the ethics of hospitality: what societies owe to strangers who arrive at their doors. It is a question my father asked me in Raqqa, and one I have lived in Beirut and in Lausanne. We came to Switzerland from Lebanon in 2024; our asylum application was not accepted, but we were provisionally admitted, because a return to Syria is not possible.

In Lausanne I help run a reading group for Arabic-speaking families at a community library. It brings together people who have lost their countries and found each other.

I want to teach and research moral and political philosophy, in Europe or in the Arab world.

For six years I worked in field teams for Egypt's water research centre, measuring salinity in the Nile Delta, often in villages where the fields had turned white with salt. I came to Basel to do the doctorate I had dreamed of all those years, on the Delta's future under rising seas.

My doctorate began in September 2024 with a mission scholarship from the Egyptian government. In spring 2026, because of the currency crisis, the government suspended payments to many scholars abroad, including me. My supervisor has written to confirm that there is no salaried position in the group until a new project starts in 2028.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,339. They include CHF 1,209 in rent plus utilities, CHF 345 for health insurance, and CHF 53 for sampling materials my fieldwork requires. My older brother, an engineer in Riyadh whose household earns around CHF 3,650, now sends me CHF 980. The gap is CHF 1,359.

And in May, our mother suffered a severe stroke in Mansoura. My brother is paying for her care too. I cannot keep asking him to carry both of us. A grant from EduAll would let me continue my research until my funding is restored, and let my brother give our mother what she needs.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I grew up in Kafr El-Sheikh, in the northern Delta, where the land meets the sea. My father was an agricultural engineer who taught me to taste the soil. "Sweet soil grows rice," he said, "salt soil grows nothing." When I was a boy, the sweet soil reached almost to the coast. Today, in many villages, it does not.

I studied soil science in Alexandria and joined the national water research centre, where I became head of a field team of nine technicians, responsible for monitoring groundwater and soil salinity across three governorates. I trained dozens of young technicians, and I learned that data only matters when farmers trust the people collecting it.

My doctoral research in Basel models how sea-level rise and upstream dams will change salinity in the Delta by 2050. It is the question I have lived with all my life.

My mother used to pack food for me every time I went to the field, even when I was thirty. She still asks me on the phone, slowly now, whether I have eaten.

After my doctorate I want to return to Egypt and help the Delta's farmers prepare for what is coming. Forty million people depend on that land.

My parents are doctors, and I grew up with medical conversations at dinner, but I was always more interested in the patients than in the illnesses: why one person recovers and another gives up.

In Bern I work as a research assistant in a lab studying resilience in adolescents with chronic illness. I code interviews, run questionnaires and help with data analysis. Now, the research has become personal: I see my sister's fear on video calls and recognise what we study.

My thesis looks at how siblings of seriously ill children cope, a group often forgotten by health systems.

After my bachelor I want to do a master's in clinical psychology and specialise in paediatric psycho-oncology.

In the second year I had a new teacher. She sat next to me for five minutes every morning, with a picture book. After three months, I was reading. After one year, I was one of the best in the class. One teacher changed everything.

I came to Switzerland in 2010 with my mother and my sisters, to join my father, who worked here. Later my parents went back to Erbil. I stayed, finished school and did an apprenticeship as a childcare worker. For five years I worked in a daycare, and I volunteered every Saturday in a homework club for refugee children.

I am in the second year of my Master's in Mathematics at the University of Zurich, with my thesis due in January 2028.

My monthly expenses are CHF 2,415, including CHF 1,318 for a studio in Wiedikon and CHF 285 for health insurance. My parents, retired teachers in Arequipa with a combined pension of around CHF 1,100, send me CHF 300 a month.

Until this spring, I tutored mathematics part-time. I stopped in March when my father was diagnosed with advanced kidney disease. He now needs dialysis three times a week, and I have travelled to Peru twice this year to help my mother organise his care. My thesis supervisor has been understanding, but I have lost months of work that I must now make up.

My parents have told me they will keep sending what they can. I know that his treatment will soon require everything they have.

When I finally found the answer, eighty-nine, he told me I had discovered the Fibonacci numbers. I felt as if I had found a hidden door in the world.

I studied mathematics in Arequipa. In 2016, when I was a student, an earthquake destroyed many schools in the region, and for two years children learned in tents and borrowed rooms. With other students I organised a weekend mathematics programme for pupils whose schools had closed, and it continued for five years in community halls. After my degree I taught for eight years, first in public secondary schools and later in a teacher training college.

In 2025, at thirty-one, I came to Zurich to pursue the master's degree I had always postponed. My thesis is in combinatorics, and my first paper, on partition identities, was accepted this year.

After my degree, I want to return to Peru to train mathematics teachers. The hidden door my father showed me should be open to every child.

My mother always told me: "Never hide your hunger from people who can feed you." So I will not hide anything.

I am in my first year of Chemistry at the University of Zurich, which I study part-time. My costs are CHF 2,085 per month. I receive a scholarship of CHF 7,782 per year from a Swiss refugee education foundation, which is a great help. I work about 13 hours a week in the chemistry department, washing and preparing laboratory glassware, and earn CHF 1,423. My friend and former colleague in Accra, a lab manager, still sends me CHF 210 every month out of a household income of about CHF 880; he says it is his way of fighting what happened to me.

Even with all this, every month there is a gap of CHF 452. My room costs CHF 722, the cheapest I found. I cook for three days at a time. I do not complain; I am free, and I am studying.

A grant from EduAll would close the gap and let me focus on the chemistry, which is the reason I came.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother was a market woman in Kumasi who sold cloth, and she could read people better than any book. When I was fifteen, she looked at me and said, "Whatever you are, you are my child." I did not understand then how much courage that sentence would need.

I studied chemistry at KNUST and worked for twelve years as a laboratory analyst for a mining company, testing water and soil for cyanide and mercury. I was the head of a team of six analysts. I was good at my work, and I was careful to be invisible outside it.

In 2023, after Ghana's parliament moved to criminalise LGBTQ people, my name was shared in a group of men who wanted to "clean" our town. I was attacked outside my house. I lost most of the sight in my left eye. I left Ghana two months later and was recognised as a refugee in Switzerland.

In Zurich I started again at thirty-eight, in a new language, as a first-year student. It is hard; German chemistry lectures move fast. But I volunteer every week at a support group for LGBTQ refugees, and I see that I am not alone.

My mother died last year. She did not see me start university again. I will finish for her, and one day I want to work on clean water for mining communities.

How long can a doctorate survive on savings? I have been asking myself this since March.

I am in my second year of a doctorate in Public Health at the University of Bern, studying access to mental health care for refugees. When I started, my supervisor told me that a project grant would pay my salary from the second year. In March the grant was rejected. My supervisor has written to confirm that no salaried position is available until a new application is decided in 2028. I now have only a small teaching assistant mandate, CHF 602 a month.

My sister in Erbil, a school headteacher, contributes CHF 600, although the whole household lives on roughly CHF 2,200.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,154. At my age health insurance alone is CHF 290, and CHF 89 goes into fieldwork materials and translation costs for interviews that my project needs. My rent is CHF 1,187 plus CHF 103 utilities.

I have lived in Switzerland for sixteen years and have worked for all of them. I did not expect, at forty-three, to find myself counting every franc again. But I have come too far in this research to stop. With EduAll's support I could continue until my funding is restored.

---

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

What happens to a mind that has seen too much? I have asked this question since I was a child in Baghdad, during the war of 1991, when my uncle came home from the front and never spoke again about what he had seen.

My parents were both teachers. I studied medicine in Baghdad, but the violence after 2003 made practising impossible for me. In 2010 I came to Switzerland. My diploma was only partly recognised, so for many years I worked as an interpreter in hospitals and asylum centres, and later as a research assistant in a public health institute.

As an interpreter, I have sat with hundreds of refugees telling their stories to doctors. I have seen how often their suffering goes untreated, because no one understands them, or because the system does not see them.

I completed a master's in public health in Bern and began my doctorate in 2024. I have published five articles on refugee mental health. My research compares access to mental health services for refugees in three Swiss cantons.

I want to make mental health care reachable for people who have survived what my uncle survived, and who deserve better than silence.

I have lived in Switzerland for sixteen years and have worked for all of them. I did not expect, at forty-three, to find myself counting every franc again. But I have come too far in this research to stop. With EduAll's support I could continue until my funding is restored.
STU000187.personal_statement:
What happens to a mind that has seen too much? I have asked this question since I was a child in Baghdad, during the war of 1991, when my uncle came home from the front and never spoke again about what he had seen.

My parents were both teachers. I studied medicine in Baghdad, but the violence after 2003 made practising impossible for me. In 2010 I came to Switzerland. My diploma was only partly recognised, so for many years I worked as an interpreter in hospitals and asylum centres, and later as a research assistant in a public health institute.

As an interpreter, I have sat with hundreds of refugees telling their stories to doctors. I have seen how often their suffering goes untreated, because no one understands them, or because the system does not see them.

I completed a master's in public health in Bern and began my doctorate in 2024. I have published five articles on refugee mental health. My research compares access to mental health services for refugees in three Swiss cantons.

I want to make mental health care reachable for people who have survived what my uncle survived, and who deserve better than silence.

For four years I worked night shifts in a bakery in Cluj before I could afford to study physics. I learned to live on very little, and I learned to count. So I will count honestly here.

The bakery where I worked opened at three in the morning. Between batches of bread I read physics books from the library: Feynman, Landau, anything I could find. My co-workers laughed at me. The baker, an old man called Domnul Pop, did not. He said: "Bread needs heat and time. So do you."

My parents are both engineers, but when I was nineteen our family collapsed: my father lost his job and began drinking, my mother fell ill, and I left my first attempt at university to earn money. I stayed at the bakery for four years, and then worked another year in a warehouse to save money. During that time I helped organise the Cluj food-sharing network, collecting unsold bread from bakeries for shelters. Every night, the bread that was not sold went somewhere it was needed.

At twenty-four I finally returned to university, finished my bachelor's in physics in Cluj, and in 2025 came to ETH for the master's. My thesis is in quantum optics, and my first paper was published this year.

I want to do a doctorate and then teach. I want to be for someone what Domnul Pop was for me.

Today my numbers still look fine, and I want to be honest about that. My costs are CHF 1,637. I was born in a village in the Mekong Delta. My parents are rice farmers and never went to school. At twenty-two I married a Vietnamese man living in Switzerland, and I came to Fribourg. For fifteen years I worked in his restaurant, in the kitchen and at the till, without a salary of my own. I learned French slowly, from customers.

Many years later, I realised that I was not happy, and that many women I knew were not either. I started to read psychology books at night. At thirty-nine, I passed the passerelle and began my bachelor. It was the first thing in my life that I did only for myself.

These last months have been the hardest. But psychology has also helped me understand what was happening to me, and to make a decision I was afraid to make for years.

I want to help other women find that courage earlier than I did.

In Zurich I am active in the Palestinian student community, and I help organise coding workshops for refugee women.

My German is still weak, and outside ETH daily life is hard. But in the lab, I am at home.

I am a doctoral student in Psychology at the University of Neuchâtel, in my second year, researching the long-term psychological effects of family separation through migration. When I was five, in Ayacucho, my mother left for Switzerland to work. She sent money, letters and cassette tapes with her voice. I listened to them every night under my blanket. For five years I grew up with my grandmother, waiting. When I finally joined my mother in Neuchâtel at ten, I barely recognised her, and she barely recognised me. Every Tuesday evening for the past two years I have sat in a small room at a Geneva community centre with elderly Vietnamese women who never learned French. I help them read their letters from the health insurance, the commune, the doctor. Sometimes we just drink tea. They call me "con", my child. It is the best part of my week.

I am a doctoral student in Public Health at the University of Geneva, in my third year. My project, on access to health care for elderly migrants, was financed by a two-year fellowship that ended in August. My supervisor has confirmed that a new grant will cover my salary from 2028; until then I have a teaching assistant mandate of CHF 765 a month.

My parents, who run a small Vietnamese restaurant in Geneva and earn around CHF 5,000 a month together, give me CHF 1,424 for rent and living costs. My costs are CHF 1,980. My rent is CHF 1,156 for a studio near the university.

My parents have always given me everything. They work twelve hours a day, six days a week, and they never had the chance to study. I want to lighten their load in these months until my funding returns, and not take from them money they need for their own old age.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My parents came to Geneva in 1998 with nothing, and opened their restaurant with money borrowed from friends. I grew up between the kitchen and the dining room, doing homework on the corner table. They never went to school beyond a few years. When I received my acceptance letter for university, and later for my doctorate, my mother framed both and hung them next to the cash register.

I studied public health because I saw, through our customers and neighbours, how many elderly migrants live alone, sick, and invisible to the health system. In my bachelor's I volunteered with the Red Cross, and during my master's I led a student initiative that trained young volunteers to accompany elderly migrants to medical appointments. We trained forty volunteers in two years.

My doctoral research documents the barriers that elderly migrants face in the Swiss health system, and tests a model of community health mediators.

I want to build a career in public health research and policy, so that the old women I meet on Tuesdays are no longer alone with their letters.

I want to explain everything honestly. I began the Master in Economics at University of Zurich in February 2026. My costs are CHF 1,808 per month, with a room of CHF 709 and health insurance of CHF 260.

My parents never went to school; my father was a rice farmer, my mother sold fish. I was the first in my family to finish school and go to university in Dakar. During my studies I worked in a call centre, and I volunteered on weekends with a youth group that organised peace and reconciliation activities between young people from different communities in Casamance.

After my bachelor I worked five years in a microfinance institution in Ziguinchor, giving small loans to women farmers.

I was born with sickle-cell disease. As a child I was in hospital so often that the nurses knew my name. Doctors told my mother I might not live past twenty. I am twenty-three now.

At school I fell behind every time I was sick, and caught up every time I was well. I became captain of our school football team, and later I coached younger children in our neighbourhood for free, because I knew what it felt like to be on the bench.

In Lagos I worked two years for an environmental NGO, organising plastic clean-ups on the beaches, and I led a youth group of fifty volunteers.

In Lausanne I study environmental science. I coach children's football at a community club, and I help organise a support group for young people with sickle-cell disease in Switzerland.

My mother died last year. She did not see me finish. But I walked in, Mama. I will walk out too.

My costs are CHF 2,061 per month. My room is CHF 1,047, including utilities. Health insurance is expensive, CHF 230.

My only support is CHF 120 per month from my nephew in Dhaka, who is an accountant and whose family lives on about CHF 670. He sends this because, years ago, I paid his school fees. I have no job at the moment and no savings.

My parents were farmers and could not read. I was the first in my family to finish school. I became a nurse, and for four years I worked in a public hospital in Dhaka, in the maternity ward. I saw thousands of births. I saw women die who should not have died.

I also volunteered for four years with an NGO training village birth attendants in hygiene and emergency signs.

At twenty-seven I decided to study medicine, because I wanted to be able to do more than assist. People told me it was too late. Perhaps. But I am here, and I have passed every year so far.

I grew up in Minya, in Upper Egypt. My father was a farmer and my mother never went to school. I was the first girl in our extended family to finish secondary school. At university in Cairo, I studied journalism and started writing about women's rights. At twenty-five I was the editor of a small online magazine, leading a team of eight young writers. I left Egypt in 2020 and came to Switzerland, where I married and slowly rebuilt my life. I learned German, worked in communications, and in 2025 I started studying philosophy.

My thesis is on freedom of expression in the work of Hannah Arendt and contemporary Arab thinkers.

After my degree, I want to do a master's in political philosophy and work on human rights and freedom of expression.

I have CHF 11,019 in savings. I earned them over three years as a geographer at a water agency in Dakar, and I brought them with me for the whole master. I also earn CHF 406 a month as an assistant at a GIS lab, a few hours a week, which is what my student permit and my full-time studies allow, and my parents in Dakar, a customs officer and a secretary with a household income of about CHF 890, send me CHF 180.

My costs are CHF 1,994 a month. The gap is CHF 1,408, and my savings pay it. At this rate they will last about a year. My master ends in July 2028, because my thesis includes a fieldwork semester on the coast in Senegal.

And there is more. My partner and our daughter, who is two, joined me in Lausanne in the spring. My partner is looking for work but has not found anything yet. Their costs are not in my budget, but of course our family's money is one money. We live in a sublet studio for CHF 1,097, which ends in December; after that we have nowhere arranged, and landlords do not like families without a Swiss salary.

I am not in crisis today. But I can see the crisis coming, and I want to be honest about both.
STU000211.personal_statement:
I am twenty-five, a geographer from Dakar, a father, and a student again.

I grew up in Rufisque, on the coast just east of Dakar, where the sea has eaten the old cemetery and the fishermen's houses. Every year the beach is narrower. My grandfather, a fisherman, showed me the place where his house stood when he was young. It is under water now.

I studied geography in Dakar and worked three years for the national water agency, mapping coastal erosion and flooding. In my neighbourhood, I helped start a community group that plants filao trees along the beach to hold back the sand. We planted more than two thousand.

In February 2026 I began my master's in environmental science at Lausanne. I want to learn to model coastal change, so that cities like Rufisque can plan instead of just losing.

My daughter was born the year I decided to apply. Every time I doubt myself, I think of her, and of the beach she will inherit.

My mother calls me every evening at nine. Sometimes the call drops because of an air-raid alert in Dnipro, and I wait, holding the phone, until she calls again. This is how my days in St. Gallen end.

I am in the second year of my Master's in Business Administration at HSG. My thesis is due in July 2028. My costs are CHF 2,502 a month: my studio costs CHF 1,010 plus CHF 137 utilities, tuition at HSG is CHF 522, and my health insurance, CHF 220.

I was twenty-two, in the final year of my bachelor's in economics. I finished it online, from shelters and trains, and after two years in a logistics company in Kyiv, organising humanitarian supply chains, I came to Switzerland in 2025.

German is still difficult for me. My master is in English, but half of the reading lists, all the administration and all the social life are in German.

My thesis is about how small Ukrainian companies kept operating during the war. I want to work in reconstruction finance, to help rebuild the businesses that kept my country alive.

I would like to be fully transparent: at present, my resources exceed my expenses.

My parents build furniture. Nobody in our family went to university. I spent my teenage years in the workshop after school, learning to measure twice and cut once. Physics felt like the same thing, only bigger.

After school, I worked two years full-time as a technician in an electronics repair company to save money for studying abroad. I also helped organise a Saturday science club for children in our neighbourhood, with borrowed telescopes and cardboard models.

I came to Lausanne in 2025, took the preparatory course, and started physics at EPFL in February 2026.

I am a doctoral student in Biology at the University of Fribourg, in my third year, studying how alpine plants respond to warming. My doctoral position has no salary: my only income is a teaching assistant contract of about 8 hours a week, which pays CHF 932 a month, and my research time is unfunded. My supervisor has confirmed in writing that no additional funding is available before a new grant decision in 2028.

My parents, a doctor and a school director in Brașov with a household income of around CHF 4,630, contribute CHF 720 a month. My monthly costs are CHF 1,905.

My fieldwork takes place every summer at high-altitude sites in the Valais Alps and requires travel, accommodation in mountain huts and equipment, costs that my department covers only in part. An EduAll grant would allow me to complete two more field seasons without asking my parents for additional support.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My grandmother kept a garden on the slopes above Brașov, where she grew plants she had collected from the mountains over fifty years. When I was small, she knew every one by name and told me which flowered first in spring. In the last years before she died, she noticed that they were flowering earlier and earlier. "The mountain is in a hurry," she said.

That sentence became my research question. I studied biology in Cluj and worked two years as a research technician on a Carpathian biodiversity project, where I coordinated a field team of five students. I have co-authored two papers on alpine plant phenology.

My doctoral research uses long-term observations and experiments in the Swiss Alps to predict how mountain plant communities will shift under climate change.

I hope to continue in research and, one day, lead a monitoring programme for mountain ecosystems in the Carpathians.

Every evening at six I collect my two children from their after-school care, cook dinner, check their homework and put them to bed. Then, from nine until midnight, I write my doctoral thesis. That is my life in Lausanne, and I love it, but it is held together by very little.

My sister in Surabaya, a nurse, sends me CHF 360 out of a household income of about CHF 1,250. My husband stayed in Indonesia with his elderly parents and sends what he can; our children live with me. My costs are CHF 2,460 a month, including our rent and the children's food and clothing.

Surabaya is a hot, loud port city of three million, where extended families live together and the old are cared for at home, by daughters. My grandmother lived with us until she died, and I watched my mother wash, feed and turn her for six years. Nobody helped my mother. Nobody even asked if she was tired.

I became a nurse at twenty-one and worked for eighteen years, first in hospitals and later as a nurse educator. In 2018 I earned a master's in nursing in Jakarta while working. In 2025 I received a doctoral position in Lausanne, and I brought my children with me.

My research asks how families from migrant backgrounds in Switzerland care for relatives with dementia, and how nurses can support them. It is my mother's story, told in a new country.

After my doctorate I want to build family caregiver programmes, in Switzerland and in Indonesia.

For five years before coming to Switzerland, I worked as a technician in a solar power company in Lahore, installing panels on rooftops of schools and clinics in poor districts. I earned a good wage for Pakistan, and I supported my parents and two sisters. When I decided to study physics at EPFL, I promised my family that I would continue to help them.

I keep that promise. I work ten hours a week as a technician at a solar start-up in Renens, earning CHF 1,114 a month. My uncle, an electrical contractor in Lahore (household income around CHF 950), sends me CHF 250. My own costs, CHF 1,630, are covered.

My father drove a rickshaw in Lahore for thirty years. My mother sewed clothes at home. Neither went to school. I was the first in my family to finish secondary school, and I did it while working in an electronics repair shop in the evenings.

At the solar company, I became team leader for a group of eight installers. We installed panels on more than a hundred schools in low-income neighbourhoods. On weekends, I volunteered to teach children in those schools how solar energy works, with small kits I built from spare parts.

In 2022, floods destroyed the homes of many of the families we had worked with. I spent two months helping with emergency power installations in camps.

At twenty-four, I began physics at EPFL. It is extremely demanding, and I am learning to study at a level I have never known. My goal is to become an engineer in renewable energy research and to bring solar power to communities that still live in darkness.

I will tell you everything, even the savings.

I have CHF 7,398 in my account. I worked for six years as a laboratory scientist in a hospital in Lagos, and I saved half of my salary for this master. I thought it would be enough, with a small job.

My costs in Zurich are CHF 1,830 per month. My room in a student house is CHF 655, one of the cheapest in Zurich. I work in the ETH library four hours a week and earn CHF 491. My younger brother, a bank clerk in Ibadan, gives me CHF 170, a large share of the roughly CHF 930 the household has.

That leaves CHF 1,169 missing every month, which my savings cover for now. But in April, my mother had a stroke. She is paralysed on one side and needs a carer. My brother and I share the cost. My savings will go there. I cannot let her lie alone.

I began my master's in February 2026. It lasts until July 2028. I am asking EduAll to help me stay, so that my mother's care and my future do not have to fight each other.
STU000229.personal_statement:
The first time I saw an electron microscope at ETH, in my first week, I stood in front of it like a child in front of a Christmas tree. In Lagos, our hospital laboratory had one old light microscope for three technicians. We diagnosed malaria, tuberculosis, typhoid by eye, and sometimes we were wrong. I always wondered how many lives we lost because of it.

My parents, a pharmacist and a teacher, always told me to learn everything I can. At the hospital I also started a volunteer programme teaching hand hygiene in primary schools near the hospital, and I was active in the women's group of my church, organising health talks.

My master's research is on antimicrobial resistance in hospital bacteria. After my master, I want to go back to Nigeria and build a modern diagnostic laboratory.

My mother always said I would do great things. Now I want her to see them.

I will start with the hardest part, because I think you need to know it first. At the moment my residence permit is not valid. I came to Basel in 2023 with a student B permit. When I applied to renew it this spring, the cantonal migration office asked me to prove that I have around CHF 2,600 every month. I cannot prove this. My renewal is still pending, and a free legal counselling service is helping me, but until there is a decision I live in a grey zone: I am still enrolled, but I am not allowed to work and I have no valid permit card. I understand this may make my application difficult, and I am writing to you anyway, because I have nobody else to ask.

Every month I need CHF 2,101 to live and study here. My older brother and his wife in Amman send me CHF 370. He is a driver and she is a nurse, and together they earn about CHF 1,480, so they give me a quarter of what they have, while raising three children. Apart from this I have nothing. No savings, no salary, no scholarship.

The biggest cost is my room: CHF 1,152 with utilities, a small studio in Kleinbasel. I know it is expensive. I moved there after the shared flat where I lived was sold, and with a pending permit almost no one would sign a lease with me. My health insurance is CHF 225. I pay it every month before anything else, because I am afraid to be without it.

Every month there is a gap of CHF 1,731. I have covered it with small loans from friends and by eating very little at the end of the month. I cannot continue like this. And there is a cruel circle: without money I cannot get my permit, and without my permit I cannot work to earn money. A grant from EduAll would count as proof of means for the migration office. It could break this circle and let me finish my degree in July 2028.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

What do you do when a child in front of you cannot read, and you do not know how to help? This question has followed me since I was a child.

I was born in Nablus, in the West Bank. My father drove a taxi and my mother cleaned houses. Neither of them finished school, but my mother always said the same sentence to me: "They can take your house, but not what you know." I did not understand it when I was a child. I understand it now.

All through secondary school, before I came to Switzerland, I helped as a volunteer in the primary school of our neighbourhood. I was not a teacher and I was not paid. I was the one who stayed after class with the children who could not read. Some of them were eleven years old and still could not write their name. I felt so helpless. I wanted to learn how to really teach them, not only to be kind to them. This is why I chose Education, and why I came to Basel, where there is a strong tradition in pedagogy and inclusive schooling.

I will be honest: my studies have been very difficult. I arrived with good English but almost no German, and most of my courses are in German. In the first years I understood maybe half of the lectures. I recorded them and listened again at night with a dictionary. My GPA is 2.34 and my average is 62.3, and I know these are not good numbers, and that they are below what you normally ask. But I have completed 24 courses, and every one of them I passed by fighting for it. My German is much better now, and my grades in the last two semesters were my best.

Since 2023 I volunteer every Saturday at a homework café for refugee children in Kleinbasel. Many of them are like the children I left in Nablus: clever, tired, and lost in a language that is not theirs. When one boy from Eritrea read a full page in German for the first time, he looked at me like he won something. I cried on the tram home. That is the moment I knew I was in the right field.

Education, for me, is not a career plan only. It is the thing my mother told me nobody can take away. Right now my permit, my security and my plans are all uncertain. What is left is four semesters. I am asking EduAll to help me finish it, so that I can become a real teacher for children who start life with less, like I did.

---

In the first years I understood maybe half of the lectures. I recorded them and listened again at night with a dictionary. My GPA is 2.34 and my average is 62.3, and I know these are not good numbers, and that they are below what you normally ask. But I have completed 24 courses, and every one of them I passed by fighting for it. My German is much better now, and my grades in the last two semesters were my best.

Since 2023 I volunteer every Saturday at a homework café for refugee children in Kleinbasel. Many of them are like the children I left in Nablus: clever, tired, and lost in a language that is not theirs. When one boy from Eritrea read a full page in German for the first time, he looked at me like he won something. I cried on the tram home. That is the moment I knew I was in the right field.

Education, for me, is not a career plan only. It is the thing my mother told me nobody can take away. Right now my permit, my security and my plans are all uncertain. What is left is four semesters. I am asking EduAll to help me finish it, so that I can become a real teacher for children who start life with less, like I did.

My monthly costs are CHF 1,873, and every month I cover them with a patchwork: CHF 826 from my job as a hospital porter, CHF 440 from my older brother, and a small scholarship of CHF 3,912 a year from a Moroccan professional association. The patchwork is about to come apart. My room in Altstetten, for which I pay CHF 775, is in a building that will be renovated from December, and all tenants have been given notice. I came to Fribourg at sixteen, to live with my uncle, after my mother died of kidney failure in Dhaka. She needed dialysis, and we could not afford it regularly. I was fifteen when she died. I have wanted to understand how the kidney works, and fails, ever since.

My father is an engineer, and he sent me to Switzerland because he believed I would have a better chance here. The first years were very hard: a new language, a new country, grief. I learned French, finished the collège, and studied biochemistry at the University of Fribourg while working nights.

For many years I have volunteered with a kidney patients' association in Fribourg, helping organise transport to dialysis for older patients who cannot drive.

My master's research focuses on proteins involved in kidney disease. I want to continue to a PhD and work in biomedical research on chronic kidney disease, which affects millions of people in South Asia who cannot afford treatment.

Materials science matters because every technology we rely on is limited by what we can build it from. My interest began at fourteen, when I took apart my grandfather's old Soviet radio in Plovdiv and found that its components, made in the 1970s, still worked better than my three-year-old phone. I wanted to know why.

I came to Fribourg at four, when my parents took up positions at the hospital. I grew up bilingual and studied at the Collège Saint-Michel before beginning materials science.

For the past three summers I have worked as an intern at a precision engineering company in the Jura, testing the fatigue resistance of metal components. It taught me the difference between theory and what actually breaks in practice.

My thesis examines the recyclability of rare-earth magnets. After my bachelor's, I plan a master's in sustainable materials, with the goal of reducing Europe's dependence on newly mined critical materials.

## Section 4 — Financial Need Statement

Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

For eleven years I worked as a lab technician at a water treatment plant in Zaporizhzhia, testing the water that half a million people drank. When the dam at Kakhovka was destroyed in June 2023, I was on shift. I will never forget the sound of the phones.

I must tell you honestly that today I do not need money in the usual sense. I study part-time and work about 19 hours a week in a water-testing laboratory, where I earn CHF 2,169. My partner, a software engineer in Zurich, earns around CHF 9,020 a month and pays CHF 380 of my costs. My costs are CHF 1,607. I have CHF 3,092 in savings. I have more than I need.

I am applying for something else. In summer 2028 I want to spend six weeks in southern Ukraine doing fieldwork on water contamination after the dam's destruction, which will become my bachelor thesis. For those weeks I cannot work, my university does not fund fieldwork in war zones, and my partner is frightened for me and does not want to pay for it. I want to pay for it myself.

If the committee decides that my application does not fit, I will understand. There are others who need this for food and rent, and they should come first.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother cleaned floors at the plant where I later worked. My father drove a tram. Neither went to university. When I was twelve, my mother took me to the laboratory on a Saturday, and a chemist let me look at a drop of river water under the microscope. I saw it was alive. I never stopped looking.

I could not afford university after school, so I trained as a technician and worked. I was good at it. When the war started, I stayed and kept the water safe as long as I could. In 2023, after the dam, the plant was shelled. I left.

In Zurich I started environmental science at thirty-one. My grades are the best I have ever had, but that is not because it is easy. It is because I have waited so long.

I want to work on water safety in post-war reconstruction.

---

- 2008–2011: Technical college diploma in Chemical Analysis, Zaporizhzhia

- 2024–present: Laboratory assistant, water-testing laboratory (about 19 hours a week), Zurich
- 2012–2024: Laboratory technician, water treatment plant, Zaporizhzhia

I am in the first year of the Master's in Architecture at EPFL, and I will complete my degree in July 2028.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,367, including CHF 1,241 for a studio in Renens and CHF 243 for tuition. I work part-time as a model-maker for an architecture office and earn CHF 458 a month. My older brother, a civil engineer in Jaipur, gives me CHF 370, a large share of the roughly CHF 1,820 the household has.

The gap is CHF 1,539 a month. The final year of my master's, including the diploma project, brings heavy costs for models, printing and site visits.

A grant from EduAll would allow me to complete my diploma without increasing my working hours.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Jaipur is a city built of pink sandstone and courtyards, designed in the eighteenth century for a desert climate. Its old houses stay cool without machines: thick walls, shaded courtyards, jali screens that catch the wind. The new buildings around them are concrete boxes with air conditioners on every wall. Walking between the two, as a child, I understood that architecture is a choice.

I studied architecture in Jaipur and worked for six years in a firm that restored heritage buildings and designed low-cost housing. In my free time I helped organise heritage walks for school children in the old city, so that they would see their own streets differently.

In 2026 I came to EPFL to deepen my knowledge of climate-responsive design. French has been the hardest part: studio critiques move fast, and I often understand only half. But I learn every week.

My diploma project adapts traditional passive cooling to affordable housing in Rajasthan.

I want to be honest about my money. My costs are CHF 1,944 per month. I work as a teaching assistant in an after-school programme and earn CHF 1,118. My brother in Kaolack, a small shop owner whose family lives on about CHF 880, sends me CHF 150. So I miss CHF 676 per month. I have no savings.

The bigger problem is my room. I rent it from a family who have told me they will sell the flat in December. I have looked since June. Everything I find in Bern costs much more than my room now, and I need a deposit.

I could work a few more hours, but my final teaching placement takes three days a week, and I also must write my thesis.

Kaolack is a city of salt and peanuts, in the heart of Senegal. The salt flats shine white in the sun. My mother worked there, carrying salt on her head for twenty years. My father was a teacher, and he taught me to read before I went to school.

At twelve, my father died. My mother kept us alive with the salt. I left school for two years to help her, then went back and finished. After teacher training I worked for two years as a primary school teacher in Kaolack, and I coordinated the reading programme of the lower grades, with five teachers.

In 2024 I came to Bern to study education, to learn how to teach children who do not speak the school language, like so many in Senegal, where school is in French and home is in Wolof.

My thesis compares how Swiss and Senegalese schools support multilingual children.

STU000246.personal_statement:
Kaolack is a city of salt and peanuts, in the heart of Senegal. The salt flats shine white in the sun. My mother worked there, carrying salt on her head for twenty years. My father was a teacher, and he taught me to read before I went to school.

After teacher training I worked for two years as a primary school teacher in Kaolack, and I coordinated the reading programme of the lower grades, with five teachers.

In 2024 I came to Bern to study education, to learn how to teach children who do not speak the school language, like so many in Senegal, where school is in French and home is in Wolof.

My thesis compares how Swiss and Senegalese schools support multilingual children.

My parents worked in a textile factory in Botoșani until it closed in 2003. Neither of them went to university. After that, my father left for Italy to work on construction sites, and I did not see him for years. At sixteen I left school and followed him. For five years I worked on building sites in Italy and Germany, first as a labourer, then as a crane operator, and in the last year as foreman of a team of eight.

At twenty-one I decided to study. I did an engineering bachelor's in Bucharest while working, and then came to Bern for the master's. I published my first paper this year, on structural health monitoring of bridges.

I grew up in Nyalenda, an informal settlement in Kisumu, where cholera came almost every rainy season. My mother sold vegetables in the market and my father was a boda-boda driver who died in a road accident when I was ten. Neither had gone to secondary school.

When I was sixteen, I started volunteering with a community health programme, going door to door explaining how to treat water and recognise dehydration. At twenty I was elected youth coordinator for the programme, leading forty young volunteers. We reduced cholera cases in our area by more than half in two years, and I co-authored a short paper with a researcher from the university who evaluated our work.

I studied public health in Kisumu on a scholarship while working as a data clerk at the county health office.

In Geneva I want to learn how to design and evaluate programmes at scale, so that what worked in Nyalenda can work in other settlements.

My parents did not go to school for long, but they want me to study more than anything. I learned German, worked in a warehouse, and did the passerelle.

In St. Gallen I study data science. It is hard, the mathematics and the programming in German, but I like to see patterns in chaos. My thesis is about predicting demand for a supply chain.

I am a doctoral student in Environmental Science at the University of Bern, in my third year. In January 2023, I spent my first winter in Bern. Walking to the institute on icy pavements with crutches, I fell twice in one week. A stranger helped me up the second time, carried my bag to the door and said, "Next time, take the tram, it stops right there." It was such a small kindness, but I remember it every day.

I was born in a village near Palu, in Central Sulawesi. My parents are farmers and never went to school. At fourteen, I developed transverse myelitis, an inflammation of the spinal cord, which left my legs weak. I walk with crutches.

In 2018 an earthquake and tsunami destroyed Palu. My family lost our house and my father's land. I was working as a researcher at a local university at the time, studying land use, and I helped coordinate emergency surveys of damaged areas.

My doctoral research is on land-use change and landslide risk in Sulawesi. I want to return to Indonesia and help make rebuilding safer.

I co-authored three reports and articles on the protection of civilians.

In 2024, after our office was destroyed and several colleagues were killed, I was evacuated with the help of an international scholars' network.

My doctoral research examines the legal protection of civilian infrastructure, water, electricity and hospitals, in armed conflict.

For eighteen years I worked as a notary's assistant in Chernihiv, drafting contracts, wills and property deeds for ordinary families. I know how much a single document can protect or destroy a household.

I started the Master of Law at the University of Neuchâtel in February 2026, part-time, to requalify in Swiss law. I work about 16 hours a week as an administrative assistant in a notary's office in Neuchâtel and earn CHF 1,787. My costs are CHF 1,845 a month. My husband, who works as an engineer in a watch company in Neuchâtel and earns about CHF 5,860, contributes CHF 420. I also receive a small scholarship of CHF 3,243 a year from a foundation supporting Ukrainian professionals.

From September 2027 I will study full-time, to finish in January 2029 rather than July 2029. The programme includes an internship period in a law firm, which is unpaid, and I will keep only a few hours at the notary's office, about CHF 340 a month. I would like to use an EduAll grant for that year and for a required language certificate in legal French.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

In March 2022, our apartment building in Chernihiv was hit during the siege. My husband and I spent five weeks in the basement with our neighbours. I organised water and food distribution for the forty people there, and I kept a list of every family's documents, because I knew that without them, nobody could prove what they had lost.

I was eighteen when the occupation of our village began. For eight months we lived under it. I finished my first year of university online, from my bedroom, with the curtains closed, afraid of every car that stopped outside. When the village was liberated, we found the school burned and the library destroyed.

When the village was free, I was elected to coordinate the youth council's rebuilding of the school library, which we reopened with two thousand donated books.

I completed my bachelor's in computer science in Kyiv and came to Lugano in 2026. My master's is in data science, and I want to use it for something very concrete: mapping mined agricultural land in Ukraine from satellite data, so that farmers like my father know where it is safe to walk.

In 2026 I came to Geneva for the master. My thesis is about proteins involved in autoimmune inflammation, and one article with my supervisor is already published.

In Khulna I volunteered with a youth group that taught computer basics to girls in our neighbourhood.

Every Saturday and Sunday since I was sixteen, I have worked. First stacking shelves in a supermarket in Renens, then in a warehouse, and now as a technician in a small engineering firm, where I earn CHF 820 a month. I have almost never had a free weekend since. I am not complaining; I am only explaining.

I study Mechanical Engineering at EPFL, in my final master's semester. My costs are CHF 2,113 a month. My mother, who cleans offices in Lausanne and earns about CHF 1,620 part-time, gives me CHF 500, almost a third of what she earns. I have no savings. The gap is CHF 793 every month, which until now I covered by working more in the summer.

This year my laboratory courses are full-time, and I cannot work the summer hours that usually save me. I am determined to finish. I want my mother to stop cleaning offices at night, and for that I need to finish.

I came to Lausanne at twelve, from Kumasi, to join my mother. She had left when I was six. For six years we spoke on the phone every Sunday. When I arrived, she was almost a stranger, and so was the language, the cold, the school. I was put in the lowest class. A teacher told me engineering was "not realistic".

My mother never went to school. She cleaned offices at night, and I often went with her, doing my homework in empty meeting rooms under fluorescent lights. I remember reading about bridges in a textbook on a conference table at two in the morning.

I finished the maturité, then studied mechanical engineering at EPFL. My master's thesis on heat exchangers for low-cost refrigeration has led to a co-authored conference paper. My GPA is 3.62.

I want to design cooling systems for vaccines and food in regions without reliable electricity, like parts of Ghana.

Every month, CHF 1,399 more leaves my account than enters it. I can calculate exactly when my savings will end: in about ten months.

I began my doctorate in Microbiology at the University of Bern in February 2026. My only funding is teaching, about 8 hours a week, which pays CHF 912 a month; my supervisor has confirmed in writing that the remaining funding depends on a grant to be decided in 2028. My father, a retired school teacher in Peshawar living on a pension of about CHF 890 with my mother and grandmother, sends me CHF 210.

I stayed and carried samples for hours. Some of them I had seen in our neighbourhood. I did not sleep for two days. I think that was the day I decided that I wanted to do something with my life that saves people, not only reports on them.

My father taught mathematics for forty years. He taught me that knowledge is a responsibility. After my master's, I became laboratory manager of a private diagnostic centre, leading a team of nine technicians, and introduced molecular testing for tuberculosis.

My doctoral research is on how tuberculosis bacteria survive antibiotic treatment. It is slow, careful work, and I love it.

I grew up in a small town in Punjab. I am transgender and non-binary, and at sixteen, when my family discovered who I was, my life became dangerous. My father and uncles threatened to kill me. With the help of my aunt, I left India, and in Switzerland I was recognised as a refugee.

The years after were hard. I had to learn French, finish school, and survive depression. For a long time I could not work or study at all. What saved me was a community: a small group of LGBTQ refugees in Fribourg, which I later helped to organise and which now meets every week.

In 2024, at twenty-nine, I finally started university. Biology is my home now. I love the patience of plants.

I want to work in plant research, maybe on crops that grow in poor and salty soils, like the fields of Punjab.

I am in the second year of my Bachelor's in Educational Sciences at the University of Bern. My monthly expenses are low, CHF 1,417, because I live in a shared flat for CHF 481. My older brother and I were the first to finish secondary school, and we did it by studying under a streetlight near our house in Lahore, because the electricity was cut every evening.

In 2023 I came to Bern to study education formally, to understand the theory behind what I had done by instinct. My research interest is adult literacy and second-language learning among migrant women.

I will be honest from the first line: I do not need money for rent or food.

I came to Neuchâtel in 2024 on a student permit, for a year of French and bridging courses in mathematics before the master. During that year the insurance company where I tutored staff in statistics offered me a 60% contract as a data assistant, about 24 hours a week. I accepted, my permit was changed to a work permit, and in 2025 I began the master part-time. I earn CHF 2,650. He needs private treatment and a supported living place, which the Romanian system does not provide in time. My parents are pensioners. My partner and I are paying. I want to use the money I earn for him. I cannot reduce my contract for my thesis year, because my permit depends on it, so the thesis will have to fit into evenings and weekends until January 2029. A grant would let me buy some of that time back, for example by taking unpaid days for my thesis.

I understand if you decide that my case does not fit. Many applicants need help for food and rent. They should come first.

I left school at seventeen, after our father's accident at the factory, to work. For many years I worked in shops and warehouses, and I volunteered with an organisation supporting people with mental illness, perhaps because I already saw something in my brother that nobody wanted to name. I also helped organise a community garden in our neighbourhood.

At thirty-three I finally went to university in Timișoara, and at thirty-eight I came to Neuchâtel, with the master as my goal. My first paper, on graph theory, was published this year.

I want to teach mathematics, and to work on mental health support for students.

How do you study to become a doctor at forty-five while raising a child alone? One day at a time, and with a very careful budget.

I am in the first year of the Joint Medical Master in St. Gallen. My costs are CHF 1,996 a month, and my room share is CHF 616. I work as a nursing assistant in a care home on weekends and earn CHF 1,169. My cousin in Amman, a teacher whose household lives on about CHF 990, sends me CHF 170. I also have a scholarship of CHF 5,985 a year from a medical foundation.

What these numbers do not show is my daughter. She is twelve. Her costs are not in my budget, but every franc I earn is shared with her. From October, my final clinical rotations begin: full days, sometimes nights, in the hospital. I will have to give up most of my weekend shifts, and with them most of my income.

I want to finish. I am so close. A grant would let me finish without my daughter paying for it.

What makes a nurse decide, at thirty-eight, to become a doctor? For me it was a night in Gaza in 2014, in the hospital where I had worked for eleven years. The electricity failed during an operation. The surgeon kept working by the light of our phones. We saved the patient. Afterwards the surgeon said to me: "You should have been a doctor." I laughed. But I never forgot.

In 2015 I came to Switzerland with my daughter, then a baby. My marriage ended soon after. For years I worked as a nursing assistant and learned German at night. My Palestinian nursing diploma was not enough, so I started again: bachelor of medicine in Zurich, and now the master in St. Gallen.

My daughter does her homework next to me every evening. She says she will be a doctor too. I tell her: first sleep.

After my studies I want to work in emergency medicine.

For eleven years I worked as a mountain guide assistant in the Atlas, carrying bags, cooking for trekking groups, and later leading groups of tourists up Toubkal. I learned every rock on the path. I did not know their names.

I want to be honest: today I do not have a monthly deficit. I study part-time and work as a cleaner in a hospital, about 18 hours a week in the evenings, and earn CHF 2,028. I apply because I want to reduce my evening work, to have the time to catch up and pass my retakes. My husband's salary also supports his parents in Marrakech, and we cannot afford for me to fail and lose a year. My bachelor ends in January 2032.

I grew up in a Berber village in the High Atlas. My parents were shepherds; my mother could not read. But my father had studied at a teachers' college in Marrakech before he returned to the land, and he taught me to read with old newspapers. At twelve I left school to work.

The mountains were my school. As a guide assistant, I saw floods destroy villages and landslides close roads. After the earthquake of 2023, I went back to my village and spent three months helping rebuild with the association of our valley, which I have been part of for many years. I saw that houses built on the wrong ground fell, and others stood.

I came to Switzerland in 2014 after my marriage. At thirty-seven, I began to study geology, to learn the names of the rocks I walked on all my life, and why the ground moves.

I want to work on landslide and earthquake risk in mountain villages, in Morocco and in the Alps.

I began the Bachelor's in Physics at the University of Geneva in September 2025. My monthly costs are CHF 2,222, mostly my room at CHF 1,145. I work as a kitchen assistant six hours a week and earn CHF 687. My mother, a shea butter trader in Tamale, gives me CHF 310, a large share of the roughly CHF 1,090 the household has. The gap is CHF 1,225 a month.

My academic record in the first year is poor: my GPA is 2.08, and I am at risk. The move from Ghana to Geneva, the French language and the pace of the physics courses overwhelmed me, and I failed two courses. I am retaking them this autumn, and I have joined a tutoring programme.

I work because I must, but it costs me study time. A grant would allow me to reduce my kitchen hours in the second year, when I need to prove that my first year was not my limit.
STU000317.personal_statement:
What changes a life? For me, it was a torch. When I was nine, in a village near Tamale, there was no electricity, and a teacher gave me a solar torch for winning a mathematics contest. For the first time, I could read at night. I took the torch apart to see how it worked. I have been curious about physics ever since.

My parents never went to school. I grew up helping my mother sell shea butter at the market. At sixteen I founded a study club in our town, where older students taught younger ones; it now has sixty members. I volunteered with a solar lamp project, and worked two years in a phone repair shop to save money.

I know my first year was weak. But I am the first person in my family to go to university, and I will not waste it.

Philosophy matters because it asks what we owe each other, a question every refugee camp, every border and every city answers badly or well. For three years I worked as a microbiologist at the Central Public Health Laboratory in Kabul. I tested water after floods, stool samples during cholera outbreaks, blood during measles epidemics. In August 2021, I went to the laboratory for the last time. Women were no longer allowed to work there.

I want to be transparent about my finances. My costs are CHF 2,312 a month. My studio costs CHF 1,351; it is expensive, but it was the only place I could find quickly when I arrived. I studied biology in Kabul and did my master's in India on a scholarship. At the Central Public Health Laboratory, I trained young technicians, most of them women, and published two papers on waterborne diseases.

After 2021, I stayed at home for two years, teaching my nieces in secret. In 2023 I received a place in a programme for Afghan scientists and came to Switzerland.

French is my fourth language, and every lecture is exhausting. But I understand the science, and my supervisor trusts me.

I want to continue research on waterborne diseases, and to train the women scientists that Afghanistan will need again one day.

I also have no job, and I want to be honest about why, and about the fact that I have never had a paid job. For most of my adult life I cared for my father, who had Parkinson's disease, and for our home in Accra. After he died in 2022, I was finally free to study again. When I came to Bern, my German was too weak for most jobs, and I have put all my energy into my master's.

I know that my CV is thin compared with other applicants, and that I have no long list of activities to show. My master's in Environmental Science ends in July 2028.

My costs are CHF 2,401 a month. My studio in Écublens costs CHF 1,277. I took it in a hurry when I arrived, and it is too expensive; I am on the waiting list for student housing. My health insurance is CHF 300.

I work as a data assistant for a humanitarian organisation, remotely, about seven hours a week, and earn CHF 752. My brother in Tehran, an engineer whose family lives on about CHF 740, sends me CHF 110.

The gap is CHF 1,539 each month, and I have no savings. I must also be honest about my grades: my GPA is 2.74. The first semester at EPFL was very hard for me, after years away from mathematics.

I have four semesters left. My thesis is due in July 2028.
STU000328.personal_statement:
The first time I saw snow in Lausanne, in December 2024, I stood outside the Rolex Learning Center and laughed like a child. In Herat it snows rarely. For a moment I forgot everything: the war, my family far away, the exam I had failed that morning.

My father was an engineer and my mother a teacher. In 2021, when the Taliban took Herat, I was working as a data officer for an international NGO, mapping schools and clinics. My name was on lists of people who worked with foreigners. I hid for four months, moving between relatives' houses, before I could leave through Iran.

For four years in Herat I volunteered teaching computer skills to girls, and I helped organise a community library. In Lausanne I help Afghan newcomers with administration and translation.

My thesis is on using satellite data to estimate access to health services in Afghanistan. One paper has already been accepted.

I want to work in humanitarian data science.

My monthly costs are CHF 1,955, and my monthly income is CHF 710. The difference, CHF 1,245, is what I am asking EduAll to help with, and I want to explain it fully.

I am a doctoral student in Biology at Università della Svizzera Italiana (USI), in my second semester. I studied biotechnology in Lahore on scholarships, and worked for three years as a research assistant, publishing three papers on plant disease resistance. When I was twenty-two, my father died, and I became responsible for my two younger sisters' education. Both are now at university.

I am in the first year of the Master's in Educational Sciences at the University of Fribourg, and I will complete it in July 2028.

My mother, a hospital doctor in Lviv, and my stepfather, an engineer, have a household income of around CHF 3,020 and contribute CHF 730 to my costs. I work as a teaching assistant at a Ukrainian community school and at a daycare centre, earning CHF 1,140. My monthly expenses are CHF 2,340.

On my first morning in Fribourg in 2022, I heard the church bells ring and instinctively looked for the nearest shelter. A woman at the bus stop saw my face, and without a word, she offered me her umbrella. I was nineteen, alone, and that small kindness is still with me.

I grew up in Lviv. My mother is a doctor and my stepfather an engineer; my father died when I was twelve. When the war began, my school class scattered across Europe. I came to Fribourg to finish my studies, and since then I have worked with children in a daycare centre and at a Ukrainian Saturday school, where children who had lost everything came to learn their own language.

My research is on how schools maintain education in wartime: underground classrooms, online teaching, and what children lose and gain.

I want to work in education reconstruction in Ukraine after the war.

I want to lay everything out honestly, because I think it is the only way to ask for help.

My costs are CHF 2,183 a month. My only regular support is CHF 190 from my sister, a teacher in Jos whose household lives on around CHF 660, and a small scholarship of CHF 1,004 a year from a Nigerian sociological association. I have no job.

I do have CHF 11,869 in savings. They come from the sale of my late father's land, which my siblings agreed to use for my studies. I use them to pay the gap of CHF 1,993 every month. They will be gone before the end of my master's in January 2028, probably in the spring.

Jos was once called the "home of peace and tourism." When I was fourteen, in 2010, it became again a city of riots. My school was burned. My neighbours, Christians and Muslims who had shared meals for decades, killed each other in the streets. My father, a secondary school headmaster, hid a Muslim family in our house for a week.

That week shaped my life. After university, I spent six years volunteering with an interfaith peace organisation, documenting violence and organising dialogue groups between young people from both communities. We published two studies on the causes of violence in the Middle Belt. I also led a community radio programme on reconciliation.

In Zurich I study sociology to understand why neighbours turn against each other, and how communities rebuild trust.

I want to return to Jos and help build lasting peace.

My parents, a civil engineer and a teacher who came to Zurich from Basra, earn around CHF 6,200 together and contribute CHF 810 to my costs. I work as an IT support technician for a school, earning CHF 1,092. My monthly costs are CHF 1,728.

In my final semester, I will take part in a software project with a humanitarian organisation in Geneva that requires regular travel and some equipment. A grant from EduAll would allow me to take this opportunity while reducing my working hours during the thesis period.
STU000368.personal_statement:
Computer science matters to me because it can make information reach people who have none. When my family arrived in Zurich in 2014, my parents struggled for months with forms, letters and official websites in German. I was fourteen, and I became the family's translator and IT support. I learned that technology can be a wall or a door.

At school I founded a coding club for newcomer children, and since 2020 I have volunteered teaching digital skills to older migrants at a community centre. At the university, I was elected president of the computer science students' association, organising hackathons for social projects.

My thesis builds a multilingual chatbot that helps refugees understand official letters.

After my degree I want to work on accessible digital public services.

My parents never went to school. In 2021, our family left Afghanistan; my father stayed behind to protect the shop, and I have not seen him since. I came to Switzerland with my mother and sisters. Our asylum application was rejected, but we were provisionally admitted, because we could not be sent back to Afghanistan.

In the refugee centre, I organised a small study group for Afghan teenagers, teaching mathematics and German. Later I was elected spokesperson of the young residents. I work in a shop in St. Gallen and help new Afghan families with administration.

Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

I want to tell you about my life here honestly, because it is complicated.

I am in the first year of the Master in Health Sciences at the University of Lucerne. My student B permit expired in July, and I applied for renewal on time. But the migration office asks me to prove that I have about CHF 2,600 every month. My only regular support is CHF 190 from my uncle in Sylhet, a teacher whose household earns around CHF 810. So my renewal is pending, and while it is pending, I am not allowed to work.

My costs are CHF 2,070 per month. My room costs CHF 975. I have type 1 diabetes, and my insulin and sensors cost more than my insurance covers.

In June my father in Sylhet lost his small shop in a flood. My family cannot help me anymore.

Every month I miss CHF 1,880. I have no savings. I am determined to finish. With a grant, I could show the migration office my means and finish my degree in July 2028.

I want to tell you the truth about my situation, even though today I have no gap.

My costs are CHF 2,010 a month. I study part-time and work about 14 hours a week as a data analyst intern at a humanitarian organisation, earning CHF 1,610, and my partner, a nurse in Zurich who earns around CHF 5,900, contributes CHF 530 to my costs. I have no savings.

But I am afraid of the next year. My internship ends in December, and the organisation can offer me only a smaller contract, about CHF 1,040 a month from September 2027. Then CHF 440 a month is missing. My partner's income is already stretched: we send money every month to my mother and my younger sister in Erbil.

I apply to EduAll because I want to finish this degree, in January 2029, without losing the balance we have fought for.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Data science matters to me because data decides who is counted. In 2014, when ISIS came to our town near Sinjar, my family was not on any list. We were Yazidis, farmers who had never gone to school, and no one knew where we had gone. We lived for three years in a camp near Duhok, uncounted.

In the camp I volunteered as a registration assistant for an aid organisation, helping families register for food and medical care. I learned how a missing name can mean a missing meal. Later I worked for that organisation as a data officer, and I organised a youth group that taught English to children in the camp.

In 2019 I came to Switzerland to join my partner, whom I met when they worked as a nurse for a medical team in the camp; I received my permit through family reunification. German has been hard, and it still is. I learned programming at night.

I want to build humanitarian data systems that never leave anyone uncounted.

I want to be honest: my money is enough at this moment. I study part-time and work about 19 hours a week, from home, as an online tutor for mathematics and physics, and I earn CHF 2,155. In February 2026, in my first week in Fribourg, I slipped on the ice with my crutches in front of the university. A physics professor helped me up. Two weeks later he offered me a place in his laboratory. I still smile when I think how we met.

I have cerebral palsy, which affects my legs. My parents worked in a factory in Galați and did not go to university. They carried me to school on their backs when the buses were not accessible.

In Romania I worked as a tutor for mathematics and physics for five years, and I led a student group for disability rights at my university. In Fribourg I help in the parents' association of my son's crèche.

My thesis is about optical sensors. I want to become a researcher in photonics.
