I am in the first year of the Master's in Physics at the University of Bern. My monthly costs are CHF 2,434, including CHF 1,127 for a room and CHF 445 for health insurance. My only regular support is CHF 80 a month from my uncle in Kabul, a shopkeeper whose household earns about CHF 270.

I have CHF 9,091 in savings, from a scholarship for scholars at risk that ended this summer, and from the sale of my late father's books and instruments. I am using them to cover the monthly gap of CHF 2,354, which means they will last only about four months.

I have no work history, and I do not currently work. I have a hearing impairment and use hearing aids, which makes many student jobs difficult for me. I realise my savings may make my situation look less urgent than it is; I wanted you to see the full picture.
STU000413.personal_statement:
My father taught physics at Kabul University for twenty-five years. When I was a child, he explained the stars to me on the roof of our house. My mother was a teacher.

In 2017, a bomb exploded near the university library where I was studying. I survived, but I lost most of my hearing. My father told me: "Physics does not need ears."

After 2021, my father lost his position and fell ill. He died in 2024. My younger brother, who stayed in Kabul, was arrested in March this year and is still detained. My mother depends on my uncle.

I left Afghanistan in 2023 with a scholarship. I study theoretical physics, which needs pen, paper and silence. I have all three.

What does a nurse do when the hospital is bombed? You keep working in the basement. I learned this in Homs in 2012, when I was twenty. Our hospital was hit three times. We moved the patients underground and continued by torchlight.

My father taught mathematics and my mother was a midwife. I trained as a nurse in Damascus, worked five years in hospitals under siege, and volunteered in a mobile clinic that reached villages cut off by the fighting. In 2017 I came to Switzerland, learned French, and worked as a nurse in a care home while completing a master's degree.

In Lausanne I help lead a group of Arabic-speaking nurses who support refugee families with health information.

My doctoral research studies how nurses in conflict zones cope with moral distress. I want this knowledge to protect nurses in future crises.

For four years, before I started medicine, I worked as an ambulance technician in Iași. On a night shift you learn quickly what is urgent and what can wait. I will try to apply the same standard to my own application.

My parents run a small construction company in Iași. Their combined income is around CHF 5,030 a month in good years, and they send me CHF 1,170. I come from Iași, in the north-east of Romania. My parents started their construction company after the revolution with one van and two workers. Neither of them went to university. They wanted me to take over the company one day, and I spent my school holidays on building sites.

At nineteen, I took a course as an ambulance technician instead, and for four years I worked on emergency crews covering the city and the villages around it. Public health is the reason I am here, and it is also the reason I work. Two long shifts a week, about 13 hours, I am a care assistant in a nursing home in Kriens, and I earn CHF 1,425 a month. My husband works in a hotel kitchen and earns around CHF 3,700. From this he gives CHF 380 each month for my study costs, and it is a lot for us.

My costs are CHF 1,990 a month. Rent for my part of our small flat is CHF 853, health insurance CHF 330, food CHF 344, and tuition CHF 180. The rest is transport, phone and study materials. Every month I am CHF 185 short, and I cover it with extra night shifts.

I have studied part-time until now. From September 2027 I want to study full-time and finish in July 2028, one year earlier. I will write my bachelor thesis on vaccination among migrant families in central Switzerland; I have started interviews with mothers from five communities. I will keep one weekend shift, about CHF 1,240, and I will be CHF 370 short each month.

I have looked for other help. The cantonal grants are closed to me because I began my studies after age 35. A grant from EduAll would let me stop the extra night shifts until I finish.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I believe that most people who die too early die of something we already know how to prevent. I learned this in Sylhet, in Bangladesh, where my father taught biology at a secondary school and my mother was a village nurse. When I was twelve, a cholera outbreak came to our town after the floods. My mother worked day and night. She came home and cried for the children she could not save.

After school I became a community health worker. For ten years I travelled by boat and on foot to villages that are cut off in the rainy season, weighing babies, giving vaccines, teaching mothers about clean water. In 2007 a cyclone destroyed the clinic where I worked and our family home. We rebuilt both. I learned then that I can start again from nothing.

In 2016 I came to Switzerland with my husband. I did not speak German. I cleaned offices, then became a care assistant, and every evening I studied. In 2023, at thirty-eight, I began my degree. I have completed twenty courses.

In Lucerne I also help run health evenings for Bengali-speaking women, about check-ups, vaccines and how the Swiss health system works. Many of them had never had a smear test.

I want to work in maternal and child health, in Switzerland or with an international organisation. For me, education is the way to do at large scale what my mother did in one village.

I am applying to EduAll for support during the last four semesters of my Bachelor's in Medicine at the University of Zurich, which I will complete in July 2028 before continuing to the master's programme.

My monthly expenses total CHF 2,213. The largest item is rent, CHF 1,197 for a room in a shared flat in Oerlikon, followed by food at CHF 328 and tuition and semester fees at CHF 203. The remainder covers health insurance, transport, phone and study materials.

My only regular income is CHF 495 a month from my elder brother, who works as a delivery driver in Zurich and earns around CHF 3,900. He shares a small flat with two colleagues and sends me more than he can comfortably spare. This leaves a monthly shortfall of CHF 1,718.

Until last year I covered this gap by working evenings in a restaurant kitchen and on weekend cleaning shifts. From this semester onwards, however, my timetable includes clinical skills training, bedside teaching and preparation for the bachelor's examinations, which make regular paid work impossible without jeopardising my studies. I stopped working in the spring and have been covering my costs from the last of my earnings, which are now exhausted.

My housing is also insecure. My current sublet ends in December, and without a stable income I cannot sign a lease of my own. An EduAll grant would allow me to secure a room for the coming year and to concentrate fully on the examinations that will determine whether I can continue into the clinical master's programme.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was nine, my grandmother fell ill in our village near Barisal. The nearest doctor was across the river, and the ferry did not run in the monsoon. My father carried her to the landing twice, and twice we turned back. I remember sitting beside her mat that night, fanning her, not understanding why no one could come. She recovered, slowly, but I never forgot the feeling of a problem that had a solution just out of reach.

My parents farm rice on a small plot of land, and neither of them completed primary school. I was the first in my family to finish secondary school, and the first to attend university. I came to Switzerland in 2019, at eighteen, and have lived here under provisional admission since then. My asylum application was rejected, but I cannot be sent back: my family belongs to the Urdu-speaking Bihari minority, and the Bangladeshi authorities have refused to issue me a passport. For my first years I learned German in intensive courses while working in restaurant kitchens, and in February 2024 I began my medical studies in Zurich.

The past two and a half years have tested me academically and practically. I have moved house five times, twice at very short notice, and for several weeks in 2024 I slept on friends' floors while searching for a room. Through all of this I have completed twenty-two courses and have not interrupted my studies once.

Since 2023 I have been part of a health information project for newly arrived Bengali-speaking families, helping them understand how to register with a doctor, use the emergency services and apply for health insurance subsidies. Many of them are where I was a few years ago.

I intend to specialise in general internal medicine and, in the long term, to work in rural primary care. For me, education is what stands between a problem and its solution, and I hope to become the doctor who crosses the river.

---

I start my master in Materials Science in Basel in February 2026. It is a programme of two and a half years, with an internship semester, until July 2028.

My costs each month are CHF 2,109. The room is CHF 962, health insurance is CHF 345, food is CHF 370, and the semester fees are CHF 142. Other things are transport, phone and materials for the lab.

My brother lives in Istanbul and works in a small shop. He earns around CHF 500 in a month and still he send me CHF 90. I know this is a big part of what he has. I do not have other income now, so each month I miss CHF 2,019.

Before the master I work for three years as a cleaner and in a warehouse in Basel. With this money I paid the German courses and the first months of study. Now the master has lab practicals every day, and it is not possible to work many hours. My room is also only a sublet until December, and the owner wants it back.

With the support of EduAll I can rent a room for the full year and study without to count every franc. I will do everything to finish the degree in time.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

It was in March 2026, in the first week of the semester. The professor gave us a sample of a new polymer and asked what we would test first. I answered in German, slowly, but correct. After the class a classmate asked me where I learned polymer chemistry. I told him: in Kabul, ten years ago. He did not believe me.

I am from Kabul. I studied chemical engineering at Kabul Polytechnic University and then I worked five years as an engineer in a factory for plastic pipes, controlling the quality of material. I was proud of this work. Water pipes are important in a city where many people have no clean water.

After 2021 everything changed and the factory closed. In 2022 I came to Switzerland to join my sister, who lives in Basel since many years. I was 27 and I started from zero: new language, no recognised diploma, no work in my field. I cleaned offices, then I worked in a warehouse. In the evenings I learned German, from A1 to C1 in three years.

I moved five times in these years. Sometimes I slept at my sister's family, sometimes in a room for only one month. But I never stopped to study.

In Basel the university recognised my diploma, and I could start the master. My dream is to work on materials for water infrastructure, pipes that last longer and are cheaper. Maybe one day it helps in Afghanistan, maybe in other places with the same problem.

For me education is the thing nobody could take from me, when everything else was taken.

Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

My doctoral research at EPFL concerns low-cost water treatment membranes, and my long-term goal is to see them manufactured in West Africa. The financial position I describe here is what stands between that goal and the next three years of work.

Unlike most doctoral candidates at EPFL, I am not employed as a doctoral assistant. I was admitted in 2025 on the basis of a project I proposed myself, with the agreement that my supervisor would seek dedicated funding for it. A first application to a national funding agency was not successful, and a resubmission is under review, with a decision expected in 2028. Until then, I am enrolled as a self-funded candidate.

My monthly expenses are CHF 2,472. Rent is CHF 1,255 for a studio in Renens, health insurance CHF 455, food CHF 334 and utilities CHF 140; the remainder covers transport, phone, materials and fees. Against this, I receive CHF 310 a month from my sibling in Lagos, whose household lives on about CHF 1,130, and I earn CHF 213 a month through occasional technical translation. I also hold a scholarship of CHF 1,739 a year from a professional engineering association. Before that scholarship, my monthly shortfall is CHF 1,949.

The conditions of my provisional admission, together with the demands of full-time laboratory work, limit how much additional employment I can undertake. I have applied to three further foundations and continue to pursue other options.

EduAll support during this bridging period would allow me to keep my research on schedule until project funding is secured, and to complete my doctorate in July 2029 as planned.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

By 2040, I would like to see a factory in Nigeria producing water filtration membranes that cost a tenth of today's imports. It is an ambitious goal, but it rests on something simple: every year, diarrhoeal disease from contaminated water kills tens of thousands of children in my country, and the technology to prevent this already exists. It is simply too expensive.

I was born in Kaduna and trained as a chemical engineer at Ahmadu Bello University. For four years I worked in water treatment, first for a state water board and later for an engineering firm, designing small treatment units for towns and schools. I saw how often imported equipment failed because spare parts were unavailable or unaffordable. That experience shaped the question I now pursue.

My path to Switzerland was not straightforward. In 2019 I had to leave Nigeria at short notice, for reasons connected to my personal safety, and I have lived in Switzerland since then under provisional admission. My asylum application was not accepted, but the authorities recognised that I could not safely be returned. I spent my first years learning French and working in a warehouse, while preparing a research proposal in my evenings. Completing a master's-level bridging programme and being accepted into a doctoral programme at EPFL in my early thirties is the achievement of which I am proudest.

In my first year I completed my first three doctoral courses and built the first laboratory prototype of a ceramic-polymer membrane using locally available clays.

Education, for me, is not a step on a career ladder. It is a way to return, with something useful, to the places that formed me.

---

*Instructions: Describe your financial situation and explain why you need EduAll support to pursue your studies in Switzerland. Address why paying for your education is difficult, which costs are most challenging for you, what would happen to your studies without support, and whether you have exhausted other funding options (300–400 words).*

One day I want to open a practice in Cairo where people can speak about their mental health without shame, and pay what they can. That is a long way from here. But this application is about the next year and a half, so let me be honest about where I am.

Right now my income covers my costs. I earn CHF 1,180 a month as a night receptionist in a hotel in Bern, and my older sister in Zurich sends me CHF 790 from her household income of about CHF 4,800. My costs are CHF 1,625. I know that on paper this looks comfortable.

It is not comfortable, because the money from my sister is not really for me. In June my father had a stroke in Alexandria. He cannot work any more and he needs care at home. My sister sends me the money, and I send most of it on to my mother, for the nurse and the medicines. So what is left for my own life is my salary, and some months not even that.

I have no savings and no scholarship. I do not want to leave my studies, and I do not want to stop helping my parents. Your support would let me do both without working more nights. I already work the fifteen hours a week my permit allows, mostly nights, and my body tells me it is enough.

I will understand if you decide that other students need it more.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I was not a good student at school in Alexandria. I was a good listener. My friends came to me with everything, and I did not know then that this could be a profession.

At twenty-two I finished a degree in commerce because my father wanted it. I worked three years in a bank and I was very unhappy. When I came to Switzerland in 2021 to join my sister, I decided I would try, finally, what I wanted. I learned German, first in courses and then from the guests at the hotel, and I volunteered on the telephone of a helpline for Arabic-speaking people in crisis. There I understood: I want to do this with training, not only with heart.

My first three semesters in psychology have been the happiest time I ever had as a student. I love statistics, which surprises everyone.

This summer was the hardest time. When my father had his stroke, I flew to Alexandria and I sat by his bed for ten days. He could not speak. I held his hand and told him I am studying psychology, not commerce any more. I think he smiled. I came back for my exams, and I passed all of them.

Education for me means that I can one day give people what I could not give my father: someone who knows how to help.

I am in the first year of my Master in Computer Science at University of Neuchâtel, part-time.

My costs are CHF 1,638 each month. The biggest part is rent, CHF 623 for my part of a small flat, and health insurance CHF 235. Food is CHF 371 and fees CHF 173. The rest is transport, phone, materials and small things.

I work about 20 hours a week as IT support in a school, in the mornings, and earn CHF 2,219. My partner earns around CHF 5,000 as a bus driver and gives CHF 380 for my costs. The rest of this income is for our two children and the household. I have a scholarship of CHF 5,734 per year from a foundation for Latin American students.

From September 2027 I want to study full-time, so I finish in January 2029 and not January 2030. I will keep only a few hours, about CHF 560, because I also take care of the children after school. Then CHF 698 is missing each month. With EduAll I can finish my thesis in calm.

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Computer science is for me a way to open doors. When I was a child in Ayacucho, there was one computer in the whole school, and only the director could touch it. Today I write my master thesis about software that can read Quechua voice messages and translate them into Spanish for health workers. My grandmother spoke only Quechua. In the hospital nobody understood her.

My parents are farmers. They did not go to school after primary. I was the first in my family who finished secondary school and went to university. I studied systems engineering in Lima in the evenings, and it took me eight years, because my first child was born during my studies.

In 2019 we came to Switzerland because of my partner's family. The first years were very difficult. We moved four times in two years, one time we lived three months in one room with the two children, because no one gave a flat to a family without Swiss income history. I learned French with the children, from their school books.

Since 2020 I give free computer classes to Spanish-speaking women in Neuchâtel, every Saturday. Many of them clean houses and want to learn to write CV, use e-banking, talk with the school of their children by email. Some of them now have better jobs.

I want to work on language technology for indigenous languages. For me, education is the proof that a child from Ayacucho can also build the computer, not only look at it.

On a rainy evening last February, a week before my doctorate began, I stood outside a building in Kleinbasel with two suitcases, having just learned that the room I had rented online did not exist. I spent that night in a hostel and the following six weeks in three different temporary rooms. I begin with this because it explains why I am applying, even though my budget currently balances.

I should be transparent about my situation. My wife, who works as a nursing assistant in Basel and earns about CHF 4,900 a month, contributes CHF 1,978 towards my costs. My monthly expenses are CHF 2,001, so at the moment there is no gap. I also have savings of CHF 5,944, which remain from my previous job in Jakarta.

The difficulty is that my doctoral position is not yet funded. My supervisor has applied for a project grant that would employ me as a doctoral assistant; the decision is expected in spring 2028. Until then I am enrolled without a salary, and our household depends on a single income, with a fixed-term contract that ends in March 2027. If her contract is not renewed before the grant decision, we would have to live on our savings, which would last only a few months.

I am also still paying for the consequences of my housing problems: a rent deposit I lost, and short-term rooms at a higher price. We finally found a stable flat in July.

I would ask EduAll to consider my application as insurance against a bridging period, rather than a current shortfall. If the committee sees more urgent needs, I will fully understand.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I grew up in Bandung, where my father repaired electrical equipment in a market stall and my mother sold food. I was the kind of child who took apart radios. At Bandung Institute of Technology I discovered chemistry, and I stayed for a master's in catalysis.

For five years I worked as a process chemist for a palm oil refinery near Jakarta. I was good at the work, but I became increasingly uncomfortable with its environmental cost. In 2021 I applied for a research position on biomass catalysts. That path eventually led me, after difficult personal circumstances that I prefer not to detail, to Switzerland in late 2025.

My doctoral project in Basel concerns catalysts that convert agricultural waste into chemicals. I have completed my first two doctoral courses.

My greatest difficulty is language. My research is in English, which I speak well, but everything else in daily life, from the housing office to my wife's employer, is in German. I am at level A2, and I attend evening classes twice a week. When I lost the room in February, I could not even read the complaint form.

I want to build a research career that connects Southeast Asia's agricultural economies with cleaner chemistry. Education, for me, is the long way to make up for the years I spent optimising a process I no longer believed in.

In ten years I want to work in a laboratory that tests water for arsenic. In Bangladesh millions of people drink water from tube wells with arsenic, and they do not know it. My grandfather had spots on his hands from this water. When I was small I did not understand why.

I am from Khulna. My father has a small pharmacy and my mother takes care of the house. They did not go to university, but they always told me: study, study. I am the first in my family at university.

After school I worked one year in my father's shop. I learned to talk with people about medicine and illness, and I saw how many patients came with problems from the water. Then I got admission in Fribourg. I learned French in Dhaka before, and one more year here.

The first semesters were a big change. Cold winter, new food, new language in the lab. But I like it very much. Last semester I did a small project about bacteria in river water, and I understood that this is what I want to do.

This summer I worked on a farm, picking vegetables. It was hard work, but I learned many words in Swiss German and I made friends.

For me, education is a way to bring something back. My father sells medicine to people who are ill. I want to help that they don't get ill.

My income now is a little more than my costs. I want to explain why I still apply.

My costs are CHF 2,176 a month. Rent is CHF 1,050 for a room in Neuchâtel, utilities CHF 126, food CHF 317, fees CHF 173, and the rest is health insurance, transport, phone and materials. A grant from EduAll would help me to stay in the programme while my family pays for my mother.

After high school I went to Switzerland as an au pair, at seventeen, for a family in Neuchâtel. I took care of three children, and I discovered I love to teach. I helped the children with homework in French, and I learned French at the same time as them.

After the au pair year I stayed as a nanny and prepared the university entrance. In 2025 I started the Bachelor in Education. I want to become a primary school teacher. It is a big thing for my family. When I told my mother I was admitted at the university, she cried in the market.

The first semesters were not easy. I read every text two or three times. But I like the practical part very much, in the classroom I feel at home.

Now my mother is sick, and I am far. I call her every day. She tells me to not come home, to finish the studies. I will do it for her.

For me education means to give children the same chance that the Swiss family gave to me.

The professor made a joke, and I laughed at the same time as everyone else. I nearly cried in the lecture hall. For nine months, I had been laughing a few seconds late.

I grew up in Lahore, in a small flat above a tailor's shop. My mother raised me and my two younger siblings alone. She taught me that you do not waste anything, not food, not time, not a chance.

I came to Switzerland at nineteen, and I live here now under provisional admission: my asylum application was rejected, but the authorities recognised that I could not safely return to the people who had threatened our family. I started my studies in February 2025. German was, and still is, my biggest challenge. I record every lecture, and I read the slides twice, once for the words and once for the meaning.

Even so, I have found a home. I am the elected coordinator of the international students' group in the computer science student association, and I organise our study tandems, where German-speaking students help newcomers and newcomers help with programming. I also volunteer every Saturday at a coding club for refugee teenagers in Altstetten. When a fourteen-year-old shows me the first game they made, I remember why I love this field.

I want to become a software engineer and one day build tools that help people learn languages faster, so that nobody has to laugh a few seconds late for months.

For many years I worked as a technician in a nuclear power plant in Kozloduy, and later in a medical physics department in Bern. I start with this because it explains also my money situation, which is not bad.

I will be honest. My wife is a pharmacist in Bern and our household income is about CHF 9,500. She pays CHF 1,110 of my costs, which is mostly my part of the rent and the household. I study part-time and work also 30% as a technician in a radiotherapy department, and earn CHF 1,439. My costs are CHF 2,371. So, in the moment, there is no gap.

Why I apply: from September 2027 I want to study full-time, because the master thesis in a research group in Bern is full-time. Then I finish in July 2028 and not July 2029. I would reduce my job to one day in two weeks, about CHF 560. Then CHF 701 a month is missing. My wife can pay more, but we send also money to my parents in Bulgaria, both have small pensions and my father has heart problems. We have no savings, because the move to Switzerland and my first years of study took all.

I understand very well if other students have bigger needs. If EduAll can help with even a part, it would let me finish my thesis without worry.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I was born in Vratsa, in the north-west of Bulgaria. My father worked in a cement factory, my mother was a cook in a school. Nobody in my family studied at university.

After technical school I worked at the Kozloduy nuclear plant, in radiation protection. I measured doses, calibrated instruments. I was good, but I always wanted to know why, not only how. In 2012 the plant reduced staff, and I lost my job. It was a difficult time, I had no work for one year and I was ashamed to tell my parents.

In 2014 my wife got a job in Bern, and I followed her. I did not speak German. I cleaned in a hospital for two years, and then, because of my experience, I got a position as technician in radiotherapy. There, the physicists explained me many things, and one of them said: "You should study physics. You already think like one."

At 37 I went back to school. I had only the Bulgarian technical diploma, so I did first the passerelle and bridging courses in physics, and in 2024 the university accepted me in the master, with some bachelor courses added. It was hard to study again after twenty years. I have now 5 courses. My grades are okay, not the best, GPA 3.18, but I am proud.

I want to become a medical physicist in radiotherapy. For me, education came late, but it came.

I am 25, I study physics at ETH Zurich, and I grew up in Davao, on the island of Mindanao.

My parents are coconut farmers. They did not go to secondary school. I was the first in my family to finish high school, and a teacher lent me her own university textbooks in physics because the school library did not have any.

When I was nineteen, I became involved in a student group that documented land conflicts in our region. Some members of the group were threatened, and one was killed. My family decided it was not safe for me to stay. I came to Switzerland in 2021, where my aunt already lived, and I was granted protection. This was the most painful decision of my life, and I still miss my parents every day.

In Zurich I learned German and passed the university entrance exam. I started at ETH in autumn 2025. It is very hard, and I am honest that I am not the best in my class. But when I solve a problem after hours of work, I feel something I have never felt before.

I help at a Filipino community centre in Zurich, where I give homework support to children on Saturdays, and I am part of a group that helps newly arrived Filipino workers with administration and German.

I want to become a physics teacher, maybe one day in Mindanao. Education for me means that where you are born does not decide what you can understand.

I am entering the second year of my Master's in Physics at EPFL, which I will complete in July 2028 with a thesis in experimental condensed matter physics.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Mazar-i-Sharif is a city of blue domes, dust and pigeons. In the courtyard of the Blue Mosque, thousands of white doves gather every morning, and as a child I used to count them with my father, a carpet trader who never had the chance to finish school. My mother, who learned to read as an adult, taught me the alphabet at the kitchen table.

In my city, few girls and boys from families like mine could hope to study science. My school had one physics teacher for six hundred pupils and no laboratory. What we had were questions, and a teacher who took them seriously.

At seventeen I won a scholarship to study physics at the Middle East Technical University in Ankara, where I completed my bachelor's degree in 2024. Studying in Turkish and English, far from my family, taught me that I can adapt to almost anything. In the autumn of 2025 I began my master's at EPFL.

Lausanne brought a new challenge: French. My courses are taught in English, but everything outside the lecture hall, from the housing office to my part-time job, is in French. I have progressed from beginner level to B1 in one year, and I now tutor first-year students in the language they speak best.

Alongside my studies, I have co-authored a publication on thin-film superconductors and helped found an informal network that supports Afghan students arriving in Switzerland with applications, housing searches and paperwork.

My goal is a doctorate in experimental physics, and ultimately to help build scientific education in Afghanistan when conditions allow. Education, for me, is the courtyard of doves: something that belongs to everyone who is patient enough to count.

I am applying for support during the remaining semesters of my Bachelor's in Materials Science at the University of Basel, which I will complete in July 2028.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My mother sold vegetables in Gikomba market in Nairobi for twenty-five years. She left home before dawn and came back after dark, and she still found time every evening to check my homework, although she herself had left school at twelve. When I told her I had been admitted to a university in Switzerland, she asked me only one question: "Will you learn how to make things that last?"

That question led me to materials science. In Gikomba, nothing lasts: plastic sheeting cracks in the sun, roofs rust through, water containers split. I want to understand why materials fail, and how to make durable ones cheaply.

Before coming to Basel, I worked for three years in a plastics recycling cooperative in Nairobi, first sorting waste and later managing quality control. That experience gave me practical knowledge that I use every day in the laboratory, and a clear sense of why this field matters.

I began my studies in Basel in 2024. Earlier this year my mother was diagnosed with diabetes and developed complications that stopped her from working. As the only child, I have coordinated her care from here, by telephone with doctors in Nairobi, while continuing my studies without interruption.

In Basel I co-organise a monthly repair and recycling workshop with a student sustainability group, where students learn to fix rather than throw away. It connects my studies with the people around me.

After graduating, I intend to pursue a master's degree in polymer science and, ultimately, to work on affordable, durable materials for East African markets. Education, for me, is my mother's question, and I am still working on the answer.

I grew up in Cusco. My father was an engineer at the regional water company and my mother taught secondary school biology.

I studied medicine at the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia in Lima. During my residency in emergency medicine, I saw many patients from the Andes arrive too late with complications of diabetes and high blood pressure. Most had never been diagnosed.

For seven years I worked in emergency departments in Lima. In the last two I led a shift team of twelve doctors and nurses. I also set up a monthly screening day for high blood pressure in a market in San Juan de Lurigancho, with colleagues from our hospital. In two years we screened over three thousand people.

I came to Zurich in 2025 because ETH has a strong group in digital health. My doctoral project develops a simple screening tool for rural health posts, using a smartphone and machine learning. I have completed one doctoral courses.

I miss clinical work. But I believe that a good tool can reach more people than I can in one shift.

Education, for me, is how I can multiply what I did in one hospital.

I am in the third semester of my Bachelor's in Physics at the University of Zurich, and I expect to graduate in January 2031.

My monthly expenses total CHF 2,047, of which rent accounts for CHF 977, food for CHF 368 and university fees for CHF 203. The remaining costs are health insurance, public transport, phone and study materials.

Until this spring, I worked twenty hours a week in a warehouse and covered almost all of my costs myself. In April, my father suffered a serious stroke in Senegal. I travelled home, and after my return I moved to part-time study and reduced my warehouse work to about 16 hours a week, in order to catch up on my courses and to support my family remotely, by phone and administratively, in arranging his care. I now earn CHF 1,777. My sister in Dakar, whose household lives on around CHF 900, sends CHF 120. This leaves a monthly gap of CHF 150.

The gap is small, but it exists only because I work every hour I can. My remaining nine semesters include laboratory courses and a bachelor thesis that require time I cannot give while working long shifts. An EduAll grant would allow me to complete my degree on schedule while my family recovers from this crisis.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

I am twenty-nine, I grew up in Thiès, in Senegal, and I study physics because I have always wanted to understand how the sun could be made to work for people.

In Thiès, the electricity cut out almost every evening. I did my homework by the light of a kerosene lamp, and I remember wondering why a country with so much sunshine had so little light. That question still drives me.

I came to Switzerland in 2015, at eighteen, to join my mother, who worked in Zurich as a caregiver. My first years here were devoted to learning German and securing a vocational qualification as a logistics specialist, which allowed me to support myself. For several years I worked in warehouses in Zurich, often in early shifts, while preparing for the university entrance examination in the evenings.

In 2025 I began my physics studies at the University of Zurich. Returning to mathematics after years in logistics was demanding, but I have completed nine courses, and this year I was able to join a research seminar on photovoltaic materials.

The past months have tested me. My father's stroke brought the distance between Zurich and Senegal painfully close. Yet I kept up with my courses, and my determination to finish has only grown.

My aim is to pursue a master's degree in energy science and to work on solar technologies adapted to West African conditions. Education, for me, is the light I did not have in the evenings in Thiès.

For three years I was the elected head of the residents' committee of a large housing complex in Alexandria, with around 200 families, and I managed the budget for maintenance and repairs. So I know how to plan money, and I want to explain my budget openly.

I am from Alexandria. I studied English literature there, and after that I stayed at home for many years to care for my parents, who were both ill. In our housing complex I was elected head of the residents' committee. We repaired the water tanks, organised the lifts, and argued with the building company. I discovered that I like organising, numbers, and to make decisions.

In 2020 we came to Switzerland, because my husband's family is in Basel. I decided to study economics, something completely new. I was 35.

The biggest problem was the language. I learned German for two years before university, but the lectures are fast, and the exams are with many texts. Sometimes I understood the economics but I could not write it correct in the time. My grades show this.

Still, I am proud. I am in the fifth semester, I passed 14 courses, and in the student council of the faculty I am the representative of mature students. We organised a quiet study room and a mentoring evening for older students.

After my degree I want to work in the finance of a non-profit organisation.

For me education means that it is never too late, even when it is difficult.

Pontianak sits exactly on the equator, on the banks of the Kapuas, the longest river in Indonesia. I grew up in a stilt house on its bank, where the river rose into our kitchen every rainy season and the smoke of burning peatland turned the sky orange every dry one. Children in my neighbourhood coughed for months. Nobody told us why.

My parents sold dried fish and had little schooling. I was the first in my family to finish secondary school, but university was out of reach. For twenty years I cared for my parents and younger siblings, and later for my father through a long illness. During those years I spent my free time in the forests along the river with a local conservation group, replanting mangroves and helping biologists count orangutan nests. They lent me their field guides, and I read every one.

After my father's death, I came to Switzerland in 2023 to join my partner. Learning French at forty was humbling, but it opened the door I had been waiting behind for most of my life. In Fribourg I volunteer at the natural history museum's education workshops for children on Saturdays.

I want to study the ecology of tropical peatlands and help restore them. My first semester has shown me how much I still have to learn. It has also shown me that I can.

Education, for me, is permission to ask the question my neighbours never had answered: why the sky turned orange.

My parents never went to secondary school. My father worked in construction in Israel when it was possible, and when it was not possible, he did not work. I am the first of seven children to go to university.

The language is still my biggest problem. I understand the content, but writing an exam of two hours in German is very difficult. I am improving. My last two exams were my best.

I want to work in water and sanitation programmes, maybe with an international organisation, maybe one day in the camps where I grew up.

Nobody knows what happened to him. I sat in the reading room and I felt that history is not about kings, it is about people like him, and like me.

I am from Chittagong, the big port city of Bangladesh. My father is a dock worker and my mother sells vegetables. Nobody in my family went to university. My grandmother told me stories about the partition and the war of 1971, and I always wanted to know if they were true.

I came to Neuchâtel in 2023 with a scholarship, and started the bachelor in 2025 after one year of French. I passed 19 courses. French is now my language for history.

Since 2024 I have volunteered with a reading club for migrant children at the city library, and I help at the Bangladeshi community association with translation and events. At the museum I work as a guide, and I like best the school visits.

My thesis is about South Asian workers in Swiss watch industry before 1914. I want to continue with a master in migration history.

For me education means to find the people history forgot, and to give them their names back.

I am in the second year of my Master of Law at the University of St. Gallen, which I expect to complete in July 2028.

My monthly expenses are CHF 2,455. The largest items are rent (CHF 1,025 for a small flat I share with my two children), health insurance (CHF 220) and food (CHF 390), followed by fees of CHF 522, utilities, transport, phone and study materials. I have deliberately kept a reserve to cover the first months after graduation, while I sit the bar-equivalent examinations and look for a traineeship, because my children depend entirely on me.

I have not been able to take paid work during my master's. My children are eleven and fourteen, and as a single parent I am responsible for them every afternoon and evening. My final semester involves a thesis and a moot court competition, which will take all remaining hours.

An EduAll grant would allow me to finish my degree without spending the reserve that must carry our family through the transition into work.

I am forty-five, a parent of two, and a student of law, in that order of seniority and not always in that order of priority.

I grew up in a village in Maharashtra, where my father was a farm labourer and my mother a domestic worker. I was the first in my family to finish school, and in my late twenties I completed a law degree in Pune by distance learning. I never practised. Instead, I found my way into law through my community: I led a women's self-help federation of more than forty groups, which negotiated microcredit terms with banks and helped members claim land titles in their own names. There, I learned that the law is only as strong as the people who know how to use it.

In 2019 my family moved to Switzerland for my then-spouse's work. After our separation, I decided to turn my experience into formal qualifications, and I was admitted to the master's programme in St. Gallen in 2024. The first year was difficult, balancing new legal traditions, a new language and two children adjusting to a new school. My results are solid rather than outstanding, but I have completed five courses and have never missed an exam.

I also co-ordinate a legal information circle for migrant women in St. Gallen, where we explain rights around residence, divorce and custody.

I intend to specialise in family and migration law and to practise with a legal aid organisation. For me, education is the difference between knowing you have rights and being able to use them.

Nobody in my family went to university. When I was twelve, my parents went to work in Italy and I stayed with my grandmother. We spoke on the phone on Sundays.

At fifteen I found an old computer at the town library and taught myself to program from online tutorials. I won a regional informatics competition, and a teacher helped me apply for a scholarship to a high school in Iași.

In 2016 I came to Switzerland, to Neuchâtel, where my aunt lived. I finished my school here, which was hard in French, and did my bachelor in computer science. In 2026 I started the master.

I should say at the outset that my current budget is balanced, and that my family is in a stronger financial position than many applicants'.

I study part-time and earn CHF 1,325 a month as a laboratory assistant in a plant pathology group, about 12 hours a week. My parents, who run a dental practice in Timișoara together with my aunt, have a combined income of around CHF 4,100 a month, and they contribute CHF 1,130 towards my costs. In June 2023, on a field course above Gruyères, our lecturer stopped the group in a meadow and asked us to count the species in a one-metre square. I found forty-one. I had grown up in a city where the only green was the park by our block, and I remember kneeling there, astonished, realising that I wanted to spend my life studying exactly this: how such diversity survives, and how quickly it can be lost.

I came to Switzerland at eighteen, in 2017, to study in French, a language I had learned at a bilingual school in Timișoara. My first attempt, in medicine, lasted a year before I admitted it was my parents' dream rather than mine. Changing to biology in 2022 was the best decision I have made.

Alongside my studies, I work in a plant pathology laboratory, preparing samples and maintaining greenhouse cultures. Since 2023 I have volunteered with a regional nature conservation association, monitoring orchid populations in dry meadows, and I help coordinate a community seed library in Fribourg where residents exchange local and heirloom varieties.

I have completed twenty-one courses and will write my bachelor thesis on the effects of drought on meadow plant communities.

For me, education is the discipline of looking closely at what others walk past.

I started my Master in History at the University of Neuchâtel in February 2026, part-time.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,368. The biggest items are rent (CHF 1,046), health insurance (CHF 415, because I had to change to a plan with low deductible after my operation last year) and food (CHF 391). The rest is fees, utilities, transport, phone and books.

I grew up in Villa El Salvador, a district on the sand south of Lima. It was built by families who came from the mountains in the 1970s, my grandparents among them. When I was a child there were still streets without water pipes, and the community organised everything itself: kitchens, schools, even a newspaper. I think this is why I love history. My neighbourhood made its own.

My parents sell shoes at a market stall. Nobody in my family went to university. In 2014, when I was fifteen, my mother came to work in Switzerland as a cleaner, and one year later I joined her in Neuchâtel. I did not speak French. School was very hard, and my mother had to go back to Peru after two years for health reasons. I stayed with a host family, finished my apprenticeship as a bookseller, and worked full-time in a bookshop for six years, the last three as deputy branch manager.

I did my bachelor in history part-time while working, and started the master this year. Academic French is still difficult for me. I write slowly and I need my texts checked. My first semester results were average, and I know I need to improve.

I volunteer at a homework club for Latin American children, and I co-founded a small association of Peruvian families in Neuchâtel that organises cultural events and helps newcomers.

For me education is a way to write down the history of people like my grandparents, who built a city from sand and are in no book.

I started my Master in History at the University of Neuchâtel in February 2026, part-time.

From September 2027 I want to study full-time, so that I finish in January 2029 instead of January 2030. I will keep only Saturdays at the bookshop, about CHF 1,010, and CHF 758 will be missing every month.

I want to be honest that I have savings of CHF 14,789. I saved this money over six years of full-time work before the master. STU000486.personal_statement:
I grew up in Villa El Salvador, a district on the sand south of Lima. It was built by families who came from the mountains in the 1970s, my grandparents among them. When I was a child there were still streets without water pipes, and the community organised everything itself: kitchens, schools, even a newspaper. I think this is why I love history. My neighbourhood made its own.

My parents sell shoes at a market stall. Nobody in my family went to university. In 2014, when I was fifteen, my mother came to work in Switzerland as a cleaner, and one year later I joined her in Neuchâtel. I did not speak French. School was very hard, and my mother had to go back to Peru after two years for health reasons. I stayed with a host family, finished my apprenticeship as a bookseller, and worked full-time in a bookshop for six years, the last three as deputy branch manager.

I did my bachelor in history part-time while working, and started the master this year. Academic French is still difficult for me. I write slowly and I need my texts checked. My first semester results were average, and I know I need to improve.

I volunteer at a homework club for Latin American children, and I co-founded a small association of Peruvian families in Neuchâtel that organises cultural events and helps newcomers.

For me education is a way to write down the history of people like my grandparents, who built a city from sand and are in no book.

I am in the second year of my Bachelor's in Chemistry at the University of Basel, which I study part-time and expect to complete in January 2031.

My monthly expenses are CHF 2,091. Rent for a room in a shared flat is CHF 1,032, food CHF 380 and university fees CHF 142, with the remainder covering health insurance, transport, phone, laboratory materials and other essentials.

Until this year, my uncle in Basel helped me with housing, but his family moved to a smaller flat, and I had to find my own room. I therefore reduced my course load and took a job as a sales assistant in a pharmacy, about 20 hours a week, where I earn CHF 2,222. My parents in Peshawar send CHF 102 a month from a household income of about CHF 420; since my father's accident this spring, even this has become uncertain.

From September 2027 the chemistry curriculum has laboratory courses almost every afternoon, and I will have to reduce my hours to about CHF 1,680, leaving CHF 291 a month uncovered. An EduAll grant would allow me to keep my attention on my studies, where my results so far have shown what I can achieve.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

Peshawar is a city of bazaars and dust, of spice markets and brick kilns on the outskirts where entire families work from dawn. My father ran a small stall selling cooking oil in the Qissa Khwani bazaar, and my mother never learned to read. When I was a child, I used to watch the oil turn cloudy in the winter cold and ask my father why. He did not know. I have been asking questions like that ever since.

Neither of my parents went beyond primary school. When I was fifteen, it became clear that I could not continue my education safely at home, and my family sent me to live with my uncle in Basel. I have been here under provisional admission since then: my asylum application was rejected, but as a minor I could not be sent back without anyone to receive me safely. I arrived knowing a little English and no German at all.

Within three years I had learned enough German to pass the university entrance examination, and I began my chemistry studies in the autumn of 2025, aged eighteen. In my first year I completed all eight courses, with results among the best in my cohort. Scientific German is still a daily effort, but I have found that the language of chemistry, formulas and structures, is the same everywhere.

This spring my father was badly injured in a traffic accident and can no longer work at the stall. From a distance, I have helped my family arrange his care, while continuing my studies without interruption.

On Saturdays, I volunteer as a tutor for younger newcomers learning German and mathematics at a youth centre.

I hope to pursue research in green chemistry, perhaps on cleaner processes for small industries like the brick kilns of my childhood. Education, for me, is where every question I asked at my father's stall finally gets an answer.

I will be as open as I can about my finances, because I think you can only help if you see the whole picture.

I am in the first year of my Master's in Education at the University of Bern, and I finish in July 2028. Each month I need CHF 2,466. I have not worked during my master, and I want to be honest about why. The first year after my mother's death I could barely manage my courses. My grades from that time are weak, a GPA of 2.78, and I needed all my strength just to stay enrolled. Now I am stronger, and I am ready to finish.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

When I was seven, my mother took me to her classroom on a Saturday. She taught at a primary school in Ibadan, and she needed to mark exercise books. I sat at a desk in the empty room and wrote my name on the blackboard, again and again, in large careful letters. She came and stood behind me, and she said, "One day you will stand here for real." I have never forgotten her voice.

My mother died of a stroke in 2024, suddenly, at fifty-one, in my first months in Bern. I flew home for the funeral, and when I came back I did not know if I could continue. The winter was very dark. I did not tell anyone at the university. I went to lectures and could not remember a word afterwards. What kept me going was the thought of her standing behind me at the blackboard.

Slowly, with the help of a counsellor at the university and a few kind classmates, I found my way back. This year I have passed every course, and I have started my master's thesis on how primary teachers in Nigeria and Switzerland support grieving children in their classes. I chose this topic because nobody knew how to support me, and I think teachers should.

I want to become a teacher trainer. Education, for me, is my mother's classroom. I want to stand in it for real.

After school I trained as a construction technician and worked for six years, first on building sites in Sofia and later in Switzerland, as a site foreman for a construction company in the Vaud region. I also help organise a monthly repair workshop for the neighbourhood in Renens, and I give free advice on small renovation projects to families who cannot pay an architect.

After two years I was responsible for a shift of twenty miners. I saw accidents that should never happen: tunnels without supports, mercury in the rivers. I wanted to understand the rocks we were digging in, and to make mining safer.

In 2017 I came to Switzerland through my uncle. I worked in construction and learned German. It took me three years to pass the university entrance exam. My German is good in daily life, but scientific German is still difficult, and my written exams take me longer than my classmates. My grades are average, but I have not failed a semester.

In 2024 I started geology in Bern. In the field courses in the Alps, I am the one who knows how to move safely on unstable ground.

I want to work in mining safety and environmental geology, and one day in East Africa, where artisanal mining employs millions of people without protection.

My income is low at the moment. I work a few hours a week as a sample preparation assistant in the geology institute and earn CHF 319. My mother in Kisumu sends CHF 180 when she can, from a household income of about CHF 650. That leaves a gap of CHF 1,346 each month.

I have savings of CHF 14,667, and I want to be honest about them. I saved this money over seven years of work, first in a gold mine in western Kenya and later in construction in Switzerland. Since starting university I have been using it for my gap, and it is what is left. I plan to use it for the master in geology, which I want to start in September 2028 and which will take two more years. If I use it now for my last semesters, I will start the master with almost nothing.

I understand that my savings mean I am not in the most urgent situation. But support for these semesters would let me continue into the master with some security.
STU000492.personal_statement:
I am 29 years old, from Kisumu, on Lake Victoria in Kenya. I study geology.

My mother sells fish at the lake shore and my father, who died when I was twelve, was a fisherman. Nobody in my family went to university. After secondary school I went to work in a small-scale gold mine near Migori, because that was the work that paid. I started as a digger. After two years I was responsible for a shift of twenty miners. I saw accidents that should never happen: tunnels without supports, mercury in the rivers. I wanted to understand the rocks we were digging in, and to make mining safer.

In 2017 I came to Switzerland through my uncle. I worked in construction and learned German. It took me three years to pass the university entrance exam. My German is good in daily life, but scientific German is still difficult, and my written exams take me longer than my classmates. My grades are average, but I have not failed a semester.

In 2024 I started geology in Bern. In the field courses in the Alps, I am the one who knows how to move safely on unstable ground.

I want to work in mining safety and environmental geology, and one day in East Africa, where artisanal mining employs millions of people without protection.

Education for me means that the next boy who goes to work in a mine at nineteen goes into a safe one.

In November 2022, I woke up in the Inselspital in Bern, and the doctor told me that I might not walk properly again. A shelf had collapsed on me at the warehouse where I worked. I was twenty-four. I lay there for weeks and I thought: if I cannot work with my body, I must work with my head.

I grew up in Aleppo. My father was an electrical engineer and my mother a teacher. I had just finished school and wanted to study mechanical engineering at the University of Aleppo, but the war made it impossible. I came to Switzerland in 2016, and I have lived here with provisional admission since then. My asylum application was rejected, but a return to Syria is not possible. I learned German, and for five years I worked in warehouses and on delivery vans.

After the accident, I had two operations and a year of rehabilitation. I walk with a stick now, and I have chronic pain in my back and my left leg. Long periods of sitting are difficult, so in lectures I stand at the back sometimes. But in 2025 I finally started my engineering studies, in German. I have passed nine courses so far, and I am proud of that.

On Sundays I volunteer with a group that helps young Syrians in Bern with their German and maths homework. I tell them my story, so they know it is never too late.

I want to become an engineer who designs safer workplaces, so that what happened to me happens to fewer people.

I am in the second year of my Bachelor's in Physics at the University of Zurich, which I study part-time and expect to complete in July 2030.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,949: rent of CHF 836 for a room in a shared flat, food at CHF 414, health insurance at CHF 240 and university fees at CHF 203, with the remainder for transport, phone and books. I earn CHF 2,222 a month as a receptionist at a community health centre, about 20 hours a week, and my younger brother in Abuja sends CHF 100 from a household income of about CHF 660.

In the interest of full transparency, I have savings of CHF 8,743, built up over nineteen years of work as a laboratory technician and later as a care worker in Zurich. My grandmother could not read, but she could predict the rain. She would stand in the yard of our compound in Jos, study the sky and the shape of the clouds over the plateau, and tell us to bring in the washing an hour before the first drop fell. As a child, I thought it was magic. Later I understood it was observation, patient and precise, and I think that is where my love of physics began.

Neither of my parents finished secondary school. My father was a tin miner and my mother traded cloth. I completed a diploma in science laboratory technology and worked for eight years in a university laboratory in Jos, preparing experiments for physics students I secretly envied. In 2011, after violence in our city destroyed our neighbourhood, I came to Switzerland to join my husband. We separated a few years later, and I rebuilt my life alone, learning German and working as a care worker.

For six years I served as chair of an association of African women in Zurich, organising language courses, legal information evenings and a mentoring programme for young women considering vocational training or university. Encouraging others eventually gave me the courage to follow my own advice.

At forty-two I passed the university entrance examination and began physics in February 2025. I have completed seven courses with a GPA of 3.54, results I did not dare to hope for.

I hope to work in atmospheric physics, on weather prediction for regions where farmers still rely on grandmothers who read the sky. Education, for me, is my grandmother's gift, made precise.

My grandmother could not read, but she could predict the rain. She would stand in the yard of our compound in Jos, study the sky and the shape of the clouds over the plateau, and tell us to bring in the washing an hour before the first drop fell. As a child, I thought it was magic. Later I understood it was observation, patient and precise, and I think that is where my love of physics began.

Neither of my parents finished secondary school. My father was a tin miner and my mother traded cloth. I completed a diploma in science laboratory technology and worked for eight years in a university laboratory in Jos, preparing experiments for physics students I secretly envied. In 2011, after violence in our city destroyed our neighbourhood, I came to Switzerland to join my husband. We separated a few years later, and I rebuilt my life alone, learning German and working as a care worker.

For six years I served as chair of an association of African women in Zurich, organising language courses, legal information evenings and a mentoring programme for young women considering vocational training or university. Encouraging others eventually gave me the courage to follow my own advice.

At forty-two I passed the university entrance examination and began physics in February 2025. I have completed seven courses with a GPA of 3.54, results I did not dare to hope for.

I hope to work in atmospheric physics, on weather prediction for regions where farmers still rely on grandmothers who read the sky. Education, for me, is my grandmother's gift, made precise.

I am in the second year of my Bachelor's in Materials Science at EPFL, which I will complete in July 2028.

My monthly expenses are CHF 1,526. Rent is CHF 488 for a small flat in a cooperative in Renens, which I share with my daughter, followed by food at CHF 299, health insurance at CHF 295 and EPFL fees at CHF 243. The remainder covers transport, phone and study materials.

My income comes from three sources. I work as a part-time cleaner in offices in the early mornings and earn CHF 822. My mother in Faisalabad sends CHF 150 a month from a household income of about CHF 590. I also receive a scholarship of CHF 6,057 a year from a charitable foundation in Lausanne. Before this scholarship, my monthly shortfall is CHF 554.

My residence permit had to be renewed this summer, now as a student permit, and the renewal is pending. I understand that it can only be approved if I show resources of around CHF 2,600 a month. An EduAll grant would therefore not only close my monthly gap, but also strengthen my permit application, and with it the stability of my daughter's life in Switzerland.

In my last semester I will write my bachelor project in a polymer laboratory. The support would allow me to reduce my cleaning hours and give the project the time it requires.

---

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

My daughter is nine, and she wants to be an astronaut. When she was six, she asked me why I go to university when other mothers go only to work. I told her: because one day I want to make materials for rockets. She has held me to that promise ever since.

I grew up in Faisalabad, the textile city of Pakistan. My father worked a loom in a mill and my mother embroidered at home. Neither completed school. I was married at nineteen and had no chance to study. When my marriage ended, I came to Switzerland in 2019 with my daughter, to live near my cousin, and I began from nothing: no French, no qualifications recognised, no income.

For the first three years I cleaned offices and hotel rooms and studied French in the evenings, with my daughter doing her homework beside me. In 2025 I passed the entrance examination for EPFL. I remember reading the result on my phone in a hotel corridor, holding a bucket, and crying.

The past year and a half has been demanding. I study at night, after my daughter is asleep, and I have completed twelve courses while working and raising her alone. I have learned to use every hour well.

My goal is to work on sustainable textile materials, fibres that do not pollute rivers the way the mills of my childhood did. For me, education is the promise I made to my daughter, and I intend to keep it.

I started the Bachelor in Physics at the University of Bern in February 2026, part-time.

My monthly costs are CHF 2,134. Rent is CHF 1,061, health insurance CHF 265, food CHF 380, fees CHF 158, and the rest is transport, phone and books. I used to work full-time as an interpreter for Dari and Pashto at the cantonal migration services; now I work about 19 hours a week and earn CHF 2,114. My sister in Hamburg sends CHF 70 from her household income of about CHF 3,000. Today my costs are covered.

From September 2027 I want to study full-time. Part-time, my bachelor would last until July 2031; full-time, it ends in January 2030. At forty-three, this difference matters. I will keep only occasional assignments, about CHF 230, and CHF 1,834 will be missing every month.

To be honest, I do not have savings, and I have no scholarship yet. The cantonal study grant rejected my application because of my age. My room is also a problem: it is a temporary room through a social housing association, and I must leave it at the end of the year.

A grant from EduAll would make the full-time year possible and let me look for a stable room without panic.

## Section 5 — Personal Statement

*Instructions: Tell us who you are and where you come from, describe your educational goals and aspirations, share any personal challenges or circumstances you wish to (optional), and explain what education means to you (max. 500 words).*

The first time I saw the night sky in the Swiss mountains, on a trip with my German class near Grindelwald in 2014, I stood in the snow for an hour. In Kabul I had loved the stars, but the city lights and the dust hid most of them. Here I could see the Milky Way. I decided then that one day I would study physics, even if it took me many years. It took me twelve.

I grew up in Kabul. My father was a driver and my mother did not go to school. I finished school in 2001, but in those years there was no possibility for me to go to university. I worked as an interpreter for international organisations for ten years, and I led a small team of translators for a health programme.

In 2013 I had to leave Afghanistan because of threats connected to my work. I applied for asylum in Switzerland and was recognised as a refugee. The first years I lived in asylum centres and then in shared rooms, and I moved seven times. I still do not have a stable home.

I learned German and worked as an interpreter again, for the migration services and hospitals. For eight years I also volunteered as a mentor for newly arrived refugees, and I helped to build an interpreters' network in Bern.

At forty-two I passed the university entrance exam. Now I sit in lectures with students who are twenty. Sometimes it is hard, but I am happy.

For me education is finally the chance to look at the stars not only with wonder, but with understanding.
